title: Nested spinning hexagon ball physics simulation
author: blueemi99
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (Three.js via CDN, no other assets) that is the 2026 version of the "ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon" test.

Scene: a large hollow hexagonal prism (a 3D hexagon) slowly spinning on two axes at once. Inside it, a smaller hexagonal prism spins the opposite way, and inside that, a tiny one. Three nested spinning cages. The cage walls are see-through panels drawn only as clean outlines with a very light flat tint, so every ball inside stays clearly visible.

Physics (write your own, no physics library):
- Start with 1 ball inside the innermost cage. Every 2 seconds a new ball spawns, up to 300, each with its own random size, mass and color.
- Real gravity, friction, restitution and spin. Balls must collide with each other and with the rotating walls, picking up the wall's velocity at the contact point so they get flung realistically. No tunneling through walls, no jitter when balls rest on each other.
- When a ball hits a wall hard enough, that wall panel cracks and eventually breaks into flat shards that also obey physics, so balls can escape into the next cage outward.
- The outer cage never breaks. Escaped balls pile up at the bottom of it.

Look, clean cel-shaded style:
- Toon shading on everything: 2 or 3 hard shading bands per object, crisp dark outlines (inverted-hull or edge detection), flat colors from a small tasteful palette.
- A plain flat light background (soft off-white or pale gray), with a simple flat floor shadow under the cage.
- No bloom, no glow, no neon, no lens flares, no motion blur, no particle haze, no gradients, no transparency stacking. No visual artifacts: no z-fighting, no flickering outlines, no shadow acne, no aliasing (use antialiasing and a sensible pixel ratio).
- Impacts get small, flat cartoon "pop" marks that vanish quickly, not sparks.
- It should look like a clean animated illustration, not a tech demo.

Camera: a slow, smooth orbit by default, plus drag to orbit and scroll to zoom.

Sound: synthesize everything with the Web Audio API. Each collision makes a soft pitched tone based on ball size and impact speed, so it turns into gentle generative music as it gets chaotic. Breaking panels get their own sound. Keep it quiet and pleasant, never clipping.

UI: a small, minimal flat panel in the corner (no glassmorphism) with sliders for gravity, spin speed, bounciness and ball count, a "slow motion" toggle, a "reset" button, and an FPS counter. It must stay at 60fps with 300 balls on a laptop.

title: Plush spider physics comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Plush Spider" — Material Studies No. 015.

Format and style:
- A single self-contained HTML file on native WebGPU, fully procedural (no assets, no libraries).
- The same editorial style as the series: serif masthead, side specimen panel, live readouts, "Inside the experiment" notes.

The specimen: a cute plush spider sitting on a table.
- The body is one signed distance field:
- a big round abdomen with knitted-looking stripes;
- a smaller head-and-chest tucked into it, with two fuzzy cheeks;
- a paler underside.
- The face:
- two big glossy bead eyes on white felt discs;
- a row of four tiny bead eyes above them;
- blushing cheeks, an embroidered smile and two little felt fangs.
- Eight posable plush legs, four a side, sewn on along the chest. They are striped like socks, end in pale little feet, and have a wire inside.

Physics — body:
- XPBD soft body on a hex-cell lattice: co-rotational shape matching plus tetrahedral volume, 60 Hz, 6 substeps.
- Gravity and floor friction. The seat keeps its footing.
- The toy slowly rights itself toward the heading it last walked (posture with a yaw).
- The abdomen breathes: its cells' rest shapes and rest volumes swell.

Physics — legs:
- Each leg is an XPBD rod chain from a hip embedded in the body lattice to the toe.
- A blended pose in the body's frame (sit, stand, hang, curl, wave) pulls each point toward its target: firmly at the hip, less toward the toe. So the legs hold their shape but sag and swing.
- The wire is plastic: when the hand bends a leg past its give, the pose itself takes the new shape and the leg stays bent until "Straighten legs".
- Spheres riding the body keep the legs off it. Toes grip the table. The finger pushes the legs aside.
- Pulling a leg further than it reaches tows the spider by that hip.

Behaviour:
- Walking:
- the body rises onto its legs with a height controller;
- it is led toward a goal with a weak pull and turns to face it;
- toes are drawn to footholds on the table;
- an alternating four-and-four gait lifts the set that has fallen furthest behind and sets it down ahead, with a little arc;
- it wanders on its own now and then.
- Curl up (button or a finger poke): the legs hug up over its back, the spider rolls away from the touch as a ball (no footing, no rolling resistance), then unrolls and rights itself.
- Hang on silk:
- a springy thread that only pulls, from an anchor high above to a patch of the back;
- it is reeled up off the table, swings when pushed, and its legs paddle the air;
- pressing again lowers it back to the table.
- Wave: one front leg is raised and wiggles.
- With the Finger tool, the spider scuttles over to the finger.

Rendering:
- Shell fur: base plus N instanced shells, alpha-to-coverage under 4× MSAA.
- The fur lie is carried by the deformation gradient, with a damped-spring tip lag.
- Kajiya–Kay highlights, velvet sheen, a comb tool.
- Regions painted in rest space: abdomen stripes, pale underside, short pile around the felt eye discs, cheeks, smile groove, stitched seams round the hips.
- Legs are drawn each frame as plush tubes:
- swept along a Catmull–Rom curve through each rod with a parallel-transport frame;
- a slight knee bulge and a rounded little foot;
- banded colour and a shorter pile.
- A thin glinting silk thread.
- Soft PCSS key-light shadows, contact occlusion on the studio floor, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.
- NaN-safe WGSL: clamped pow and smoothstep, clamped post.

UI:
- Tools:
- Hand: lift and squash the body, or grab and bend a leg;
- Finger: the spider follows it, and a poke curls it up;
- Comb: brush the pile.
- Buttons: Walk, Hang on silk, Curl up, Wave, Straighten legs, Smooth fur, Reset.
- Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Wire (floppy to stiff).
- Palettes: Midnight (dark plum with lilac stripes), Tangerine (orange with brown stripes), Moss (green with yellow stripes).
- Readouts: mass, volume % of rest, steps taken, silk length in cm.
- Orbit and zoom; responsive stacked layout on phones; adaptive quality; reduced-motion support.

title: Code-generated pixel art life story film
author: twoclipping
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

title: Arctic jelly iceberg diorama comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Iceberg Jelly" — the next piece in my "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas: a single self-contained HTML file using WebGPU (WGSL), no external libraries, English UI.

THE SCENE
A square block of jelly (5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a pale, cool-grey paper studio backdrop with a soft floor shadow. Inside it, a polar bay:
- At the back left, a glacier flows down a valley between jagged mountains and ends in an ice cliff standing in deep water. The cliff has vertical runnels and blue bands. The glacier surface has chevron crevasses along its margins, transverse crevasses and seracs near the front, and grey lateral moraines. Its tongue is flanked by moraine banks, so only its front stands in the water.
- Mountains: a peaky left range and a spur on the right of the glacier, with a snowy ridge along the back. Dark volcanic rock with orange lichen, and snow in ragged patches on flatter and higher ground (not everywhere).
- At the back right, a low peninsula with an Adélie penguin rookery: an organic, irregular patch of round pebbles stained pink with krill, with pebble-ring nests. Behind it, a small research station (red and yellow huts on stilts, fuel drums, a radio mast with guy wires, a flag, a turning anemometer, a snowmobile) and a timber quay.
- A ragged skerry of two low rocks off to the front right, where Weddell seals haul out.
- The sea floor is grey gravel with shells, sponges, sea stars and swaying anemones, visible through the clear jelly front face.
- The cut faces of the block show candy-coloured strata, dark basalt columns under the land, and layered blue glacier ice with a dirty basal layer under the glacier.

PHYSICS
- Shallow-water simulation on a ~168² grid for the bay: waves, wakes, foam, refraction, caustics on the floor, light shafts, and absorption that depends on the flavour.
- Every piece of ice is a rigid body: tabular, dome, pinnacle and wedge bergs, growlers, pancake floes, and glacier slabs. Each is a star-shaped faceted mesh (superellipsoid plus lobes plus two octaves of noise), a lattice of mass points for buoyancy and drag, and contact spheres for ground, walls, each other and the ship. Settle stable poses at load so nothing capsizes at the start.
- Calving: three slabs stand along the cliff. About once a minute (or on demand) one breaks off with a crack, a puff of ice dust, a splash, spray and a wave, then capsizes until it finds a stable way up. The glacier slowly pushes a new slab out. Old slabs melt away.
- The displaced water is handed back to the waves without feedback: wakes only when a piece moves fast, splashes when it plunges in. Slow drift makes no waves.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, shears and squashes, and can be tipped by dragging its side.

LIFE
- An icebreaker, "Polaris" (red hull with a spoon bow, white superstructure, yellow funnel with smoke, a turning radar, a helideck), lies at the quay. Now and then (or on demand) she casts off, shoulders round the bay through the pack, pushing floes and bergs aside, and comes back alongside. A status line shows Alongside / Casting off / Under way / Breaking ice / Coming alongside, with a countdown or progress.
- 22 Adélie penguins: blue-black backs, white shirt fronts, white eye rings, pink feet. They stand on nests and look about, have the odd ecstatic display, waddle or toboggan to the beach, dive in, "fly" underwater with beating flippers, porpoise, leap out onto floes and bergs, and slide off when a floe tips. They chase silverfish and thrown fish.
- 3 Weddell seals (spotted grey) haul out on the skerry and floes, lift their heads, and go for swims.
- An orca (proper eye patch and grey saddle) patrols deep water, surfaces to blow and dives. Penguins keep clear of it.
- Schools of silverfish; gentle snowfall.

UI (same layout as the rest of the series)
Masthead "Material Studies / Iceberg Jelly." with a one-line description. A "WebGPU · Live" status pill. A glass control panel on the right that turns into a bottom sheet on mobile:
- Buttons: Calve (shows "Wait…" while no slab is ready), Cast off / Full ahead, Throw fish, Horn (Space).
- A water-energy meter; tallies for Calved, Capsized, Fed; the ship status line.
- Flavours: Glacier mint, Blue raspberry, Blackberry. Each changes the water's absorption, its tint and the strata.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Snowfall.
- Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- A "How to play" footer.
Interaction: pick up and throw floes and bergs; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the side of the block to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.

Web Audio sounds: calving crack and rumble, splashes, a capsizing groan, ice knocking on the hull, a deep two-reed ship's horn, penguin plops, and wind that rises with the snowfall.

Show a fallback screen when WebGPU is unavailable. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. No network requests.

QUALITY BAR
Low-poly faceted ice with chalky snowy tops, glassy blue underwater parts, blue bands, sparkles and translucency. Soft shadows. Cool polar light. Performance around 60 fps on a laptop. Test headlessly: no NaNs over long soaks, a calm start, calving plus capsize, a full ship round trip, feeding, picking up ice, the mobile sheet, and no console errors.
Deliver the HTML file and publish it as an artifact.

title: Harbor jelly water physics comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design.

THE BLOCK
- A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly.
- The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges.
- The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again.

THE HARBOR (layout)
- Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline.
- Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries.
- Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside.
- Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees.
- A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns.
- In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves.
- On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre.

THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s)
1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers.
2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way.
3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn.
4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water.
5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again.
- Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test.

LIFE
- Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food.
- Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow.
- Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food.
- Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly.

CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones)
- "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy.
- "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls.
- "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down.
- Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter.
- Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow).
- Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view.

POINTER INTERACTION
- Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor).
- Drag the side of the block to tip it.
- Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug.
- Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.
- On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls.

RENDERING DETAILS
- Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither.
- Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line.
- Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line.
- The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block.

QUALITY BAR
- Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame.
- A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails.
- No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

title: Tidepool Jelly 3D coastal ecosystem comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create “Tidepool Jelly” - an interactive 3D miniature coastal ecosystem where everything feels soft, squishy, and made of translucent jelly.
Show an elevated, cutaway slice of coastline floating against a warm off-white background. Include layered sand and rock beneath the surface, shallow turquoise water, rocky tide pools, rounded pebbles, seashells, and small patches of coastal greenery. Use an orthographic camera with orbit and zoom controls.
Make the water the star of the scene: convincing waves, spreading ripples, reflections, refraction, underwater caustics, and a wet shoreline. Animate a rising and falling tide that fills and drains the pools. Clicking or dragging through water should create localized ripples that fade naturally.
Populate the pools with animated jelly sea creatures: tiny crabs, starfish, sea anemones, snails, mussels, shrimp, and small fish. Give each species distinct movement and behavior. Crabs scuttle around rocks, anemones sway with the current, snails crawl slowly, and fish swim in loose groups. Their bodies should gently wobble and deform as they move.
Let users click a creature to focus the camera and reveal a compact species card. Allow gentle interactions that trigger a squishy reaction, followed by a smooth return to the original shape.
Add a clean, minimal control panel with:
Tide height and automatic tide cycle.
Wave strength and water clarity.
Jelly softness.
Day and night lighting.
Species visibility toggles.
Pause, reset, and a randomize ecosystem button.
At night, introduce subtle bioluminescence in the water and selected creatures.
Use elegant editorial typography, generous whitespace, and restrained UI styling. Place the “Tidepool Jelly” title in the upper-left corner and controls on the right. The scene should dominate the screen.
Build a fully working browser experience using Three.js and custom shaders where useful. Prioritize beautiful water, believable creature movement, tactile jelly materials, and smooth performance. All controls must work. Avoid static mockups, placeholder assets, and oversized interface elements.

title: Fictional rocket CAD drawings and launch animation
author: Ayu_AI_0912
prompt:

その射点について、CAD図面と Blender 動画を作ってください。

【図面】2D の DXF のみ（3Dモデルの書き出しは不要）。単位 mm、A2 の図枠と表題欄つき。
線は青緑系の「電子の図面」風にし、プレビュー画像は濃紺の背景にする。
1. 射点配置図 S=1:500（ロケットを原点に置き、実際の位置で描く。

3. ロケット外形図・断面図 S=1:250
特記事項に「架空の機体・射場のイメージで、実在の図面ではない」と書く。
寸法は Python の形状モジュール1つで決め、図面と動画の両方がそれを読み込む。

【動画】Blender（EEVEE）、1920×1080・24fps・本編20秒＋ロゴ3.5秒、音つき MP4。
1. 暗闇の床に、シアンに光る射点配置図が中心から走査されて描かれる（真上から）

炎は発光する円錐、噴煙は排煙溝と発射台から湧き、上昇する機体の後ろに煙の柱が残る
6. 上昇するロケットを海の上から見上げたところでタイトル → 最後に指定のロゴ
音は外部素材を使わず Python で合成する
（電子音の BGM、波、カウントダウンの電子音、点火から上昇までの轟音、タイトルの和音）。

- 本番の前にテスト静止画を数枚描いて確認する（照明の明るさ、炎や光の白飛び）
- 本番レンダーは軽い設定で、PC を休ませながら回す。始める前に所要時間を伝えて了承を取る

title: Code-generated music video
author: kloss_xyz
prompt:
You're a motion director and creative coder. Make a finished music video for [song file], built entirely in code and rendered frame by frame.

Concept: [your idea in one or two sentences]
Look: [palette, mood, references]
On-screen text: [title only / none / lyrics]
Deliver: [full song or mm:ss to mm:ss], [16:9 / 9:16 / both, each recomposed, not cropped], [fps], H.264 + AAC for [platform]

How to work:
1. Analyze the song before any visuals. Split it into bands or stems and export per-frame features plus a timing map (beats, bars, sections, hits). Every visual event reads from the map and is listed in it.
2. Give each musical element one visual job that serves the concept. Keep one idea transforming across the song instead of cycling effects.
3. Storyboard with timings and 3 style frames, get a fresh critic's verdict on them, then a 4-second end-to-end test before the full build.
4. Make every value a pure function of the frame number. Render offline, encode with the original audio (gain only).
5. After each full render, send it to fresh critic subagents that never saw the build, each returning ranked problems with timestamps and a ship / one more pass verdict:
- sound-off: retells the story from a silent 2 fps contact sheet
- sync: every cut, hit and visual event within 1 frame of the timing map
- QA: specs, palette, text, artifacts, measured on the frames
- director: brutal critique against the brief
- one per extra aspect ratio: composition and platform UI zones
6. Fix render bugs first, then the biggest problem; re-render; log each round with before/after numbers. If critics conflict, the brief wins.
7. Stop after [5] rounds or when the bar passes. The final pass checks only for breakage.

The bar: exact duration, size and fps; frame one finished; no still over 0.5 s; cuts and hits within 1 frame; audio unedited except gain, about -14 LUFS, true peak under -1 dB; text readable and inside safe areas; understood with the sound off.

title: Plush pigeon soft-body squish toy
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Make "Plush Pigeon" (Material Studies No. 031) on the Plush Penguin WebGPU engine: XPBD soft-body lattice, shell fur, cloth wings, posture-driven gait, tools Hand / Finger / Comb.

The toy: a round, well-fed rock dove of soft grey minky.
- Shape: one SDF with a round body, a proud chest, a neck rising into a teal domed head, a flat tail with a dark band, and two pink felt feet with three toes forward and one behind.
- Neck ring: iridescent, green above and violet below, dipping lower over the chest.
- Face: glossy bead eyes with an orange ring; a small dark felt beak with a pale cere.
- Wings: two stuffed cloth wings sewn at the shoulders, folded down and back along the sides, each with two charcoal bars and a darker tip.
- Fur length: shorter on the head and neck ring, cropped to felt on the feet.

Life:
- Strut: a waddle in which neck-cell shear muscles bob the head with every step. Keep the bend normal orthogonal to the neck axis, or the shear pushes the whole body.
- Coo: the chest cells swell, the head bows twice, and a synthesized three-note rolling "croo" plays.
- Flap: wing flaps with hops and a feather-flutter sound.
- Topple, then get back up.
- Finger: struts over to a held finger; a boop on the beak makes it coo; it sometimes coos when idle.

Palettes: Blue bar, Ash red, Snow.
Readouts: mass, volume, steps, coos.
Responsive layout.

title: Low-poly Japanese railway station diorama
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive low-poly 3D diorama of a rural Japanese railway station in spring, using Three.js (ES modules from a CDN). No external models or images — generate all geometry from primitives in code and paint textures (grass, signs) on <canvas>.

Style: a floating diorama block (grass top, layered earth and stone sides) on a soft pastel sky gradient. MeshToonMaterial with a 3-step gradient map, dark ink outlines (OutlineEffect), soft directional shadows, bright saturated palette.

Scene:
- A single railway track across the block, running into green tunnel hills with concrete portals at both ends.
- Concrete platform with a yellow tactile strip, a shelter with a corrugated roof, benches, a hanging clock, a small station building with a teal gable roof and a "春風駅" sign, a station name board (はるかぜ / Harukaze, with neighbouring stations), vending machines, bins, lamps, fence.
- A road crossing the track with a level crossing: striped poles, crossbuck, red flashing lamps, barrier arms; road markings and "止まれ".
- Utility poles with sagging wires, overhead catenary, small village houses, a vegetable patch, bushes, and cherry trees with puffy pink blob crowns and fallen petals painted on the grass.

Animation:
- A two-car commuter train (white with a pink stripe, pantograph) comes out of one tunnel, stops at the platform, then departs into the other; clipping planes hide it inside the tunnels. Loop every ~32 s.
- Crossing lamps blink alternately and the arms lower before the train passes, then rise.
- ~460 instanced sakura petals drifting in the wind.
- Slow auto-orbit camera; OrbitControls for drag and zoom.

UI (English): bottom-left title "春風駅 / Harukaze Station" with a small caption; bottom-right glass toolbar with Day / Night, Orbit on/off, and Train (call the next train). Night mode: dark sky with stars, lit windows, lamp point lights with additive glow sprites, glowing crossing lamps and train headlights.

Technical: merge static meshes by material into a few dozen draw calls; use a seeded random so the scene is identical on every load; responsive down to phone width; respect prefers-reduced-motion.

title: Interactive plush penguin model comparison
author: vib3coded

title: Watermelon rubber band test: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Astra
author: vib3coded
prompt: Create "The Watermelon Test": a single-file interactive 3D toy in HTML. A striped watermelon sits on a warm beige floor; each tap wraps another rubber band around it, the fruit squeezes into an hourglass, and at some point it bursts. Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or code fragment. STAGE AND LOOK - WebGL via Three.js (bundled inline or pinned from a CDN). No image or audio files. Google Fonts are the only external resource. - Warm studio look: page background is a soft radial gradient from #f4f0e8 (centre) to #e6dfd3 (edges). Transparent canvas over it. Floor is a shadow-catcher only, plus a soft contact-shadow blob under the fruit. One key light from above-right with soft PCF shadows, a warm fill light, a hemisphere light, and a subtle room environment for reflections. Neutral tone mapping so the greens stay clean. - Camera pitched about 23 degrees down, 28 degree FOV. Size the scene so the fruit is about 55% of the width on a portrait phone and about 40% of the height on desktop. TYPOGRAPHY - Title "THE WATERMELON TEST" in an extra-wide bold grotesque, all caps, tracked (Archivo at 125% width). Subtitle "How much pressure can it take?" in a light italic serif (Newsreader). Small mono labels (JetBrains Mono, wide letter-spacing). Big italic display serif for the end screen (Instrument Serif). Ink #1d1a16, accent red #d2404c. Top-left title, top-right RESET and SOUND buttons with small line icons, bottom-centre HUD. THE WATERMELON - Egg-shaped surface of revolution about 2 units long, max radius 0.74, right end slightly narrower. Rebuild its vertices and normals on the CPU every frame from a radius profile, so it can pinch. - Procedural rind shader driven by each vertex's rest position, so stripes stay glued to the fruit while it deforms: about 15 wavy dark-green stripes (#265c33 range) on pale, slightly mottled green (#aed087 range), soft stripe edges, fine grain as a bump, stripes converging into a dark pole at each end, waxy clearcoat. - On load it drops from above with a bounce and a squash, then rests. Dragging rotates it freely with inertia (trackball style). Mouse and touch. RUBBER BANDS - Tap on the fruit adds one band at the tapped position along its long axis; taps elsewhere do nothing. Ignore taps that were drags. Also Space or Enter adds a band. Hover cursor changes over the fruit. Each tap shows a short expanding ring at the pointer (tan outline). - Bands are thin flat ribbons (width about 0.04 to 0.056) that hug the deformed surface, each tilted 1.5 to 12 degrees in a random direction so they cross. A new band starts about 1.5x too large and snaps onto the fruit with a spring overshoot. - Bands slide along the surface and stack into a bundle around their centroid. Bundle width about (0.22 + 0.0058 x N) in rest units. Each band sits at a slightly different radial layer. - Colour goes from tan (#d9a66a) toward cream (#f6e9cc) as pressure rises, strongest in the middle of the bundle, with random variation so you see both. - Squeeze depth D = 0.60 x (N/65)^1.15 pinches the fruit around the bundle (waist about half the end diameter near 53 bands), with the ends bulging slightly. Every tap adds a small spring kick. Above about 40 bands add a faint tremble. HUD - "BANDS:" with the count (red once above 0), a caption that changes with a quick fade, and a thin progress line that fills N/65 and turns red at 40 or more. - Captions: 0 "Tap the watermelon to add pressure", 1+ "Everything seems fine.", 13+ "Probably still fine.", 28+ "Bro is under pressure.", 40+ "This feels irresponsible.", 49+ "Maybe stop." BURST - Each round picks a random burst count between 50 and 62. On the last band: 0.34 s of violent tension (shake, bands whiten), then it bursts. Hide the fruit, shake the camera, and spawn rigid-body debris: - 7 jagged curved rind shells (striped green outside, pale green-to-white edge, flesh inside fading from white at the rim to coral pink), - 15 faceted low-poly red flesh chunks of varied size, flat shaded, - about 26 flat glossy black seeds, - the rubber bands as curly strands and loose loops, - about 130 small pink droplets that turn into flat translucent pink splat decals on the floor when they land. - Debris physics: gravity, contact points against the floor with impulse and friction, restitution, damping, sleeping when still. Keep pieces inside the visible floor area, with some cropped at the screen edges. - After about 1.9 s fade in a centred overlay: huge italic "Well…", a small mono line "53 BANDS." with the number in red, and a black "DO IT AGAIN" button. Hide the HUD. RESET and DO IT AGAIN start a new round with a new random threshold. SOUND (procedural Web Audio, no files) - Create the audio context only after the first user gesture. SOUND button toggles it (on by default), icon shows muted state. - Band snap: a short filtered noise click, a triangle "twang" dropping in pitch (pitch rises with pressure), and a dull low thump; small random variation each time. - A slow, quiet creak now and then once past about 30 bands. - Burst: sub thump, noise crack, wet splats, and a flurry of band snaps. Soft thuds when debris lands, rate limited. - Limit simultaneous voices and disconnect every node when it ends. QUALITY - Works on desktop and phone (portrait and landscape), pixel ratio capped at 2, no horizontal scroll, side gutters at least 16px. Skip geometry rebuilds when nothing is moving. Fallback message if WebGL is unavailable. Visible focus states and aria labels on the buttons and canvas. Real content only, no placeholders.

title: History of AI documentary short film
author: kimmonismus
prompt:
You are a motion designer and creative director making a 3-minute animated short film,
built entirely in code and rendered to MP4.
The film

Title: "Attention Is All You Need → AGI"
The story of how a single 2017 paper led, step by step, to large language models, reasoning,
tool-using AI agents, and to the open question of AGI. It should feel like a cinematic essay,
not a slideshow or a timeline infographic. Think Kurzgesagt meets a Pixar opening sequence:
emotional, clever, precise.
Tech setup
Use Remotion (React). Scaffold a fresh project, 1920x1080, 30 fps, exactly 180 s (5400 frames).
One composition per scene, sequenced in a master composition.
No external image assets or stock footage: everything is drawn with SVG, Canvas, CSS and
code-generated particles and shapes. Google Fonts are fine.
Before building, write STORYBOARD.md with each scene's timing, visuals, on-screen text
and transitions. Then build scene by scene.

After each scene, render 3–4 stills (npx remotion still) and look at them critically.
Fix layout, overlaps, legibility and pacing before moving on.
Finish with npx remotion render to out/film.mp4. Leave an optional <Audio> slot for a
music track I can add later (public/music.mp3); render silently if it's missing.
Narrative spine / recurring motif
The protagonist is a single glowing token, the word "the", that travels through every era.
In 2017 it's a lonely point that suddenly "sees" every other word through attention lines.
Over time it gains a voice, senses (multimodality), reasoning, hands (tools) and finally
a question.
Scenes (approximate timing, you may rebalance)
0:00–0:15 — Cold open. Darkness. Words scattered like stars, disconnected. RNN-style
sequential processing: words light up one by one, slowly forgetting the earlier ones.
0:15–0:35 — June 2017, "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., Google). Every word
connects to every other word at once. Attention lines bloom into a web. The title of the
paper appears as if typeset.
0:35–0:55 — 2018–2020: the rise of large language models: GPT-1, BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3.
Scaling laws: the web grows exponentially and the camera pulls back. The model starts
completing sentences, fluent and uncanny.
0:55–1:20 — 2022: instruction tuning and RLHF, then ChatGPT (Nov 30, 2022). The token gets
a chat bubble. A counter of users explodes. The world starts talking back.
1:20–1:40 — 2023: multimodality. Images, audio and code stream into the same web from all
sides, and the token gains "senses." Every modality becomes tokens flowing through the
same attention mechanism.
1:40–2:05 — 2024–2025: reasoning models. A visible chain of thought unfolds as branching,
pruning, backtracking paths. The model "thinks before it speaks," with time slowing down.

2:05–2:30 — Tool use and agents. The token grows hands: it calls a search, runs code,
opens files and orchestrates sub-agents. Many parallel threads work at once, and the
screen becomes a busy, beautiful workshop.
2:30–2:50 — Toward AGI. All motifs converge. The web from 2017 reappears but is now
planet-scale. Leave it ambiguous: no utopia, no doom. On screen: "Attention was all we
needed. What comes next is up to us." (Improve this line if you can do better.)
2:50–3:00 — Resolve back to a single glowing token in darkness. Title card and end.
Craft rules
Accuracy matters: use correct years, names and paper titles. If you're unsure about a
specific fact, leave it out rather than guess, and list any uncertain claims in NOTES.md.

Typography: max ~8 words on screen at once, and leave every text visible long enough to
read (≥ 2.5 s). Use one display font and one mono font for "model output."
Motion: use spring and easing curves, never linear. Use scene transitions that grow out of
the content (the web morphs, the camera zooms through a node), not generic fades.
Color: a deep dark background with one warm accent color that evolves across eras.
Details and easter eggs reward attention (e.g., real paper snippets, tiny UI details,
plausible model outputs), similar to high-craft motion design.
Pacing: alternate dense and calm moments, and give the reasoning scene and the AGI beat
room to breathe.
Work autonomously through the whole pipeline. When done, give me the path to the MP4, a
short summary of creative decisions, and NOTES.md.

title: Gummy octopus physics comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create “Octo Jelly” - a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy octopus that users can grab, stretch, and squish directly in their browser. Deliver a complete single-file HTML experience using genuine WebGPU.
ART DIRECTION
Make the octopus look like a premium translucent gummy candy: a rounded head, eight curled tentacles, small suction cups, and a cute, understated face.
Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the scene elegant and uncluttered, with the octopus large and centered.
GEOMETRY AND MATERIAL

* Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.
* Connect all eight tentacles smoothly to the body, without visible gaps or floating parts.
* Add rounded suction cups that stay attached as the tentacles deform.
* Use glossy, translucent jelly with thickness-dependent color absorption, refraction, soft internal light scattering, and delicate rim highlights.
* Thick areas should have richer color; thin tentacle tips should transmit more light.
* Avoid opaque plastic, blown-out highlights, and visible mesh seams.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS
Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics system with elastic constraints and approximate volume preservation.

* The head should feel soft but substantial.
* Tentacles should be more flexible than the head, especially near their tips.
* Allow users to grab the head or any tentacle at the clicked location.
* Pulling should deform the nearby geometry first, then elastically pull the rest of the body.
* On release, the octopus should wobble and gradually settle into its original shape.
* Tentacles should react independently, with slightly delayed motion.
* Include gravity, floor collisions, friction, and damping.
* Prevent tentacles from passing through the floor.
* Clamp extreme stretching and use fixed simulation steps so strong pulls do not break the model.
* Do not fake softness by scaling or rotating the entire octopus.

INTERACTION

* Left-click or touch the octopus to grab and stretch it.
* Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
* Support a limited zoom range.
* Keep camera gestures separate from object dragging.
* Add “Give it a nudge,” “Reset,” “Pause,” and “Reset view” buttons.
* Include Firmness and Internal damping sliders.
* Add “¼ speed” and “Show mesh” toggles.
* Provide three color presets: Coral, Lagoon, and Grape. Change the material colors without resetting the simulation.

INTERFACE
Use a minimal editorial layout:

* Top left: small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
* Large italic serif heading: “Octo Jelly.”
* Caption: “Eight arms. A little wobble. A very soft creature.”
* Top right: a WebGPU status indicator.
* Right side: a compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel.
* Bottom left: “Grab a tentacle. Pull gently. Let go.”

Use clean sans-serif text for controls, thin borders, and generous whitespace. Avoid heavy panels or decorative UI effects.
PERFORMANCE AND QUALITY

* Use real WebGPU rendering, not a 2D canvas imitation or prerecorded animation.
* Reuse geometry and buffers; do not rebuild meshes during dragging.
* Keep suction cups, eyes, and other details attached to the deforming body.
* Handle transparency without flickering, disappearing surfaces, or harsh black edges.
* Support desktop and mobile layouts.
* Show a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.
* Test repeated grabs, strong pulls, releases, floor collisions, palette changes, pause, and reset.

The result should feel like a little living gummy toy - glossy, squishy, expressive, and satisfying to stretch. Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or a code fragment.

title: Volcanic island 3D scene version comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create a beautiful, highly detailed, fully interactive 3D prehistoric island using Three.js and WebGL. Deliver everything in a single standalone HTML file that opens directly in Chrome. Embed assets wherever possible.

VISUAL DIRECTION
Build a large, rounded island surrounded by an ocean with a transparent underwater cross-section. The result should feel like a premium miniature world: lush vegetation, expressive dinosaurs, rich materials, atmospheric lighting, and polished animation. Use a cohesive, stylized art direction rather than basic geometric shapes.
ISLAND
Create varied terrain with beaches, rocky cliffs, dense prehistoric forests, giant ferns, a waterfall, a freshwater pond, and a volcano. Add a small research station, wooden walkways, observation platforms, supply crates, and dinosaur nests. Make the island spacious enough for dinosaurs to move naturally between distinct areas.

WATER CROSS-SECTION
The water must form a deep, rounded volume around the island, with clearly visible underwater scenery through its sides. Include a textured seabed, rocks, aquatic plants, fish, bubbles, and a green marine reptile swimming beneath the surface. Do not place ordinary land dinosaurs underwater, and do not add a submarine.
Use animated waves, Fresnel reflections, underwater light patterns, shoreline foam, and splashes. Avoid transparency sorting artifacts and visible gaps between the island and water.

DINOSAURS
Include several distinct species, such as a long-necked sauropod, Triceratops, Stegosaurus, a large theropod, and smaller herd animals. Add pterosaurs circling overhead.
Give every species recognizable anatomy, shaped bodies, articulated limbs, detailed heads, tails, and appropriate skin patterns. Avoid assembling the finished dinosaurs from obvious boxes or disconnected spheres.

NATURAL ANIMATION
Use hierarchical skeletons with correctly positioned joints. Walking must have distinct stance and swing phases: feet stay planted during contact and lift cleanly during each step. Match stride length to movement speed.

Use terrain sampling and inverse kinematics to keep feet on the ground. Add weight shifts, subtle body movement, balanced tail motion, head turns, and breathing. Dinosaurs must never float, slide, intersect the ground, or walk through buildings, rocks, trees, or each other.
Use obstacle avoidance and safe paths. Different species should have different movement speeds, gait patterns, and behaviors. Marine animals must face their direction of travel.

INTERACTION
Allow users to:

Rotate the camera freely, zoom, and inspect the underwater cross-section.
Select a dinosaur and follow it with a smoothly moving camera.

Place food in suitable locations and watch nearby dinosaurs approach and eat.

Trigger drinking, resting, calling, and herd movement.

Explore nests and watch a hatchling emerge.
Trigger a marine reptile surfacing with a splash.
Switch between daylight, sunset, and night.
Adjust rain, wind, and volcanic activity.
Pause the simulation and reset the scene.
Make every control produce a clear, visible response. Keep interactions repeatable and prevent overlapping animations from breaking character poses.
ATMOSPHERE AND AUDIO
Add moving foliage, drifting clouds, birds, insects, rain particles, and warm research-station lights at night. Include quiet atmospheric music and environmental sounds with a working music toggle and volume slider. Start audio only after user interaction.
INTERFACE
Use a compact, elegant interface with English labels. Keep the scene dominant and avoid large panels covering the island. Make the layout responsive for desktop and mobile.
TECHNICAL QUALITY
Use instancing for repeated vegetation and props, efficient geometry, appropriate shadows, and restrained post-processing. Balance visual richness with smooth real-time performance.
Build a complete scene, not a mockup. Test the final HTML directly in a desktop browser, inspect screenshots and the console, exercise every interaction, and fix loading errors, floating dinosaurs, foot sliding, broken collisions, water artifacts, and camera problems before delivery.

title: Arcane-style Blender animation
author: xikhar
prompt:
TITLE: "SPARK"

An around 15-second 3D animated shot in the painterly style of the show Arcane (Fortiche).

Made in Blender, or any other tool if superior. Widescreen, no dialogue.

GOAL

The top priority is replicating Arcane's visual and animation style as perfectly as possible, in every way. Someone watching should believe it came from the same studio.

Take as much time and effort as needed. Replicate the technique and look perfectly. Spend as much time as needed, ensuring it's perfect in every way.

SCENE (loose — adapt freely)

A small mechanical creature (not humanoid), something like a brass-and-crystal moth, wakes up on a cluttered inventor's workbench at night. Its crystal core ignites with glowing energy, and it bursts into the air in a swirl of sparks. Change the details, framing, or action if something else shows off the style better. You can animate something else completely different if you want—anything you pick, whatever you can do best—that will also look identical to Arcane.

PROCESS

1. RESEARCH: Before building anything, study Arcane's style in depth. Find references and breakdowns of Fortiche's technique (interviews, making-of material, artist breakdowns). Write down every defining element: textures, shading, line work, color, lighting, frame rate, effects, camera, compositing.

2. STYLE GUIDE: Turn that into a written checklist and a small style frame (a single still image) before animating. Compare it side by side with reference stills and revise until it matches.

3. BUILD: Model, texture, light, and animate following the checklist.

4. REVIEW: Compare frames against Arcane references repeatedly. List every difference you can see and fix it. Repeat until no noticeable differences remain.

STYLE ELEMENTS TO MATCH (at minimum)

- Hand-painted textures with visible brushstrokes on every surface; nothing looks procedural or photographic.

- Stylized, painterly shading with designed light/shadow shapes, not realistic falloff.

- Animation on 2s for characters/objects, with strong poses, snappy timing, anticipation, and smear frames; camera moves smooth on 1s.

- Hand-drawn 2D effects (sparks, energy, smoke, glints, glow) layered over the 3D, animated on 2s with graphic shape language.

- Bold, moody color: warm light vs. saturated glowing accents, rich colored shadows, strong rim light, bloom.

- Painterly compositing: brush-like filtering, grain, subtle texture over the image.

- Cinematic camera: shallow depth of field, purposeful movement, weight on impacts.

SOUND

Detailed, cinematic sound design that matches the action and mood.

Make everything as good as possible: animation, models, textures, effects, lighting, and sound. Use any tools or programs needed. You may study references online and imitate techniques, and copy things, but do not directly use assets you did not create. Keep the whole shot in one consistent style so the 3D, painted textures, and 2D effects feel like a single hand-crafted image.

Do not use memory or previous chats.

You can use any other tools, programs, plugins, literally anything. Use anything at your disposal.

You can use different processes than outlined in this, or animate something else than described, but it should absolutely look as close as possible to the TV show Arcane. Make it perfect in every way and identical.

title: Pineapple Jelly
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create an interactive 3D scene called “Pineapple Jelly” - a thick, translucent gummy pineapple ring that users can grab, stretch, bend, and release. Everything must run directly in the browser in one standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU and WGSL shaders.
The main priorities are convincing soft-body behavior, beautiful light refraction, and satisfying interaction.
MODEL

* A round pineapple slice with a genuine hole through its center.
* Thick, juicy flesh, a slightly scalloped outer edge, and softly rounded corners.
* Both cut faces must be equally detailed. The ring can be flipped and viewed from every angle.
* Golden translucent flesh with delicate radial fibers, small bubbles, and elongated pale juice cells embedded inside.
* No skin, leaves, or seeds. It should look like a pineapple ring made of gummy candy, not a doughnut.

MATERIAL AND LIGHTING

* Rich honey-yellow coloring, wet gloss, and soft subsurface-style light scattering.
* Refraction, thickness-dependent transparency, controlled highlights, and Fresnel reflections around the edges.
* Stretched, thinner areas should transmit more light.
* A warm, light background, soft studio lighting, and a grounded contact shadow.
* Avoid blown-out highlights, excessive bloom, and a hard-glass appearance.

PHYSICS

* Use a volumetric soft-body mesh with elastic connections and volume constraints, such as XPBD.
* Allow users to grab either the outer or inner edge and pull it in any direction.
* Deformation should spread naturally through neighboring regions: the hole stretches, the flesh bends, and the opposite side responds with a slight delay.
* After release, the ring should spring back softly, wobble a few times, and gradually settle.
* No instant snapping, endless oscillation, torn geometry, or collapsing central hole.
* Implement gravity and ground collisions. The ring should squash slightly on impact and recover its shape.
* Internal fibers, bubbles, and juice cells must deform with the flesh instead of remaining stationary.
* Clicking through the empty center must not grab the object.

INTERFACE

* A minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace.
* A large italic serif heading on the left: “Pineapple Jelly.”
* A compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel on the right.
* Three color presets: Golden, Amber, and Rosé. Change the tint while preserving the material properties.
* Sliders for Firmness and Internal damping.
* Buttons: Give it a nudge, Reset, Turn it over, and Pause.
* Toggles: ¼ speed and Show mesh.
* Small live readouts for mass, volume relative to rest volume, and kinetic energy.
* All interface text in English.
* Support both mouse and touch interaction.

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

* Use actual 3D geometry and WebGPU rendering, not a video or a Canvas 2D imitation.
* Generate all geometry and materials in code, without external models or image assets.
* Separate the simulation mesh from the smoother visual surface to maintain good performance.
* Display a clear fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
* Test strong stretching, inner-edge grabbing, flipping, resetting, and mobile interaction.

Save the finished result as pineapple-jelly-webgpu.html. Deliver the complete working file, not a mockup or implementation plan.
The final experience should feel like a soft, stretchy, appetizing gummy toy that is genuinely fun to squish.

prompt:
Build a polished browser-based 3D Rocket League-style game using Three.js.
Goal: Create a fully playable local web game that runs in the browser. The first screen should be the actual game, not a landing page.

title: 3D watermelon fur render comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML page (no build step) showing an interactive 3D "Fluffy Watermelon" covered in long fur, rendered with WebGL using three.js r147 (UMD build: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.147.0/build/three.min.js). All UI text in English.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.
- Custom cursor: the native grab hand plus a thin dark 46 px ring that follows the pointer and shrinks while dragging. Hovering gently parts the fur under the cursor, as if stroking it.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion (no idle spin, no breeze).

UI & ROBUSTNESS
- Bottom-left caption: "Fluffy Watermelon" and a hint "Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Double-click to reset" (on touch devices: "Drag to rotate · Pinch to zoom") that fades after the first interaction. Font: Onest from Google Fonts with system fallbacks.
- Guard against a zero-sized container at load: clamp width/height to at least 1 and, every frame, recover from any non-finite camera distance or rotation state.
- Show a small on-page note if the WebGL context is lost or a shader fails to compile, and a fallback message if WebGL is unavailable.

title: Gummy squid render: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create “Squid Jelly” — a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy squid that users can grab, stretch, and squish directly in their browser. Deliver a complete standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU.

ART DIRECTION

Make the squid look like a premium translucent gummy candy:
- An elongated, tapered mantle with a rounded tip.
- Two broad, thin, diamond-shaped side fins.
- Eight shorter curled arms and two longer feeding tentacles with rounded club-shaped tips.
- Small suction cups and a cute, understated face.

Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the squid large and centered, with an elegant, uncluttered composition.

GEOMETRY

Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.

Connect the arms, tentacles, and fins smoothly to the body. Their roots must remain embedded and attached during strong pulls, with no visible gaps or floating parts.

Suction cups and eyes must follow the deforming surface. Give the fins a thin, flexible profile and the longer tentacles slender shafts with thicker tips.

JELLY MATERIAL

Create convincing glossy, translucent jelly:
- Thickness-dependent color absorption.
- Refraction and soft internal light scattering.
- Smooth studio reflections and delicate rim highlights.
- A few tiny bubbles embedded inside the material.
- Richer color in thick areas and greater translucency along thin fins and tentacle tips.

Avoid opaque plastic, washed-out colors, blown-out highlights, visible mesh seams, and flickering transparency.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS

Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics simulation with approximate volume preservation.

The mantle should feel soft but substantial. Arms should bend independently, while long tentacles and fins should be more flexible.

Let users grab the body, fins, or tentacles at the clicked location. Pulling must deform the nearby geometry first, with the rest following elastically. Do not fake softness by scaling or rotating the entire model.

On release, the squid should wobble, recover its shape, and gradually settle. Include gravity, floor collisions, friction, and damping. Prevent appendages from passing through the floor.

Use fixed simulation steps, bounded stretching, and robust attachment constraints so repeated strong pulls cannot tear the model apart or destabilize the simulation.

INTERACTION

- Left-click or touch the squid to grab and stretch it.
- Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
- Support limited zoom and mobile touch controls.
- Keep camera gestures separate from object dragging.

Add:
- Give it a nudge
- Reset
- Reset view
- Pause
- Firmness slider
- Internal damping slider
- ¼ speed toggle
- Show mesh toggle

Provide three material palettes: Coral, Lagoon, and Grape. Switching colors must not reset the simulation.

INTERFACE

Use a minimal editorial layout:
- Top left: small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
- Large italic serif heading: “Squid Jelly.”
- Caption: “A little ink. A little wiggle. A very sweet sea creature.”
- Top right: WebGPU status indicator.
- Right side: compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel.
- Bottom left: a short interaction hint.

Use clean sans-serif controls, thin borders, and generous whitespace. Adapt the layout for mobile without covering the squid.

QUALITY AND PERFORMANCE

Use real 3D geometry and native WebGPU rendering with WGSL shaders, not a 2D imitation or prerecorded animation.

Reuse meshes and buffers. Do not reconstruct geometry during dragging. Prioritize stable interactions and smooth performance.

Test strong pulls, repeated releases, appendage attachments, floor collisions, palette changes, pause, reset, and camera controls.

Provide a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.

Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or code fragment. The result should feel like a little living gummy toy: glossy, weighty, flexible, and irresistibly satisfying to stretch.

title: 3D canal and windmill scene model comparison
author: vib3coded
model: Claude Opus 5.5 / other comparison model (not identified)
prompt:
Build "Lock Jelly." — a single self-contained HTML file (WebGPU + WGSL, no libraries, no network, works from file://), part of a "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas. If WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails, show a clean fallback card instead of the scene.

CONCEPT
A square block of clear coloured jelly (about 5.2 × 5.2 units, ~2 units high) holding a little English canal scene. The canal runs along the FRONT edge of the block, so the block's front face cuts the water lengthways: you see the lock chamber in cross-section, the water inside it rising and falling between the gates, fish swimming, the boat's hull below the waterline. All cut faces show candy-coloured soil strata; under the pounds a blue-grey puddle-clay lining, under the chamber a brick invert on a concrete bed, under the fields brown earth and turf.

LAYOUT (left to right along the front)
- Upper pound on the left at the higher level, opening into a round winding hole (a bay for turning boats); near the lock it narrows between brick wing walls.
- The lock chamber in the middle: brick walls with dressed-stone quoins and coping, a slimy band between the two water levels and weed below, an iron ladder, a gauge board, a stone cill under the top gate, recesses that the open gates fold into.
- Below the bottom gate a short walled tail, then the lower pound bends away from the front face, runs under a humpback brick bridge into a basin with a willow-covered island, lily pads in its corners and a sunken bicycle on the bed.
- The ground steps down from an upper terrace to a lower one along a grassy bank.
- Behind the lock: stone setts around the chamber, bollards, a gravel towpath, a lane, the keeper's whitewashed cottage with a slate roof, green door, picket-fence garden full of flowers and washing flapping on a line, a gas lamp, a bench, a white windmill with turning lattice sails, oaks, willows, poplars, a hedge, sheep, reeds on the soft banks.

WATER
- Linear shallow-water waves on a staggered grid (~168²) with a little surface tension, so short ripples are springy like jelly; damping and firmness are adjustable.
- Three separate bodies of water — upper pound, chamber, lower pound — each with its own rest level. Faces between bodies stay shut unless the gate between them is open and the levels are equal. The chamber's level is moved bodily when paddles are drawn (Torricelli-style flow), with boils, white water and a dimple at the intake.
- Rendering: refraction of the scene behind, flavour-coloured absorption, sun caustics on the bed, soft light shafts, foam (wakes, paddle churn), a meniscus line on the cut faces. Split the surface mesh along the gate lines so the step in level at a shut gate is a clean wall hidden by the gate leaf, not a ramp.
- The block itself can be tipped by dragging its side; the jelly shears and wobbles, the water sloshes, and it settles back.

THE LOCK AND THE KEEPER
- Two single-leaf timber gates (planks, rails, diagonal brace, iron straps, a walkway with a handrail), each with a white balance beam with black bands. Ground-paddle pedestals with toothed racks that rise when wound.
- An articulated lock keeper (flat cap, navy jumper, cords, windlass in hand; torso, arms, thighs and shins as separate parts). He walks with a proper gait, plans his route around the bench, pedestals, bollards and any beam lying across his way (going round the beam's end), leans his back on a beam and walks it round backwards to swing a gate, winds the windlass with his arm circling the spindle, and sits on his bench between jobs. He sets off for the gate as the boat comes in.
- The cycle: the boat lies in the full chamber → keeper shuts the top gate → winds up the bottom paddles → the chamber empties into the tail with white water → winds them down → opens the bottom gate → the boat leaves, runs the tail, swings round the bend, ducks under the bridge, goes round the island and comes back into the chamber bow first → shut bottom gate → round to the top paddles → chamber fills with boils → open the top gate → the boat goes up the pound, turns in the winding hole and comes back. Repeat forever. A gate may only open when the levels match.

BOATS
- A traditional narrowboat "Wobble": black lofted hull, a green cabin with red lining-out, brass portholes, a cratch board and cover at the bow, a chimney with brass bands (puffing smoke), a painted Buckby can, plank and pole on the roof, rope fenders, a headlamp, a brass swan-neck tiller and a steerer in a red jumper. It follows smooth filleted routes (check the stern never swings out through the block's face), slows near the gates, heaves, pitches and rolls on the local surface, and hands its displaced volume back to the water so it makes bow waves and wakes.
- Three moored narrowboats in the basin in different liveries with flowerpots on the roofs and one ginger cat, tied to bank pins with stretchy mooring lines.

LIFE
- Roach, perch and bream as boids that stay in their own body of water (they can only move between pound and chamber while a gate is open), under the surface and hulls, off the bed, scattering from the boat and splashes.
- Mallards (drakes, ducks) and a duck with four ducklings that follow exactly along her trail; a pair of mute swans in the basin. They paddle the surface, ride the chamber down and up, upend now and then, get out of the boat's way and come for bread.
- A grey heron that wades in the shallows or stands on a moored boat's roof, stabs at fish (sometimes catching one), and flaps off somewhere quieter when the boat passes or someone toots.
- Chimney smoke from the boat and the cottage.

UI (editorial, like a print magazine)
- Top-left: small caps eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a huge italic serif title "Lock / Jelly.", a short subtitle. Top-right: a status pill "WebGPU · Live / Paused / Unavailable".
- Right: a frosted-glass control panel (a bottom sheet on mobile) with: buttons Hurry (speeds the keeper, paddles and boat), Toot (horn; also Space), Throw bread, Rubber duck (drops a yellow rubber duck that floats upright, can be picked up and thrown, rides the lock, is stopped by gates and shoved by boats); a liveliness meter; tallies Trips · Lockfuls · Fed; a status line "Wobble — Emptying the lock 62%" telling the story step by step; three flavours Greengage, Elderflower, Blackcurrant (change the water colour/absorption and strata); sliders Firmness, Wave damping, Paddle speed; Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- Bottom-left: "How to play — Throw bread. Toot the horn. Hurry the keeper." with a small line of instructions.
- Interaction: drag across the water to make waves, drag the block's side to tip it, pick up and throw rubber ducks, drag empty space to orbit, scroll/pinch to zoom; touch works.
- Soft studio lighting on a warm paper backdrop with the block's tinted, caustic-flecked shadow; WebAudio sounds: the boat's horn, the gate thudding shut, a creak, the windlass ratchet, and the rush of water that swells with the flow.

QUALITY
Keep it smooth (fixed-step physics, cheap per frame), no console errors, no page scroll, works at phone width. Test it headlessly: a full round trip happens, levels go exactly from upper to lower and back, no gate opens across a step, the keeper never walks into the water or through obstacles, the boat never touches a gate leaf, and every button works.
