title: Courtyard House
author: Katia Gil Guzman (OpenAI)
prompt:
Build a complete, polished, interactive landing page. Use clear, natural copy and a restrained layout with purposeful controls. Keep native scrolling, support phone and desktop layouts, keyboard controls, and reduced motion. The main interaction should work without a runtime AI call or account.

Scenario: an architectural practice presents Courtyard House, an imagined compact home organized around a planted courtyard. The visitor wants to understand the plan, how spaces connect and how daylight moves through the building. This is a focused architecture-project landing page, not an interior moodboard generator.

Art direction: gallery white, charcoal drawing lines, natural oak and one restrained terracotta accent. Architectural photography/renders, meticulous diagrams, a clear modern typeface and large whitespace. The drawing and building are the visual identity.

Hero: “A small house built around daylight.” Present one excellent exterior/axonometric image and an “Explore the house” action. Build a single geometrically coherent model and use it throughout the page.

The main interaction is a reversible scroll from exterior to roof-off cutaway to floor plan. A section-plane control then lets the visitor cut across the actual geometry to see room relationships, wall thickness, openings and the courtyard. Named room labels attach to the correct spaces and remain readable; do not put a generic render beside an unrelated invented plan.

Provide a time-of-day slider for one explicitly defined illustrative site orientation and season. Sun direction, shadows through openings and the diagram compass must agree. Use simplified lighting if necessary, but do not invent energy-use or daylight-compliance metrics. Show the time and orientation only where they help explain the view.

Visitors can select one room to see its connected interior view, compare two materially different facade/finish options, and return to the overview without losing their section/time state. Finish with a compact plan/specification summary and a “Download project sheet” action that exports the actual selected plan and views. Areas and dimensions should derive consistently from the model or be omitted.

Use authored 3D geometry with editable model or procedural source and a credible lighting setup. Do not rely entirely on image crossfades. On mobile, offer clear presets for plan/section/exterior rather than forcing difficult free-camera gestures. Verify camera bounds, clipping, labels, room mapping, sun/compass consistency, export and state restoration. The page should communicate a building beautifully and precisely.

title: Nightjar Listening Room
author: Katia Gil Guzman (OpenAI)
prompt:
Build a complete, polished, interactive landing page. Use clear, natural copy and a restrained layout with purposeful controls. Keep native scrolling, support phone and desktop layouts, keyboard controls, and reduced motion. The main interaction should work without a runtime AI call or account.

Scenario: Nightjar is an imagined listening room built around records, good speakers and comfortable seats. Visitors can preview the listening experience and explore the room. Demonstrate audiovisual craft and interface timing with a warm, tactile design.

Art direction: tobacco wood, near-black, oxblood and amber light, with excellent photography or original room renders. Use an understated serif for the venue name and a clear compact sans for the listening controls. The page should feel like a specific room at night, not a streaming-service dashboard.

Page and signature interaction:
- Hero: “A listening room for full albums.” A turntable, sleeve and speaker sit in an inviting room scene, with an obvious “Play a sample” button. Audio starts only from user action and always has visible pause/mute and volume controls.
- Offer three distinct original short instrumental samples/loops with accurately described styles and duration. Produce them procedurally with Web Audio or use properly licensed original assets. No copyrighted commercial recordings, fake artist credits, or claims that a short generated loop is an actual released album.
- Selecting a record changes the sleeve, label and sound. The tonearm lowers, platter rotates while playback runs, and subtle meter/room-light movement follows the actual audio amplitude. Pausing must stop the appropriate visual motion. The animation and playback state must stay synchronized.
- Scrolling reveals the room: a bench, a table near the speakers and the bar. Clicking one shows its view and a concise description. Keep the room layout consistent across hero and detail views.
- Include a compact authored listening programme with useful categories, and allow visitors to save a shortlist locally. Use fictional programming without presenting it as a real event booking.
- End with a clear room overview and “Replay the samples” or “View your shortlist.” A functioning preview is the destination; do not add fake ticketing.

Handle browser audio unlocking, sample switching, rapid play/pause, a tab becoming hidden, and reduced-motion preferences. Never require a microphone. Provide a visual alternative for the audio story. Make the mobile player compact and reliable. The result should combine an excellent hospitality landing page with a genuinely working miniature listening experience.

title: Tidal House

Build a complete, polished, interactive landing page. Use clear, natural copy and a restrained layout with purposeful controls. Keep native scrolling, support phone and desktop layouts, keyboard controls, and reduced motion. The main interaction should work without a runtime AI call or account.

Keep camera transitions bounded and comfortable. On mobile preserve cabin selection and useful views without requiring a drag gesture to scroll. Verify every cabin, time/tide combination, and return to the overview. Let the setting and useful exploration carry the page.

title: High-speed parkour motion previz
author: かし子🍩
prompt:
Remotionを使い、高低差と多彩なカメラワークを備えた、高速パルクールのモーションコンテを実装・レンダーしてください。計画や静止画だけで終わらず、実際に動くMP4を完成させてください。

【制作条件】
題材は「遊園地のアトラクションを渡り歩く高速パルクール」。題材の指定があれば、その舞台へ置き換えてください。
尺・画面指定がなければ、15秒、横長、SD程度、30fps、無音を初期値とします。軽量で動きを確認しやすい解像度を選んでください。
外部素材がなくても、単純な立体形状で制作を完結できる構成にしてください。

【必須技術】
TypeScriptとRemotionを使用し、useCurrentFrame()を時間の基準として、人物、背景、動く足場、カメラの状態を決定してください。
背景と人物は共通の3D座標系に置き、WebGLで奥行きと遮蔽を描画します。RemotionでプレビューとMP4のレンダーを行ってください。

コース形状、人物の移動経路、姿勢、動く足場、カメラ、描画処理を分離し、後から動作とカメラを編集できる構成にしてください。同じフレーム番号からは常に同じ状態が得られるようにします。

【人物の形と動き】
人物は1体。球形の頭と縦長のカプセル状の胴体からなる、単純な「i型」にしてください。頭と胴体は少し離し、背景から見分けやすい色にします。

四肢や衣装を作り込まず、位置移動、前傾、左右の傾き、軽い上下動、踏み切り前の圧縮、着地時の沈み込みで動作を伝えてください。
走行では短周期の接地感を入れ、加速、跳躍、着地、再加速をつなぎます。
宙返りは身体の向きが空間内で実際に回転するようにし、移動軌道と回転を別々に制御してください。

【コースとアクション】
遊具を、実際に通過・接地できる一続きの立体コースとして配置してください。

基本の流れ：
・ジェットコースターの上りレールを高速で駆け上がる
・曲線レールを急降下する
・レール間の隙間を横宙返りで越える
・ひねり跳躍で動く観覧車のゴンドラ屋根へ飛び移る
・ゴンドラから外周の足場へ跳び、観覧車上部のアーチを走る
・一段低いメリーゴーランドの屋根へ前宙で降りる
・着地ロールから起き上がり、方向転換する
・振り子アトラクションの動く平台へ飛び乗る
・平台からさらに低い屋根へ後宙で降りる
・障害物を跳び越え、曲がる水路沿いを走る
・水路を宙返りで越え、そのまま出口へ疾走する

尺に応じて動作を整理し、各動作の踏み切り、空中移動、接地が読み取れる時間を確保してください。

移動する足場は独立して動かし、接地中の人物は足場の移動へ追従させます。離れた瞬間から人物自身の跳躍軌道へ移行してください。
高さ、距離、足場の幅、回転速度は、接触が成立し、映像でも読める値を設計してください。

背景には支柱、隣接する遊具、屋根、水路、地面などを配置し、人物の移動距離とカメラの視差が分かるようにします。形状は簡素でも、遊具の種類を識別できる輪郭を持たせてください。

【カメラ演出】
次の構図を、アクションの意味に合わせて組み合わせてください。

・真後ろから、進行方向へ伸びるレール越しに追走
・やや斜め後ろから、高低差と次の足場を見せる追走
・横から並走し、跳躍距離や身体の回転を見せる構図
・着地点側に先回りし、こちらへ飛び込んでくる人物を正面で迎える構図
・高所で周囲の地形と落差を見せる広い構図
・次の足場を見る意図を伝える、短い頭部のアップ
・踏み切りや着地の接触を伝える、短い接地部のアップ

正面の迎えでは、カメラを着地点側の一定位置に構える区間を設けてください。人物とカメラの距離が実際に縮まり、人物が画面内で大きくなるようにします。

空中の回転や遊具間の移動では、全身と着地点が読める画角を確保してください。接地部のアップは接触成立後に入れ、次の移動へ素早くつなぎます。

カメラ位置、注視点、画角は連続した軌道でつないでください。背後から正面へ移る際は、人物の周囲を弧を描いて回り込みます。人物を挟んだ2地点を単純に直線補間して、カメラが人物を突き抜けることのない設計にしてください。

構図の名称だけを増やすのではなく、実際の進行方向に対するカメラ位置と、完成映像の見え方に変化を作ってください。

【見た目と速度感】
人物と遊具の形状が読みやすい、簡素な色と照明で仕上げてください。
高速感は、大きな位置変化、短い踏み切り、着地直後の再加速、前景の通過、カメラへの接近で表現します。
映像面は人物と環境で構成し、説明文や制作メモは別資料へまとめてください。

【検証と提出】
レンダー前に、以下を確認・修正してください。
・着地点に支持面があり、接地中の人物が足場へ追従する
・意図しない床抜け、支柱や遊具へのめり込みがない
・人物とカメラの位置、姿勢、画角に不連続や非数値がない
・広い構図では人物全体が画面内に収まる
・頭部と接地部のアップが対象を正しく捉える
・背後、斜め後方、側方、正面の構図が実際に成立する
・正面の迎えで人物がカメラへ接近する

MP4をレンダーした後、ffprobeで尺、解像度、fps、フレーム数、音声の有無を確認し、ffmpegで最後までデコードしてください。
完成動画から各動作とカメラ移行の代表フレームを取り出して目視確認し、可能なら通常速度でも通し再生してください。数値検査と映像の見やすさは別々に検証します。

提出物：
1. 完成したモーションコンテMP4
2. 編集可能なRemotion／TypeScriptソース
3. 動作区間、開始・終了フレーム、カメラ、出力仕様を記載したJSON
4. 再レンダー手順
5. 実施した検証と未確認事項の短い記録

最後に、完成MP4をすぐ開けるリンクを提示してください。

title: Cozy Café Fluid Studio: interactive coffee and milk simulation
author: genevieve__h
prompt:
# Role & Objective
Act as a Principal Graphics Engineer and Creative Technologist specializing in Three.js, WebGL2/WebGPU, 3D Volumetric Fluid Dynamics, and GLSL Raymarching. 

Build a browser-based, photorealistic, interactive 3D coffee & milk physics sandbox ("Cozy Café Fluid Studio") designed to look like a viral macro-lens video on X. The user can orbit the camera freely (from 90° top-down to a 0° macro side-profile view), swap custom 3D glass vessels and ice cube shapes (with procedural fallbacks and a `.glb`/`.gltf` loader for Blender assets), and pour either Espresso or Heavy Cream directly from their cursor in any order.

---

# 1. Core Visual & Physics Architecture (True 3D Volumetric Fluid)
Because the camera can view the glass from the side, top, or any oblique angle, implement a **3D Eulerian Grid Fluid Solver** (e.g., `64x96x64` or `96x128x96` tiled 2D texture atlas or WebGL2 `sampler3D` / WebGPU 3D Storage Textures) confined to the bounding volume of the active glass mesh:

1. **Two-Fluid Miscible Density & Filling System:**
   - Track two separate scalar volume fields inside the glass: $\rho_{\text{coffee}}$ (dark absorbing fluid) and $\rho_{\text{milk}}$ (bright scattering fluid), plus a dynamic **Liquid Fill Height (
$h
_{\text{fill}}$)** that rises smoothly as the user pours either liquid into the glass.
   - Allow pouring in **any order**:
     - *Coffee first, then Milk:* Pouring espresso fills the glass with dark amber-black liquid and generates a thin golden crema foam layer on the top meniscus ($y \approx h_{\text{fill}}$). Pouring cold milk next shoots a dense white plume downward that billows back up via buoyancy.
     - *Milk first, then Coffee (Dirty Latte / Macchiato style):* Pouring cold milk fills the glass with opaque ivory liquid. Pouring hot espresso on top creates dark mahogany plumes that sink through the dense milk and stratify into layered gradients around the ice.

2. **Rayleigh-Taylor & Kelvin-Helmholtz Instabilities:**
   - Implement **MacCormack (or BFECC) Advection** so thin caramel ribbons do not smear out due to numerical dissipation.
   - Inject **Baroclinic Vorticity** ($\nabla \rho \times \nabla P$) and **Vorticity Confinement** ($\epsilon (\mathbf{N} \times \boldsymbol{\omega})$) along the interface between milk and coffee so sinking/rising plumes roll up into hyper-detailed mushroom caps and curling tendrils.

3. **3D Volumetric Raymarching Shader (Beer-Lambert + Multiple Scattering Approximation):**
   - Render the fluid volume inside the glass by raymarching through the 3D density texture (`sampler3D`).
   - **Optical Physics:** Do NOT use simple RGB `mix()`. Compute physically based **Beer-Lambert Law extinction** ($\sigma_a(\lambda) = \text{vec3}(1.6, 5.4, 13.5)$ for espresso so thin edges glow ruby/caramel-amber while thick regions are pitch black) combined with **isotropic + forward Henyey-Greenstein phase function scattering** for the milk fat globules (high albedo ivory-white).
   - Add a **Dual-Lobe Subsurface Scattering (SSS)** look by sampling a lower-MIP (blurred) level of the milk density volume for ambient internal light transport, creating a soft, milky amber glow where coffee and cream meet.

---

# 2. Custom Blender Assets (Glasses & Ice) + Procedural SDF Dual-Representation
Support loading custom Blender `.glb` meshes via `GLTFLoader` while providing built-in procedural geometries (and matching Signed Distance Fields) so the app runs out-of-the-box:

1. **Glass Shapes (Vessel Selector):**
   - **Fluted Café Glass:** Ribbed vertical ridges that distort and refract the swirling fluid inside.
   - **Double-Walled Borosilicate Mug:** Suspended inner rounded chamber showing floating liquid in mid-air.
   - **Stemless Wine / Tulip Glass:** Curved tapered bowl that forces sinking milk plumes inward toward the center.
   - **Classic Rocks Tumbler:** Heavy thick crystal base with sharp vertical walls.
   - *Rendering:* Use Three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `transmission: 0.98`, `ior: 1.52`, `thickness`, dispersion/chromatic aberration, and crisp studio softbox environment reflections.
   - *Physics Boundary:* Enforce a strict no-slip/no-penetration boundary condition against the inner wall SDF of the selected glass so fluid hugs the exact contour of the vessel.

2. **Ice Cube Shapes (Ice Selector):**
   - **Large Craft Sphere:** A single giant crystal-clear sphere in the center that splits the pour stream into a ring vortex.
   - **Beveled Bistro Cubes (x3):** Stacked at angles inside the glass, creating narrow channels for cream tendrils to snake through.
   - **Hollow Cylinder / Bullet Ice:** Allows fluid to pour through the center hole and billow out the bottom.
   - **Crushed / Pebble Ice:** A porous top cluster that diffuses the pour into dozens of tiny trickling caramel fingers.
   - *Rendering & Physics:* Render ice with `ior: 1.31`, internal frost fracture planes, and real-time refraction of the raymarched fluid behind it. Stamp the ice SDFs into the 3D fluid solver's obstacle buffer so plumes physically collide with, wrap around, and slide underneath the ice cubes. Include buoyant bobbing when liquid height rises.

---

# 3. Interactive Pouring & Camera Controls
1. **Cursor-Driven Pour Stream:**
   - Raycast the mouse cursor onto a horizontal plane above the glass rim.
   - **Left-Click & Hold:** Pour a visible, glossy 3D parabolic liquid stream (rendered as a dynamic tube mesh or raymarched metaball stream) from the cursor into the glass.
   - **Mouse Speed & Scroll Wheel:** Moving the mouse whips the stream across the surface; scrolling adjusts **Pour Height / Velocity** (a high pour punches deep to the bottom of the glass with high turbulence; a low pour gently floats layers on the surface).
2. **Seamless Orbit Camera (`OrbitControls`):**
   - Right-click drag (or two-finger drag) smoothly orbits from **Macro Side View** (watching plumes dive down the glass wall) to **Top-Down Latte Art View** (watching crema swirl around the ice).
   - Include quick camera preset buttons: `[Side Profile]`, `[45° Café Angle]`, and `[Top-Down Macro]`.

---

# 4. Minimalist Cozy UI & Atmosphere
- **Environment:** A warm, sunlit wooden tabletop with soft morning window blinds casting subtle gobos/caustics, warm beige/linen background tones, and a shallow depth-of-field (`BokehPass`) on the background.
- **Minimalist Floating Dock (Bottom Center, frosted glass `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, rounded pill buttons, warm serif/sans typography):**
  - **Liquid Toggle:** `[ ☕ Pour Espresso ]` | `[ 🥛 Pour Heavy Cream ]`

  - **Simulation Controls:** `Pour Speed` slider, `Time Scale` slider (`0.1x Slow-Mo` to `1.0x`), `[ Stir with Glass Straw ]` tool, and `[ Empty Glass ]` reset button.

---

# Deliverable Instructions
Provide a complete, runnable HTML/JS/GLSL implementation (or clean modular Vite + Three.js setup) with zero missing placeholders. Prioritize the 3D raymarched Beer-Lambert coffee/milk shader, the 3D fluid advection/vorticity compute passes, and the refractive glass/ice boundary coupling so it runs at 60fps.

title: The Fields Under the Forest — LiDAR Survey
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# LiDAR Survey — Style Prompt

> Real airborne laser points of a real place, floating in the dark as a measured cloud; a scan line or a cutting plane passes through them and the points condense into a solid, raking-lit surface, which is then measured with hairline instruments. One designed camera move carries the whole film: the cloud is something you fly through, not a picture you look at.
> References (grammar only): survey and archaeology lidar visualisations (colour as height, the canopy removed); architectural section drawings (a cut, dimensioned); museum film cadence (one held reading per screen). Copy none of their layouts, ramps, typefaces or music, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The cloud is the data**: every point is a real return at its measured position; points appear, glow, lift away or give way to a surface, but are never moved into a shape.
- **Points become a surface**: a front (scan line, cutting plane) behind which the cloud condenses into a solid model of the same place.
- **Classification is a lever**: ground, vegetation, buildings, water are layers to peel, isolate and recolour.
- **Measurement in hairlines**: one reading at a time, in the accent, attached to what it measures; numbers from the points or an official source.
- **Dark, quiet, exact**: near-black ground, restrained colour, no glow except at the front.

Not Sci-fi Hologram HUD (no invented interface: the points are real, sparse where the survey was), not Satellite Briefing (photographs from above; here a 3D cloud flown through), not Blueprint, not Low-poly Isometric, not Glass Product Render.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Points**: GL points sized in world units (0.12–0.3 m), floor of one output pixel, soft discs, opaque and depth-tested (additive only for a ghost layer); colour from height or class, value from intensity; distance fog.
- **Quantise for the browser**: uint16 positions (2 cm / 1 cm) plus a byte each for height above ground, class, intensity, seed.
- **Height above ground** for every return (minus a ground model triangulated from class-2 returns) drives the colour ramp, the cutting plane and the ruler.
- **The solid surface**: a 0.5–1 m mesh of the ground or surface model, smooth normals, baked short-radius AO, a low raking sun (20–35°), faint contours, crests lightened. Display exaggeration of micro relief (×2–3) only with an on-screen note; measure on undistorted data.
- **The front**: one world-space plane (one uniform) shared by the point and surface shaders; points ahead of it brighten, a thin seam glows behind it and the surface fills in over tens of metres.
- **The cutting plane** (by height above ground): returns above it lift away and fade, a ring glows where it meets the trees, a ruler on the frame edge tracks it.
- **Marks on the surface** (traced features, section lines) are a distance field in the surface shader, kept hairline with `fwidth`; readings, leaders and charts are a 2D overlay through the same world → screen function.
- **A survey window**: outside the measured area the cloud stays as dim points instead of ending in black.
- **Post**: 2× render, high-threshold bloom (only fronts and seams), vignette; no grain (points are already fine detail; encode at a higher CRF).

## 3. Colour logic

- Background near-black with a cold tint; never pure black, never a gradient sky.
- Points: one ramp by height or class, desaturated (deep green-teal → pale; or grey → white); intensity modulates value, not hue. No rainbow elevation ramps.
- The front and seams: one cool near-white; it is light, not a colour.
- The solid surface: warm neutral (stone, clay, plaster), lit; its colour never competes with the accent.
- One accent (amber) reserved for what was found and measured: traced features, the reading, the section line. A second, cooler hue only in a comparison chart.

Example (our demo): background #05080A, canopy #1F3F35 → #5C9A7A → #E2F3DC, ground returns #C8B38C, surface #BDB5A6, front #D4FFF0, accent #FFB347, chart green #83C495.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: light condensed numerals for readings (110–130 px, e.g. Barlow Condensed 300); a monospace for instruments, coordinates, counts and source lines (19–22 px, e.g. IBM Plex Mono); a sans for labels in the film's language (24–36 px, e.g. Noto Sans SC 500). OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset to the characters used.
- **Instruments** in one corner: place, coordinates, area, data source, point count, any exaggeration; they change only when the medium does.
- **Readings** in the right third beside what they measure: label, number, source/method line; a leader when the feature is in frame; a rolling counter reports its landing value.
- **Subtitles**: a transcript strip bottom-left (2 px rule, plate fading right), one line per language measured with the real font, split rather than wrapped; if bilingual, the film's language on top.
- Nothing below 19 px at 1080p. Hold subtitles ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); labels ≥ characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5 s (CJK), letters ÷ 15 + 1.5 s (Latin).

## 5. Motion quality

- On ones, 24 fps; the camera never stops; keys as a C1 spline in target / distance / heading / pitch (no `lookAt` from nadir).
- The front moves on an ease, slowest where the subject is; a cutting plane steps on the beat (eased steps, short holds) so the layers read.
- Points appear behind a front or by height, never by random fade-in across the whole frame.
- Readings land with a small pop; traced features light up along their length in order.
- Never moves: the points relative to each other (no wobble, no noise displacement), the instruments' positions.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Locked nadir with slow push | "this is what a photo shows" | a claim to test; a before; an ending that returns to the map |
| Crane down with tilt to oblique | entering the data; the place has height | the switch from picture to cloud |
| Low oblique close to the cloud (10–20° pitch, 90–150 m) | volume; things standing up | canopy, buildings, a facade, a cliff |
| Slow orbit | studying, the plane doing the work | a peel; a scan; a held reading |
| Rising pull-back | scale reveal of what was found | a network, a site plan, a corridor |
| Lateral track | travelling a feature | a wall, a road, a pipeline, a coast |
| Push to a section | the detail that proves it | a cross-section, a clearance, a height |

Subject ≥ a third of the frame height at key moments; readings right third; instruments in a corner; nothing in the subtitle strip. Transitions are fronts and planes, never crossfades or hard cuts inside the cloud.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Instrument sounds**: FM pings, fine crackle as points arrive, noise sweeps tied to a front, ticks that divide (8ths → 16ths → 32nds) to accelerate, a descending pitched blip per peeled layer, a ratchet while a counter rolls, a ping when a reading lands.
- **Weight and synthesis**: timpani, bass drum, gran cassa for condensations and cuts, a reversed swell into the main impact; low-passed detuned-saw pads; a pulse bass with audible 2nd/3rd harmonics.
- **Dry and wet**: one option is electronics while the subject is still points, and a single organic, wooden or bowed timbre (marimba, bowed vibraphone) for the found features once the surface exists.
- **Beds**: the place's own ambience (wind in leaves, water, traffic) at the start and the end as J- and L-cuts; a thin air bed in between.
- **Silence**: a near silence (air only) before the main reveal; the first sound after it is the impact.
- **Mix**: voice ~10 dB over the music and ducking it; impacts outside the bus compressor; −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1.2 dBTP. Voice: a calm, plain narrator, short declarative lines.

## 8. Native moves

- **Photo to points.** A scan line crosses an aerial photo; behind it the place is points. *Fits content like:* a site visit before a design; what the satellite misses; a quarry's real volume.
- **The canopy peel.** A plane descends by height above ground, returns above it lift away layer by layer, a ruler tracks it. *Fits content like:* archaeology under forest; a hidden trail; flood channels; landslide scars.
- **Points condense.** A front turns the remaining points into a solid surface; found features light up in order. *Fits content like:* a building scan to a BIM shell; a cliff to a hazard model; a street to a vehicle clearance model.
- **The section.** A plane crosses one feature; the profile glows and a dimensioned chart of the real returns hangs beside it. *Fits content like:* a levee's height; a bridge's clearance; a road cut.
- **The window.** The measured area is a stage inside the unmeasured cloud. *Fits content like:* a parcel; a corridor; a site boundary.
- **The regrowth.** The removed layer returns as a ghost over what was found. *Fits content like:* an ending; a clearing before/after; a buried pipe under a street.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Finding data for a new place**: USGS 3DEP (US) as Entwine Point Tiles per project at `https://s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/usgs-lidar-public/<project>/ept.json`, projects and footprints in `boundaries/resources.geojson` of github.com/hobuinc/usgs-lidar; bare-earth scouting through the 3DEP elevation ImageServer. OpenTopography (catalogue of many collections, licence per dataset). AHN (Netherlands, CC0). National portals, e.g. England's Environment Agency LiDAR (OGL), France IGN LiDAR HD (Licence Ouverte), Spain PNOA-LiDAR (CC BY 4.0), Finland NLS (CC BY 4.0), New Zealand LINZ (CC BY 4.0); read each portal's terms. Fetch a subset by box and depth, not whole tiles.
- **Licences**: public domain, CC0, CC BY and attribution-only government licences are fine, with credit in `CREDITS`. ODbL, CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions" (not CC0) or non-commercial terms: name them to the user and ask first. Never commercial scans or Google 3D tiles. Ask the user for their own scans (a site survey, a drone or terrestrial scan, their BIM) when the film is about their asset. Never stand in a generated or invented cloud for real evidence.
- **Facts**: keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method) and deliver it with the film.
- **Coordinates**: EPT copies are often Web Mercator: convert to a local east/north/up frame first; check the vertical datum against known ground.
- **Leaf-off vs leaf-on**: leaf-off lidar reaches the ground but its canopy is sparse; say which season each layer is.
- **Classification is the provider's**: class 1 mixes vegetation, buildings and noise; drop 7 and 18; finish a cut below 0 m or low vegetation stays as stripes.
- **A dense cloud reads as a flat carpet** from afar: go close and low for volume; let the distance fog out.
- **Scan striping** is real texture; don't frame a reveal on it at grazing angles.
- **Traced features are interpretation**: say "traced", keep the tracing in a data file, snap it to the data, leave faint candidates out.
- **Privacy**: crop out houses and yards; keep the survey window on public or uninhabited land.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/film.js`: point shader (front, cutting plane, lift, ghost, window), surface shader (light, AO, contours, feature field, section), photo shader, camera spline (`camAt`), overlay (`reading`, `drawSection`, `subtitles`, readcheck registry).
- `demo/tools/`: `fetch_ept.py` (EPT subset), `terrain.py` (local frame, DTM), `walls.py` (relief model), `trace.py` (snap a tracing, measure), `profile.py` (section from raw returns), `build_data.py` (binaries + facts).
- **Extra packages and packs** (beyond `setup.sh deps voice music`): Python `laspy`, `lazrs` (LAZ decoding), `scikit-image` (relief and ridge tools), `fonttools` + `brotli` (CJK subset). They are not in the library's `.venv`: the agent installs them itself into a private venv in the project folder (the demo uses `demo/assets/raw/.venv`), never into `$LIB/.venv`. Fonts come from github.com/google/fonts (ofl/), fetched by script.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: a building scan. Points coloured by class, a vertical front sweeping the street; behind it a 1 m surface model; one reading (roof height above the street).

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the place and dataset, which classes to peel or keep, the fronts and their directions, the camera route, the readings, the accent within the colour logic, and whether a photo or a map opens the film.

- **Structures**: a corridor flown end to end with three readings; two surveys of one place (erosion, construction) swapped by a front; one object scanned, cut and dimensioned.
- **Openings**: a black frame the scan paints in line by line; a street-level photograph that dissolves into its own returns; a top-down map that tilts up into the cloud.
- **Endings**: the cloud pulls back to show the whole survey tile; the removed layer returns as a ghost; the last reading holds while the points fade to the instruments.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: 21 Keys, Opened — Exploded Teardown
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Exploded Teardown — Style Prompt

> A real product, built from its own engineering files (CAD, PCB layout, bill of materials), lit like a studio packshot and taken apart in front of the camera: the layers lift on one axis, the camera travels between them, every part is named with the numbers its files contain, and it closes again into one object.
> References (grammar only): hardware-launch exploded films (layer stagger, orbit timing), repair-guide teardowns (opening order, the macro on the part that matters), engineering drawing (leaders, dimension lines). Never copy their products, layouts, typefaces or music, or name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A frame reads as this style when:

- **the object is real and exact**: geometry, positions and counts come from the product's own files (STEP, KiCad, BOM, assembly guide). Nothing is eyeballed that a file can give;
- **it is shown apart**: layers float on one axis with even, readable gaps, each still oriented as it sits in the product;
- **it is photographed, not drawn**: physically based materials, a studio key light, a cool rim, an HDRI reflection, soft contact shadow on an invisible floor;
- **the numbers live on the object**: thin leader lines from a dot on the part, dimension lines with ticks drawn in the scene's own perspective, never a table beside it;
- **the camera never stops travelling**: one or a few continuous moves, orbit outside, macro inside.

It is not a glass product render (one object, material beauty, no disassembly), not a blueprint (line drawing on a grid, no light), not a keynote (slides, headline type, a stage), not an assembly manual (step numbers, arrows, hands).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- Real-time PBR (three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial`) at 2× and downsampled, ambient occlusion, a depth of field with one aperture for wide and macro (blur follows 1/focus − 1/z, so it grows as the camera comes close), a high-threshold bloom for emitters only, a vignette.
- Each material keeps its character: plastics with soft sheen (roughness 0.55–0.7), boards with a thin clearcoat and traces as a raised, lighter relief under the mask, metallic pads, tight highlights on machined metal, matte rubber.
- **Boards are painted from their layout files**: copper pours, every trace, via, pad and drill, silkscreen, on both sides, at 14–20 px per millimetre, with roughness, metalness and bump maps from the same drawing. Components stand at their footprint positions with their package sizes.
- Light: a warm key from above front, a cool rectangular rim behind that follows the camera so edges separate from the ground, a soft top light, a low HDRI for reflections; a practical fill only where the camera goes inside.
- Background: a dark graphite seamless sweep (screen-space radial gradient), floor visible only as soft shadow.
- Effects anchored to the world (leaders, dimension lines, glows) are projected from 3D points every frame; only subtitles and title cards live in screen space.

**Where the geometry comes from.** For the user's own product, ask for its STEP / IGES / KiCad / other CAD exports, BOM and spec sheet before anything else. For a public product, look for open hardware (GitHub, GitLab, OSHWA certification list, Hackaday.io, Printables/Thingiverse sources with the original CAD) and component datasheets from the maker. CC0, public domain, CC BY and MIT are fine with credit; CERN-OHL (-P, -W, -S), CC BY-SA, GPL hardware and "no known restrictions" are not the same thing: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. Without files, build only from published dimensions (datasheet, spec page), say on screen or in the voice that it is a model, and show no number you could not source. Never stand in a generated image for the real part.

Keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method for anything measured from the CAD) and deliver it with the film.

## 3. Colour logic

- The product brings its own colours; the frame around it is neutral and dark, so the product is always the brightest, most saturated thing.
- Interface ink is one warm white at two strengths (names at full, specs at about 60 %), plus **one accent** reserved for measured things: dimension lines, label indices and one matching detail on the product itself.
- Values are ordered: ground darkest, product mid to light, labels lightest. Never put text on a busy, bright part without a dark backing.
- Example (our demo): ground #34363a → #0d0e10, ink #f1efe9, accent #ff6b3d.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Names: a clean sans at medium weight in the film's script (28–32 px; Noto Sans SC 500 in our demo). Specs and numbers: a monospaced face (15–22 px; JetBrains Mono) so digits line up and read as measurement. A neutral grotesque (Inter) for Latin running text.
- Label structure is fixed: a two-digit index in the accent, the name, one spec line. Units always written (mm, MB, ×n for counts). A label carries at most one fact the voice does not say.
- Dimension text sits on a small dark plate, follows the line's angle and is never upside down.
- Subtitles: a centred strip at the bottom with a soft shadow and no box; if the film is bilingual, the film's language on top. Hold every cue ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); every label stays fully in frame for CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; everything is smooth and deterministic.
- **Separation**: smooth start, fast middle, long settle (ease-in-out cubed); layers leave top first, 0.15–0.2 s apart; repeated parts (keys, screws) fan out in a wave ordered by distance from a corner.
- **Closing**: bottom first, quicker (about 1 s per layer), the last layer lands with a real mechanical response (a key travels its stroke and returns; nothing bounces like rubber unless it is rubber).
- While held apart, layers may float a millimetre or two with offset phases; during macro shots they hold perfectly still.
- Labels draw in (anchor dot, leader growing, text sliding 10 px) and fade out before the parts move again.
- Never moves: the floor, the light rig's relation to the camera, the label column's x position.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Orbit while layers separate | the whole, its order of assembly | a reveal; a structure overview |
| Grazing macro dolly | touch, material, finish | an opening; a texture |
| Dive between layers | being inside | a hidden component; how it works |
| Slow push on one still part | the part that matters | a chip, a sensor, a seal |
| Rise through the stack | one subsystem to the next | a transition between stops |
| Fast pull back | return, synthesis | a closing; a before/after |
| High three-quarter drift | scale and precision | sizes, pitch, thickness |

- At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height. Labels live in a column on the free side (shift the projection with a view offset rather than moving the object), subtitles in the bottom 12 %.
- Transitions are camera moves through the object itself. No cuts to black, no slide transitions, no split screens.
- The camera path is keyed in the product's own coordinates and interpolated without overshoot (monotone cubic), so a held macro really holds.

## 7. Sound palette

- Instruments: tuned mallets (marimba, vibraphone, glockenspiel, glass), a round bass, a short synthetic kick and small dry percussion. Precise and dry outside the object; sustained and airy inside it.
- Foley is the material: hollow plastic clacks for keycaps or housings, a switch click with a low thock, dry taps for boards, inharmonic rings for small machined metal, a soft thud for the enclosure, airy swooshes for layers lifting and for camera dives, a fine pen hiss when a dimension line draws, a tiny tick per label.
- Every separation and every landing has its sound, panned to where the part is.
- Silence: at least two near-silences (room tone only) before the big separations or the turn back; the first sound after each is the most important hit around it.
- Mix: voice clearly on top (music about 10 dB under it while it speaks), music bus ducked, sub-bass kept lean (20–60 Hz well under the full band), loudness −14 LUFS.
- Voice: calm, close, unhurried, short sentences; numbers spoken as words, written as digits.

## 8. Native moves

- **The wave lift.** Repeated parts rise in a wave across the object. *Fits content like:* battery cells; solar tiles; the drawers of a modular shelf.
- **Inside the gap.** The camera enters the space between two lifted layers to see a hidden face. *Fits content like:* the back of a logic board; the inside of a drone arm; the underside of a sensor module.
- **The leader that lands on the part.** A macro label whose line ends on the component. *Fits content like:* a pressure sensor in a shoe; a gasket in a waterproof case; a motor driver.
- **Dimensions drawn on the thing.** After closing, the real outline gets dimension lines in perspective. *Fits content like:* the thickness of a laptop lid; the footprint of a router; the bore of a valve.
- **One real motion.** A part performs its true mechanical motion once (a press, a hinge, a latch). *Fits content like:* a camera shutter; a buckle; a folding hinge.
- **Lights on inside.** Emitters inside the product switch on while it is apart. *Fits content like:* status LEDs; a backlit display; an indicator ring.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Invented numbers.** A size that no file gives. Fix: measure it from the CAD and say "measured" in the facts file, or leave it out.
- **Mixed-up revisions.** Plates, cases and boards from different versions of a project. Fix: check hole positions and stack heights across the files (they must coincide), and pin the commit.
- **Panelised boards.** Layout files may hold a panel with breakaway tabs. Fix: take the outline from a plate or case of the same revision, or flood-fill from an interior point.
- **Zero-length edges.** Duplicate outline points give zero normals → NaN → black squares after bloom. Fix: clean outlines, repair zero normals, scan frames for one-frame black tiles.
- **Overshooting camera splines.** Catmull-Rom over unevenly spaced keys flies past a macro stop. Fix: monotone interpolation per component.
- **Labels too short.** Macro stops last about three seconds. Fix: one fact per label, opened before the camera settles; check with `readcheck`.
- **Over-bright light sweeps.** Area lights blow plastics to white. Fix: sweeps at a fraction of the key, bloom threshold above the brightest diffuse surface.
- **Brand marks on parts.** Chip tops and connector shells carry trademarks. Fix: plain package tops; drop logo footprints unless the product is the user's own.
- **Crushed blacks.** Black plastics against a black ground disappear. Fix: lift them to a dark grey and let the rim light separate them.

## 10. Engine

All in `demo/src/` (three.js r170, the library's `core/three/post.js` and `core/lib.js`):

- `parts.js`: `keycapGeometry(w, d, h)` (lofted shell with a spherical dish and a stem), `switchGeometries()`, `loft(rings)`, `shapeFrom(outline, holes, circles)` (KiCad outline to extrusion), `inset`, `hexSpacer`, `screwGeometry`.
- `pcbtex.js`: `paintPCB(data, side, outline, box, ppm)` paints colour, roughness/metalness and bump maps from extracted layout data.
- `comps.js`: `buildBackParts(data, group, y, materials)` places package bodies at footprint positions and returns anchors.
- `overlay.js`: anchored labels (`label`), perspective dimension lines (`dimension`), subtitles, title card, readcheck texts, subtitle width check.
- `main.js`: layers, explode and gap functions, the camera keys (orbit or eye/target, monotone), lights, `window.EV` for the mixer.
- `tools/extract_pcb.py`, `kicad_geom.py`, `sexp.py`: read any `.kicad_pcb` (outlines, tracks, zones, pads, silkscreen, footprints; plain Python). `tools/step2mesh.mjs`: STEP to mesh.

**Extra packages and packs**, beyond `setup.sh deps [voice] [music]`: `occt-import-js` (npm, LGPL-2.1, not in the library's package.json) to triangulate STEP files, and the studio HDRI (`sh tools/fetch.sh hdri`). Install the npm package yourself into a private `node_modules` in the project folder (as `tools/fetch_cad.sh` does in a temp folder), never into `$LIB`.

Minimal example, not in the demo: read a plate file with `extract_pcb.py`, extrude `shapeFrom(outline, cutouts)` 1.5 mm as aluminium (`metalness: 1, roughness: .35`) and orbit it with three `CAM` keys.

## 11. Variation space

Decided per film: which product and revision, which layers to separate and in what order, how many stops inside and which parts deserve them, the camera route, whether to open from the whole or from a detail, the product's palette and the accent, the voice.

- **Three structures**: one orbit with two stops; a "how it works" path following a signal or flow through the layers; two revisions taken apart side by side, each held still before a difference is named.
- **Three openings**: a part performing its real motion in macro; the closed product turning in silence on the seamless; a single component floating alone before the rest of the product assembles around it.
- **Three endings**: closed with its dimensions drawn on it; closing into a top view that becomes a technical drawing; apart one last time, frozen, every part labelled like a printable sheet.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: The Map Still Says Sea — Satellite Briefing
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Satellite Briefing — Style Prompt

> Real satellite imagery of a real place, graded down to an analyst's grey, with thin white measurement lines drawn on the ground: a lock-on reticle, outlines, a range line, one reading. One continuous zoom built from stacked imagery plates carries the viewer from orbit to the ground and back, and time can run inside one locked frame.
> References (grammar only): open-source investigation films that annotate satellite pictures (thin lines on imagery, one claim per screen, measuring as the plot); the Eameses' *Powers of Ten* (one continuous change of scale with a readout); NASA Earth Observatory's *World of Change* (one place, time running). Copy none of their layouts, typefaces, icons or music; never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The ground is a photograph**: real, licence-clean, georeferenced satellite or aerial imagery of the actual place. Nothing on the ground is drawn, stylised or generated.
- **Two layers, two truths**: the imagery is what the satellite saw; the hairlines are what the analyst measured. Marks are thin, white, sparse, and sit on real coordinates.
- **The grade moves with the story**: orbit in true colour, the analysis layer in grey, colour back only where the story turns.
- **Scale is the camera**: one zoom from orbit to the ground built from nested plates, with an altitude readout and a scale bar from the same camera.
- **One finding per screen**, in the single accent colour.

Not Data Storytelling (a chart on paper), not Sci-fi Hologram HUD (no glowing wireframes or invented chrome), not Blueprint, not Isometric Infographic (real nadir or oblique views, no diorama), not a keynote (no slides, header bars or chapter numbers).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Plates**: georeferenced rasters with a lon/lat box, sampled in a shader where the camera ray hits the ground, nested by resolution (world → region → detail) with feathered edges so finer plates dissolve in as the camera descends.
- **Globe**: ray–sphere from a perspective camera, a thin atmosphere rim, limb shading at orbit only; compute |C|² − R² in double precision (float32 fails below a few tens of km).
- **Time**: dated plates share one grid. A soft scan front (a satellite pass, never a hairline) swaps them: north → south forward, south → north for a rewind. Growth can run outward from the old edge, ordered by a distance map.
- **The analyst's grade** (one uniform from colour to grey): luminance with local contrast and clarity, a shoulder so salt, snow and cloud stay below white, toned blue-black → cool silver up to ~65 % grey, a fifth of the chroma. White belongs to the marks.
- **Marks**: a 2D overlay through the same world → screen function: hairlines 1.2–2.6 px with a dark halo, dashes for history and claims, brackets, ticks, leader lines. Lines draw on; outlines print behind the scan.
- **Screen space only for instruments** (altitude, scale bar, imagery credit) and the transcript strip. Everything else is anchored to the ground.
- **The claim layer** is a printed map drawn in the shader from a distance field of the old outline: paper grain a few pixels wide at any zoom, halftone ink, coast and waterlines, graticule, the serif name.
- **Post**: light grain in ffmpeg, a vignette, directional blur only on whip pans.

## 3. Colour logic

- Neutral ground: grey, roughly 3–65 % in value. White means *measured*.
- One accent (warm, e.g. amber) for the single reading on screen, never decoration.
- A second hue may mark the **claim** the imagery tests (a map, a plan, a promise): flat, cartographic, never used for anything measured.
- True colour is evidence: at orbit, and again only where the story turns (the field that greened, the water that returned).
- No false-colour ramps over the imagery.

Example (our demo): ground #070B0E → #A1A7A9, marks #F2F5F6, reading #FFBE55, map blue rgb(46, 112, 206).

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a light condensed grotesk for the reading (96–130 px, e.g. Barlow Condensed); a monospace for instruments and dates (20–34 px, e.g. IBM Plex Mono); a sans for labels in the film's language (24–42 px); a serif only for the claim layer and the title. OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset to the characters used.
- **Labels attach to the ground** with a leader line. The reading sits in the right third beside what it measures, label above, source note below ("Landsat, measured").
- **Subtitles are a transcript strip** at the bottom left: a 2 px white rule, a dark plate fading right, left-aligned, each line on one line (measure with the real font, `nowrap`; split a long sentence into two cues). If the film is bilingual, the film's language on top.
- Nothing below 20 px at 1080p, the imagery credit included.
- Hold subtitles ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); a rolling counter reports its landing value; labels stay ≥ characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5 s (CJK).

## 5. Motion quality

- The camera never stops: distance interpolates in log space, segments ease, holds keep a 2–5 % creep or a slow rotation. No frozen frame longer than a second.
- Marks arrive by being made: a line grows, an outline prints behind the scan, a counter rolls and lands with a small pop, a reticle snaps with overshoot.
- Time changes are scans, never dissolves; their spacing tells the speed, and the camera moves with them (accelerating as the steps shorten, braking on the last).
- Never moves: the ground under its annotations, the instrument positions.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Oblique orbit, limb in frame | scale, context, distance | an opening; a return; a title card |
| Dive (log zoom, tilt to nadir) | going to look for yourself | a reveal; checking a claim |
| Locked nadir frame, slow creep | evidence, comparison | time running in one place; a measurement |
| Push-in on a point | singling out | one town, one dam, one field |
| Track along a line | travelling a distance | measuring; a river, a road, a border |
| Whip pan with blur | a new subject at the same altitude | the counter-example; "meanwhile" |
| Climb back to orbit | consequence, perspective | an ending; a summary |

At key moments the subject fills a third of the frame height; reading right, subtitles bottom left, instruments in the corners. Transitions: scan-line swaps, a map layer switched off, zooming through plates, whip pans, the reticle opening into a title card. No crossfades between unrelated places, no hard cuts inside a zoom.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Telemetry**: FM pings (a lock-on ping worth bringing back), dry ticks on the grid that divide to accelerate, noise scans (rising for a rewind, falling forward), servo whines, a ratchet for a range line.
- **Weight**: timpani, bass drum, gran cassa, bowed cymbal, a tam-tam reversed when time runs backwards. Measurements land on a pitched hit.
- **Synthesis**: a pulse bass with audible 2nd and 3rd harmonics, detuned-saw pads under a low-pass, risers for dives.
- **Beds**: orbit hum, radio hiss, data chatter; the place's own ambience (wind, water, a far horn), sparingly, often as J- or L-cuts.
- **One option for the shape**: keep the palette dry (electronics, skins, metal) and let one wet timbre (glass, water, bowed metal) mark the turn.
- **Silence**: music and foley stop, a thin bed stays, impacts may decay into it; the first sound after it is the turn. A short suck-out (0.2–0.45 s, music and foley down ~25 dB) before the heaviest impacts makes them land.
- **Mix**: voice ~10 dB over music; the two or three designed impacts are the loudest moments (out of the bus compressor, with mid-range body, e.g. a low-brass stab); 20–60 Hz about 15 dB under the full band (high-pass ~40 Hz, impact weight at 60–120 Hz); −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1.2 dB. Voice: a calm analyst, short declarative lines.

## 8. Native moves

- **The map against the photograph.** The camera falls into the printed map of the claim; a scanner bar tears it away and the ground is underneath; the name outlives the page. *Fits content like:* a lake still on maps but gone; a cleared concession forest; a planned city never built.
- **Time rings in a locked frame.** Dated plates scan in one by one; each leaves its outline, the band lost between two rings flashes. *Fits content like:* a glacier's retreat; a city's sprawl; a fire scar season after season.
- **The range line.** Mark the destination, grow a ticked line from A to B, chase the tip while the reading counts up, land on the number, pull back to show the whole distance. *Fits content like:* how far a shore moved; a village to its well; a camp to the border.
- **The dive and the climb.** One zoom from orbit to the ground, or back. *Fits content like:* locating anything; a scale reveal; an ending that returns one place to the planet.
- **Colour returns where the story turns.** Only the subject regains true colour inside the grey. *Fits content like:* an irrigated field; a refilled reservoir; a regrown forest.
- **The reticle becomes the frame**: the lock-on brackets open out to frame a title card or the last reading.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Licences**: not usable: Google Earth/Maps, Bing, Esri World Imagery, Mapbox Satellite, Planet, Maxar, news photos, AI-generated imagery. EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless is CC BY 4.0 only for 2016 (2018 onward is NC). Raw Copernicus Sentinel data need "Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data [year]"; check the user's rules. Public domain or free with credit: USGS Landsat (1972 on, worldwide), USGS NAIP (US, ~1 m), NASA Blue Marble, MODIS, VIIRS. Burn a readable credit into the picture and list every asset in `CREDITS`.
- **Finding imagery for a new place**: search by bounding box and date in the Planetary Computer STAC (Landsat C2, Sentinel-2 L2A; no account) or USGS EarthExplorer; MODIS/VIIRS and Blue Marble from NASA GIBS; outlines from Natural Earth. Log every request. OSM (ODbL), CC BY-SA and "no known restrictions" are not CC0: name the terms and ask the user first. Ask for the user's own surveys or GIS layers when the place is theirs. Never fill a gap with generated imagery presented as evidence.
- **Seams**: paths imaged on other days disagree. One date per path, each scene gain-matched on stable land, feathered overlaps, holes filled from the same year only.
- **Old sensors**: Landsat MSS (to 1992) has no blue or SWIR and drops scan lines: nearest-neighbour resampling, near-zero rows as nodata filled from same-year scenes, scan-angle streaks cleaned on land only. Inspect every year at full contrast.
- **Plumes and haze** cross water as bright diagonal bands: swap the scene for another date of the same year rather than painting it out.
- **Edges**: resampling against nodata darkens scene rims (erode the mask); drop contour pieces along a plate border. Real straight edges (dikes, polders) can read as seams: frame them out or label them.
- **Grey mush at close range**: raise local contrast for that altitude only and dim outside the measured corridor.
- **Water and cloud**: MNDWI where shortwave infrared exists, only the basin you measure; clouds read as features in grey, so use the dry season.
- **Facts**: keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method with scene IDs and dates) and deliver it with the film. Measure on the date you show.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/engine.js`: `makeCamera({lat, lon, d, tilt, heading, sx, sy})`, `project()` / `unproject()`, the WebGL2 plate shader (nested plates, time scans, growth map, analyst grade, printed-map layer, whip blur).
- `demo/overlay.js`: hairlines, brackets, `readout`, the measured single-line `subtitle` strip, `text` with a registry for `window.TEXTS`.
- `demo/tools/`: `fetch_landsat.py` (STAC, one date per path, same-year gap fill), `plates.py` (normalisation, streak cleaning, water masks, areas), `vectors.py` (shorelines, distances), `mapfield.py` (the printed map), `growth.py`.
- **Extra packages and packs**: none beyond `setup.sh deps voice` and the sample packs the score uses (`sh tools/fetch.sh instruments <lib>` for vsco2ce, vcsl, freepats in the demo). Imagery uses only the standard library, numpy, SciPy, Pillow (no GDAL); allow 3–4 GB for cached scenes. Anything more (rasterio, pyproj) goes in a private venv in the project folder, not `$LIB/.venv`.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the place or places, whether there is a claim layer, which dates, the structure, the camera path, the accent hue and where colour comes back.

- **Structures**: a locked time-lapse of one place ending in a push-in; a river followed from source to mouth with a reading at each stop; two places compared at one scale with whip pans.
- **Openings**: a ground-level detail that climbs to reveal its scale; a black frame a scan line paints in; an oblique orbit with a searching reticle.
- **Endings**: the climb back to orbit; a last measurement that lands and holds in silence; the claim layer redrawn to match the ground.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: Midnight at the Starlight Hotel — Art Deco
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Art Deco — Style Prompt

> Black lacquer, engraved gold line and airbrushed geometry: a 1930s poster that moves. Every composition has a centre axis, transitions open or close along it, and light arrives as bulbs switching on one by one.
> References (grammar only): **A. M. Cassandre** posters (giant geometry, steep perspective, airbrush inside hard edges); **Chrysler Building / Rockefeller Center ornament** (setbacks, sunbursts, chevrons); **Busby Berkeley** overhead numbers overheads (human kaleidoscopes); **The Great Gatsby (2013) title sequence** (gold line drawing itself on black); **Gershwin-era symphonic jazz** (clarinet, piano, muted trumpet). Never copy a poster layout, a real building, a character, a typeface design or a melody.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A world built from **gold keylines on warm black**, filled with **airbrushed hard-edged volumes** (Cassandre, Lempicka), organised around **one vertical axis**. Ornament *is* the picture: sunbursts are backgrounds, stepped arches are frames, a dial is a progress bar, a bulb marquee is a reveal. Motion is **mechanical and symmetrical**: things unfold from the centre, doors split along the seam, lights switch on in counted order. Native register: glamour with a clock ticking (an event, a deadline, a launch).

Not a gold-foil slideshow (things move and have volume), not Art Nouveau (no whiplash curves, no flowers), not a flat vector poster (volumes are airbrushed and rimmed), not a 60s spy title (no silhouettes on flat colour).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Ground**: warm lacquer black, never neutral grey-black; a night sky may drift toward a deep emerald near the horizon.
- **Gold is a banded metal gradient** (dark – light – hot – light – dark); animate its `sheen` offset for a light sweep.
- **The signature stroke** (`gline`): a dark engraved underline ~1.6 px wider than the line, the gold gradient line, and a hairline highlight on top. Optional glow and a parallel twin (`double`). Nothing gets a black cartoon outline.
- **Volumes**: hard edge + airbrush (`airbrush`): a directional gradient from shade to light inside the shape, one consistent light direction (upper left by default), a thin gold rim on the lit side.
- **Motifs** (sunburst, stepped arch / ziggurat, fish-scale, chevrons, fan, four-point sparkle, speed lines, clock face, dial) are structural (a background, a frame, a transition), not stickers.
- **Perspective is real**: true one-point (mode-7 floors) and two-point perspective through a pinhole camera, so dolly, tilt and pan change perspective instead of scaling flats.
- **Characters are deco too**: about 7 heads tall, tapered streamline bodies, faceted lacquer planes (Lempicka), almond or arc eyes, a one-stroke nose, airbrush + gold rim. Give each lead one or two silhouette marks readable at a quarter of frame height.

## 3. Colour logic

- Three constants: **warm black ground, gold line and metal, ivory** for paper, gloves, light and type.
- **One saturated accent reserved for the protagonist** (or the one object the story follows). It is the only large saturated area, so the eye finds it in any wide shot. A cooler jewel tone may carry secondary surfaces, never competing in area.
- **The one-colour exception**: any single element can be drawn in its own colour through the same fill + keyline + glow (`color` option) while everything else stays gold.
- Always expand hex to six digits in code (three-digit hex breaks colour mixing).
- Examples of the triad (accent / jewel / metal): burgundy / emerald / gold; coral / sapphire / pale gold; jade / plum / rose gold. Our demo's actual values are in DEMO.md.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Type (OFL)**: Limelight (titles), Poiret One (numbers, sign skeletons, plaques), Josefin Sans (subtitles, labels), Italiana (numerals).
- **Titles are architecture**: a stepped gold title bar over an arch or sunburst, optional badge and wings; drawn on in gold, then a sheen sweep.
- **Subtitle card** (`subtitleCard`): a lacquer bar (~88 % black) with stepped ends like the title bar, double gold keyline, Josefin Sans SemiBold ~40–42 px ivory, an optional small speaker icon per voice. It **unfolds from the centre** like every other title, so titles, subtitles and transitions are one system. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- Numbers carry plot without narration: dials, clock faces, floor medallions, badges.

## 5. Motion quality

- **Characters step on twos (12 fps)**; camera, light, bulbs, gold draw-on and sheen run on ones (24 fps). A stepped camera reads as stutter.
- **Everything unfolds from the centre**: a point → a hairline → bars open symmetrically → text rises → wings and sparkle.
- **Draw-on follows the music**: a gold line grows at the speed of the phrase under it and lands on the hit.
- **Bulbs have an ignition overshoot** (~1.6× flash settling in ~0.18 s) and a relay "chunk"; once a sign is lit, a fast chase may run across it.
- **Mechanical easing**: doors, dials and hands move with firm ease-in-out and a small settle, like machinery; nothing floats.
- **Performance beats get anticipation** and escalation in threes (once, twice, mash).
- What never moves: the centre axis of a composition. Symmetry may rotate or open, but it never drifts off-centre.

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric split (two door leaves hinged at the edges; or a revolving-door wipe) | a threshold crossed | a new place; a new chapter; a reveal behind a façade |
| Leaves sliding shut over the live shot | a door closing on a moment | leaving; a decision made; the end of an era |
| Extreme low-angle Cassandre tilt | scale and aspiration | a goal far above; a tower, a rocket, a monument |
| Architectural section (pull out to a cutaway of the whole building) | progress through a structure | climbing, descending, a process in stages; a company's floors |
| Busby Berkeley overhead, mirrored and rotating | people become pattern | a team, a release, a celebration, a system of parts |
| Push-in on a dial, medallion or clock | the number is the plot | a deadline; a count; a milestone |
| Match-cut on shape (circle → circle, ray → ray) | two places, one rhyme | jumping between departments, cities, eras |
| Low oblique along a sign or marquee | light travelling letter by letter | a name revealed; a launch; a score being counted |
| Pull back from detail to skyline | where the moment sits in the world | aftermath; a city-wide effect; scale |

Framing: the centre axis is sacred; an asymmetric frame must resolve to it within the shot. At an emotional peak the protagonist fills ≥ ~1/3 of frame height (smaller, the face reads as a prop in the ornament). Transitions: splits, revolves, arch openings, shape matches; never a generic dissolve or slide.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Symphonic jazz of the 1920s–30s, not a 60s big band.** Options: stride or concert piano, clarinet (trill; a glissando by time-varying resampling of a long note), strings (tremolo, rushes, pizzicato), muted trumpet commentary, trombone and sax section, walking pizz bass, brushes or sticks, tubular bells, harp glissandi, banjo, xylophone runs, celesta.
- Rhythm families to choose from: foxtrot, Charleston, tango, a slow torch-song ballad, a fanfare in the manner of a newsreel.
- **Techniques (options)**: one hit per unit of counted light; accelerate by dividing the beat; plant a theme in fragments so its full statement is a payoff; low-pass a band that is physically far away and open it as we approach; move a period narrator through acoustic spaces (horn, radio, PA, live mic) to make distance audible.
- **Foley by material**: brass clicks, bronze clang + chain, iron treads, marble heels, silver trays, wooden doors + spring twang, paper flutter, knife-switch "chunk" + filament hum, relay ticks, elevator ding, champagne cork.
- **Silence as a tool**: before the most important sound, drop to one small diegetic sound (a clock tick, wind) and cut back in with that sound alone.
- **J/L-cuts** carry architecture: the next room's sound enters a bar before its door opens.
- Mix: duck music ~−9 dB under voice (less under a period announcer who is part of the texture), beds −6 dB, −14 LUFS, light film grain.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **Counted light.** A bulb sign lights one letter per beat or per event, so the audience can count. *Fits content like:* the countdown to a product launch; the letters of a city name lighting as a train arrives; votes tallied into a winner.
- **Threshold doors.** Every scene change is a door split along the seam. *Fits content like:* the departments of a company; the rooms of a museum; stages of a career.
- **Machine kaleidoscope.** People or objects become a mirrored, rotating pattern that locks into a symbol. *Fits content like:* a team becoming a logo; gears of a supply chain; a choir becoming a clock.
- **Dials carry the plot.** A floor indicator, a clock or a gauge moves instead of narration. *Fits content like:* a funding thermometer; the altitude of a climb; a stock ticker at the opening bell.
- **The architectural cutaway.** Pull out until a building is a section and the protagonist a coloured dot with speed lines. *Fits content like:* data moving through a server stack; a letter through a post office; a skier down a resort.
- **Sheen sweep / draw-on.** Light crosses a gold object on a hit; a gold line engraves itself at the speed of a glissando. *Fits content like:* unveiling a trophy; a map route; a signature on a treaty.
- **The one colour.** One element keeps its own colour in a gold world. *Fits content like:* the one product among competitors; the patient among doctors; the new idea in an old firm.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Bulb signs from glyph skeletons break on curves (G, S, R): Zhang–Suen staircase pixels fool a neighbour-count junction test → use the **crossing number** and weld chain ends within ~14 px.
- A generic cartoon character looks pasted in → characters are deco (§2).
- Fish-scale reads as brickwork → lower half-circles row by row, each overlapping the previous row, plus an inner arc.
- Door leaves over a flat "interior" read as a blank frame → draw only the leaves, closing over the live shot.
- A gold point on pure black trips `blackdetect` → lift the background wedges and glow slightly.
- Period loudspeaker distortion is unintelligible under music → gentle drive; whisper-check every line on the final mix.

## 10. Engine

Canvas2D, deterministic in `t`, in `demo/engine/`: `deco.js` (gold gradient, `gline`, `airbrush`, motifs, `drawShape` for any path in the deco manner, `color` for the one-colour exception), `type.js` (title bar, digits, badges, dial, clock, `subtitleCard`), `bulbs.js` (any text → bulb sign, `litSequence`), `cam.js` (pinhole camera, `cardTransform`). `demo/frames.js` renders model sheets and style frames from the real engine. Signatures and a minimal example that draws something not in the demo: DEMO.md "Engine reference".

## 11. Variation space

You decide the structure, the characters (or none), the settings, the opening, the ending, the camera path, the pacing, the accent colour and what gets counted. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **the exhibition** (five pavilions of a world's fair, one idea of the topic behind each door); **the ocean liner** (three decks from engine room to ballroom, a horn per stage); **the trophy night** (nominees as sunburst panels, the winner revealed in light).
- Openings: **the machine room** (gold gears and pistons building to the first beat); **the engraved map** (a gold route crosses a continent before anyone appears); **the telegram** (ticker tape types the premise).
- Endings: **the lights go out** (letters switch off in reverse until one bulb remains); **the dawn** (lacquer black warms to a pale sky); **the poster** (the last shot flattens into a printed poster with a date).

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: Geese at twilight: a continuous thirty-second marsh camera loop
author: loktar00
prompt:
THE SHOT SEQUENCE, one continuous move of about 30 seconds that then repeats seamlessly (the last frame flows straight into the first):
  1. ESTABLISHING: wide and low, just above the water among the cattails, slowly dollying forward through a gap in the reeds as the
  afterglow fills the sky and the first V of geese appears small over the far tree line.
  2. THE APPROACH: a slow crane up and a smooth pan as the lens lengthens, picking up the V in silhouette against the brightest part of the
  sky and tracking it as it comes closer and the birds begin to break formation.
  3. THE LANDING: the camera eases back down to just above the water at a normal lens, side-on to the geese as they cup their wings, drop
  their feet and skid onto the water in a spray, their wakes spreading toward the lens with the reflections of the sky rippling.
  4. THE SETTLE: a slow pull back and rise to a wide view of the whole marsh, the landed geese small on the glowing water, the next skein
  appearing far off, and the camera drifting back into the cattails to the first view as the loop closes.
  As the shots play, the light very slowly deepens toward twilight and then gently returns, so the loop restarts without a jump. Add a
  gentle synthesized ambience with Web Audio if you like (soft wind through the reeds, distant goose calls, a splash as they land); if so,
  show a small, unobtrusive "click for sound" hint and never block the scene behind it.
