title: Hand-drawn educational video remake with layered GPT assets and Opus animation
author: wadezone
model: Claude Opus 5.5 / GPT (image model unspecified) / Codex (model unspecified)
prompt:
补一下这条 5 分 4 秒视频的制作流程，方便想试的朋友参考。

1）先拆原片
抽帧，对照时间轴整理构图、角色、字幕、动作和切点。这次整理成 51 个场景、6 个章节，字幕也做了改写。每个镜头都要说明“谁在干什么、什么时候动、什么时候停”。

2）用 GPT 生成手绘素材
第一版直接用代码画人物，线条和造型太规整，手绘感不够。后来改成让 GPT 生成透明 PNG：人物、器官、道具分别准备，需要躺下、握拳、惊吓等动作，就补对应的姿态和表情图。文字留到组装时单独排版。

3）先做 15 秒样片
先把几个镜头拼起来，检查人物比例、笔触、字体、遮挡和动作节奏。样片看着顺了，再扩展到全片。这一步能早点发现风格问题。

4）把风格写进工程
把确认过的样片作为参考，固定角色素材、裁切位置、图层顺序、颜色、字体、字号和标题栏位置。
这次标题用站酷快乐体，字幕用 Noto Sans SC 真粗体。它们是接近原片的选型，原片的具体字体还没确认。后面新增素材和镜头，都按这套参数检查。

5）让 Opus 5.5 组装完整视频
让 Opus 写 HTML/GSAP 动画，用 HyperFrames 渲染。代码负责位置、遮挡、姿态切换、呼吸、点头、碰撞和字幕时序。
例如床铺、人物、前景被子分层，脸和手要露出来；人物躺下用真正的躺姿素材。按拆好的时间轴逐镜头完成，再导出完整无声版。Codex 负责串起素材准备、比对检查、渲染和必要的修正。

6）加自己的声音和原片音效
用 ElevenLabs 已有的本人克隆音色分段配音，这次生成 40 个单元。通过重录和调整停顿对齐画面。
原片只有混合音轨，用本地 HDemucs 分离非人声底轨，再和新旁白混音。讲话时压低背景，动作空隙保留音效。分离后的底轨可能带着背景音乐和细微残影，并非作者提供的纯音效文件。

7）对照检查，再导出
检查关键帧、切点、字体、字幕、素材边缘和声音时序，用 FFmpeg 合成最终 MP4。配音版保留已经确认的画面，再做解码、时长、响度和同步检查。

这次最有用的经验：先把美术素材和样片定下来，再扩展完整时间轴。GPT 负责手绘素材，Opus 负责动效组装，分开后更容易控制画风。

补充：rev 这次主要用于早期版本代码的静态分析。画面是重新制作的，过程中没有恢复出原作者的 AE 工程。原作作者是画渣花小烙，原片链接在主推文。

title: Measured Blue — Microscope Story
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Microscope Story — Style Prompt

> Real, licence-clean microscopy of a real specimen, seen as it is, and one continuous change of scale that carries the viewer from the glass slide in the hand to a single cell. Focus breathes when the magnification changes, a focal plane sweeps when the camera lands, and every scale bar, field of view and reading comes from the image's own metadata.
> References (grammar only): Charles and Ray Eames' *Powers of Ten* (one continuous change of scale with a readout riding along); premium microscope launch films (dark bench, glass catching light, restrained marks, clean instrument sound); digital-pathology viewers' instruments (scale bar, field of view, magnification). Copy none of their layouts, interfaces, typefaces or music; never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The specimen is a photograph**: a real micrograph or whole-slide scan of the actual sample, CC0, public domain or CC BY. Nothing on the specimen is drawn, retouched or generated. A whole-slide image (WSI) is the ideal source: one sample, one registered pyramid from millimetres to microns, with the pixel size in its metadata.
- **Scale is the camera**: one log-space dive (and, when the story wants it, the climb back) through nested plates of the same sample. The scale bar shortens and jumps in a 1-2-5 sequence, the field-of-view readout rolls, the magnification steps.
- **Focus has a grammar**: a rack-in from soft at the start, a short breath (blur + a hint of field change) each time the magnification changes, a focal-plane sweep across the frame when the camera lands.
- **Readings are measured**: every number is computed from the file (pixel size × pixels) and the screen says how it was measured. Describe what was measured; never diagnose. Keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method) and deliver it with the film.
- **One reading per screen**, in the single accent colour.

Not Satellite Briefing (no grey grade; the stain keeps its colour), not Sci-fi HUD (no glowing wireframes or crosshairs), not Data Storytelling (no chart paper), not a keynote (no slides or header bars).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Plates**: the WSI pyramid levels as plates in one world frame (level-0 pixels), the coarse levels whole and alpha-feathered at the scan edge, the fine levels as crops around where the camera lands. Each frame draws the finest plate that is downsampled no more than ~1.45×, and blends the next level in between 2.2× and 1.45×: no seams and no visible upsampling, because every level is the same sample, already registered.
- **The naked-eye plate**: the scanner's own photo of the whole slide (many WSI files carry one), registered through the scan's area-of-interest metadata and checked against the tissue's centroid. Cut the glass out of the scanner tray, remove the line-sensor streaks, and fill any manufacturer's printed logo with the surrounding frosted glass. Below ~30 mm of field the photo would be upsampled: let the cover glass become clean glass (its dust leaves the focal plane).
- **One grade for every plate**: glass normalised to a warm white, a little density and chroma in the stain, nothing else. No false colour, no film emulation.
- **The bench**: graphite under a slow pool of light; a soft shadow under the slide.
- **Focus**: screen-space Gaussian blur on a frame rendered with a margin (so edges never go dark); the focal sweep is a tilted sharp front crossing a softened frame. A light illumination vignette, nothing more.
- **Marks** in screen space but anchored to the specimen through one world → screen function: hairlines 1.5–2.5 px with a dark or light halo, circles drawn on as arcs with cardinal ticks, dimension lines with end ticks, leader lines with one elbow. Counted pixels are shown as a mask revealed behind a scan front, then kept as a faint trace.
- **Frosted panels** (dark translucent glass over a blurred copy of the frame) for readings, instruments, subtitles and the credit: white type reads on glass and stain alike, nothing switches colour mid-shot.

## 3. Colour logic

- Glass: warm paper white. Bench: graphite. The stain is evidence and keeps its true colour (e.g. trichrome red and blue, H&E pink and purple).
- One accent, cool and away from the stain's hues (mint against red and blue; amber against a green or purple stain), only for the measured reading and the counted pixels.
- Ink on glass is near-black; type on stain sits on a frosted panel in warm white.

Example (our demo): glass #F4F1EC, bench #0B0D0F → #2A3036, ink #181B1F, panel rgba(12,14,17,0.74), accent mint rgb(120,240,205) (on stain) / rgb(0,122,99) (on glass).

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a light condensed grotesk for readings and the scale bar (40–72 px, e.g. Barlow Condensed); a monospace for instruments and pixel counts (20 px, e.g. IBM Plex Mono); a sans in the film's language for labels (20–34 px, e.g. Noto Sans SC); a serif only for the title. OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset.
- **Instruments** live in one frosted panel in a corner: scale bar with its value, field of view, magnification with a small nosepiece glyph that turns a quarter on every change. The source credit in a small panel in the opposite corner.
- **Readings** sit in a frosted panel beside what they measure, joined by a leader: a small label above ("collagen share of tissue area"), the number large in the accent, the method or the raw counts below.
- **Subtitles**: a frosted strip at the bottom; if the film is bilingual, one line per language with the film's language on top, never wrapped. Measure each line with the real font and split long lines into two cues.
- Nothing below 20 px at 1080p. Hold labels ≥ characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5 s (CJK); a reading that rolls is reported by its landing value.

## 5. Motion quality

- The camera is a similarity transform (zoom, roll, position) interpolated as a log spiral between keys (M^u about the fixed point of the two frames), so every push is a true dive towards one point and the roll is part of it. Ease the moves, creep 2–5 % during holds; never a frozen frame longer than a second.
- Magnification changes happen where the plates actually change, each with a breath of focus, a turret click and the new magnification said once, large.
- Marks arrive by being made: a dimension line grows from its centre, a circle is drawn as an arc, a scan front counts pixels while the reading rolls, the reading lands with a small spring.
- Never moves: the specimen under its marks, the instrument positions.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| The dive (log zoom with roll) | going to look for yourself | an opening; from the slide to the cell |
| Locked frame, slow creep | evidence, a measurement | a reading; a comparison |
| Truck at one magnification | a second sample of the same thing | the counter-example; "meanwhile, nearby" |
| Pull back to frame two marks | comparison | the verdict |
| Focal-plane sweep | arriving; depth | a landing; a reveal inside one frame |
| The climb (reverse dive, scale bar jumping back) | consequence, scale | an ending; a return to the eye's scale |

At key moments the measured structure fills a third of the frame height or more; instruments in a corner, subtitles bottom centre, readings beside their marks. Transitions are scale changes, trucks and focus, never cuts or crossfades between samples.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Instrument foley**: the objective turret (a click, a detent, a small metal ring), a focus servo, pen on glass for each line drawn, a band-passed scan travelling left to right with counter ticks that speed up, a soft filtered sweep for the focal plane.
- **Music**: hard-mallet vibraphone in 8ths and 16ths, marimba ticks, bowed vibraphone and water glasses for pads and the motif, glockenspiel for each reading that lands, a pulse bass with 2nd/3rd harmonics, timpani and bass drum under the landings. Harmony stays open and light; the score is the user's to shape.
- **Beds**: a quiet lab room (fan, a little mains hum).
- **Silence** before the verdict and before the climb; the first sound after it is the reading or the turn.
- **Mix**: voice ~10 dB over music, music ducked under it; −14 LUFS. Voice: a calm, exact narrator; numbers spelled out for the TTS, digits on screen.

## 8. Native moves

- **The dive.** From the slide in the hand to a cell in one camera, the turret clicking at each real change of level. *Fits content like:* a biopsy to its cells; a coated surface to its crystals; a hair or skin section to its layers.
- **Counting the colour.** Draw a circle, let a scan front cross it, light up every counted pixel and roll the share up to its landing value; show the raw counts underneath. *Fits content like:* collagen in tissue; porosity in a ceramic; coverage of a coating; pigment in a sample.
- **Two circles, one verdict.** Measure one place, truck to another at the same scale, then frame both and say what differs. *Fits content like:* treated against untreated; edge against centre; before against after.
- **The focal sweep and the ring.** Land, sweep the focal plane across the frame, ring one structure and give its size. *Fits content like:* a nucleus; a grain; a fibre's diameter.
- **The climb back.** Pull out to the eye's scale with the scale bar jumping backwards; a title card written on the glass.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Licences**: most microscopy on the web is CC BY-NC or all rights reserved. Usable: CC0 whole-slide scans (e.g. the OpenSlide test data: check each file's licence line), public-domain government micrographs (NIH, CDC PHIL, NASA, USGS), CC BY collections (Cell Image Library, Wellcome Collection), with every file listed in `CREDITS`. Not usable: CC BY-SA without agreement, NC images, journal figures, AI images.
- **Finding material for a new topic**: search by organ, stain or material plus "whole slide" in the OpenSlide test data, NCI Imaging Data Commons (TCGA/CPTAC slides, licence per collection), the Cell Image Library, Wellcome Collection, Wikimedia Commons (filter by licence) and NIH/CDC galleries; prefer a file whose metadata carries its pixel size. CC BY-SA, ODbL or "no known restrictions" are not CC0: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. For a product, a lab or a brand, ask the user for their own scans (SVS/NDPI/MRXS, SEM TIFFs with a scale) first. Never stand in a generated image for a real specimen.
- **Different samples never zoom into each other**: two micrographs of "the same thing" at two scales are two specimens. Use one pyramid; if you must join sources, cut on a focus breath and say so.
- **Pixel size**: read it from the file (XMP `ScanRes`, TIFF resolution, OME `PhysicalSizeX`); a slide-photo's resolution tag can be trusted only after checking against the scan.
- **Upsampling** shows as mush beyond ~1.6×: end the dive at the scan's real resolution.
- **Tile seams**: some scanners overlap tiles; check the joint info, frame out visible seams.
- **Labels and logos** on the slide: barcodes and IDs are part of the object; manufacturer logos are not — fill or crop them.
- **Claims**: a stain's colour means what the stain protocol says, nothing more; measured shares are of the drawn region and the stated threshold, never a clinical score.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/film.js`: log-spiral camera (`camAt`), plate selection by downsampling ratio and coverage, objective events from real level changes, focus, frosted `panel()`, marks, readings, `TEXTS` / `SUBCHECK` / `EV`.
- `demo/tools/plates.py`: slide-photo registration and cleaning, graded plates, collagen mask and the scan's cumulative curve, the tissue axis. `nucleus.py`: membrane edge on 72 rays, least-squares circle.
- **Extra packages and packs** (beyond `setup.sh deps voice`): `tifffile` + `imagecodecs` read TIFF-based slides (Ventana BIF, Aperio SVS, Hamamatsu NDPI, generic pyramidal TIFF; `demo/tools/plates.py` is written for BIF: its label page, XMP and AOI); MRXS, SCN, VMS and others need `openslide-python` with the OpenSlide library (`brew install openslide`), or an adapter of your own. Install them yourself into a private venv in the project folder, not into `$LIB/.venv`.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: a coated steel sample: one SEM pyramid, a dive to one crack, a circle counting coverage, a ring around one grain.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the specimen, the stain or modality, what is counted, the camera path, the accent, the ending.

- **Structures**: a single dive ending in one measurement; a comparison of two regions or two samples at one scale; a climb that starts on a cell and reveals the object.
- **Openings**: the slide on the bench under moving light; a cell already in focus, the climb revealing what it belongs to; a blurred field racking into focus.
- **Endings**: the title written on the glass; a last reading held in silence; the slide lifted out of frame.

---

title: Clawd Moves In — Living Screencast
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Living Screencast — Style Prompt

> A product walkthrough that looks like a real screen recording, where a low-resolution mascot lives inside a high-resolution interface and acts out what the software is doing.
> References (grammar only):
> - **Screen Studio-style product recordings:** auto-zoom to the cursor, cursor smoothing, click push-ins, and a window floating on wallpaper.
> - **Apple "Guided Tour" videos:** real interface, calm narration, one feature per sentence.
> - **Duolingo and Headspace mascot motion:** squash and stretch, anticipation, a character that performs inside the UI.
> - **The Browser Company (Arc) launch films:** playful tone and fast cutting.
>
> Never copy their characters, UI, music or footage.

A walkthrough of a piece of software, typically 45–75 s. The user gives the product and the features; you decide the story, shots, choreography, sound and music.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

The film looks like a **screen recording of the real product**, but it is not a recording. Every window, menu, diff line and button is **redrawn in 2D (HTML/CSS/SVG)**, so the camera can go anywhere, every pixel is controllable and text stays sharp at any zoom.

A **mascot made of big square pixels** lives in that high-resolution world. The clash of two resolutions, a hard-edged low-res sprite against anti-aliased UI, is the look.

The mascot is the software's agency made visible: when the software reads, it runs along the rows it reads; when it plans, it holds a pixel pencil; when it tests, it stomps the button.

**Two actors, never a hand:** the **cursor** is the user; the **mascot** is the software.

Not a dark tech keynote (no black stage, no invented abstract UI: this is the real product), not a pixel-art game (the world is hi-res vector UI; only the mascot and its props are pixels), not a real capture (nothing is a screenshot).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Real UI, redrawn**: every label, mode name and shortcut matches the real product; no screenshots, no lorem ipsum. Demo content (code, data, test output) is coherent, and the app under test really changes.
- **Pixel grid is sacred**: the mascot, its props (pencil, "!", sparkles, heart, dust) and trails share one square-pixel grid with crisp edges. It scales with the camera; its position snaps to half-pixels, so its motion feels stepped.
- **Gravity = top edges of UI**: the mascot only stands on the top edge of a real element (input box, menu, list row, code line, button, status bar, the letters of a heading). Its position comes from **measuring the live DOM** every frame, never hand-placed coordinates.
- **Window on wallpaper**: the app floats on a desktop with a soft shadow; zoom never shows beyond the monitor.
- **Depth** only where it serves attention: rack focus (blur the pane that doesn't matter), a vignette spotlight. Never blur text the viewer must read.
- **Motion blur** is derived from camera speed and applied as an anisotropic blur on an **untransformed wrapper**, only on whips. Slow moves stay sharp.

## 3. Colour logic

- The product's own interface colours rule: follow its real light and dark themes exactly.
- The mascot keeps the product's or brand's mascot colour, or one saturated hue that no UI element uses, so it finds the eye in any frame.
- Overlays (chapter pill, key HUD, captions) are neutral frosted glass; one accent at most, taken from the product.
- A theme switch can be a story event: the whole film may change state with it.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- UI type follows the product (or licence-free look-alikes such as Inter, JetBrains Mono, a serif for editorial UIs).
- **Information layers only**: a chapter pill (01–04), a KeyCastr-style keystroke HUD, frosted-glass caption pills, an optional "▶▶ 4×" time-lapse tag. Nothing else overlays the screen.
- Captions sit in a pill at the bottom, never over the element being discussed and never under the mascot; hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- A title, if any, is diegetic: it appears as part of the UI (an empty-state heading, a window title, a notification).

## 5. Motion quality

- 30 fps; UI on ones; mascot position stepped to its pixel grid.
- **Mascot acting**: jumps with anticipation crouch, stretch on take-off, tucked legs, landing squash with a damped bounce and dust. Idle breathes (a tiny squash) on the score's beat and blinks irregularly. Walks by leg alternation, flipping the sprite for direction.
- **Eyes carry the acting** (neutral / left / right / up / down / wide / happy / shut / blink): they look at what matters. Arms: down / up (cheer) / wave.
- **Cursor**: smoothed, spring-eased paths, small push on click, never teleports.
- **Cause and effect**: every mascot action triggers a real UI state change; every user action is a cursor move, click or keystroke shown on the HUD.
- UI animates like the real product (its own menus, popovers, diff reveals); don't invent flourishes the product doesn't have.

## 6. Camera grammar

A recording-software camera: one continuous take inside the screen, zoom ≥ 1, cuts only under chapter transitions. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Push-in to the cursor or caret | "this is where it happens" | typing a prompt; choosing a menu item; a setting |
| Slow drift at rest | the app is alive while we listen | a line of narration; waiting for a result |
| Whip-pan between panes (with blur) | cause here, effect there | sending a message → a result appearing; code → preview |
| Push-in + vignette freeze | the one promise to remember | a safety guarantee; a price; an undo |
| Rack focus between panes | attention moves, nothing else does | reading files; logs scrolling while chat waits |
| Pull back to the full window | the whole workflow in view | a summary; parallel tasks; before/after |
| Follow the mascot along a list | the software working through items | scanning results; a checklist; a migration |
| Split-window reframe | two things at once | parallel sessions; compare two versions |

Framing: the thing being discussed and its caption never overlap; the mascot never covers text to be read. Transitions: chapter pill wipes, pixel wipes, a theme reveal circle; never dissolves or screenshots.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Two resolutions in the music**: a hi-fi layer (piano, upright or electric bass, brushed or tight kit, glockenspiel, real samples) is the world; a chiptune square or pulse voice is the mascot. They can trade, duet or merge.
- Options: a low-passed "night" version of the band for a dark theme; a tom fill and crash at chapter seams; dropping the drums to build tension; the mascot's notes on words it lands on; a stereo split for split screens; a single held pad under a freeze.
- **Foley**: keyboard (a thock plus a click, human timing jitter), trackpad clicks, pane swishes, popup pops, notification chimes, CI ticks, a shutter for screenshots. Mascot steps, jumps and landings are 8-bit.
- **Silence**: a short drop to room tone before the key promise makes it land.
- **Voice**: calm, one feature per line; product names verified with whisper. Keep effects off word onsets. Duck music under voice; −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your walkthrough needs.

- **Match-cut origin.** The mascot is born from something already in the UI (a logo's block characters, an icon, a loading spinner) and climbs out, leaving an outline. *Fits content like:* a CLI tool moving into an app; an icon becoming an assistant; a spinner becoming a helper.
- **Diegetic title.** The name appears as a real UI element; the mascot lands on it on a downbeat. *Fits content like:* an empty state; a new-project dialog; a welcome email.
- **Moving floor.** The mascot rides a caret, a popup, a sent message, a progress bar. *Fits content like:* a message flying into a thread; an upload bar; a drag-and-drop.
- **Time-lapse with a tag.** Long work runs at N× with a flashing tag and rack focus. *Fits content like:* indexing a library; a data import; a build.
- **Spotlight freeze.** Push in and vignette the one badge that holds the promise. *Fits content like:* "Saved"; "Encrypted"; "No charges until…".
- **The film changes state.** A toggle's effect escapes the preview and takes over the whole film, and returns later. *Fits content like:* dark mode; a language switch; offline mode.
- **Cell division.** A new session or window splits the screen and the mascot splits with a pixel burst. *Fits content like:* parallel tasks; multiple accounts; team members.
- **Cursor and mascot as characters.** The cursor pets, pokes or drags the mascot, and it reacts. *Fits content like:* approving a suggestion; undoing; onboarding delight.
- **Karaoke-ball words.** The mascot hops from word to word as they are spoken. *Fits content like:* a slogan; a shortcut list; step names.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Invented features or renamed modes → check every button, mode and shortcut against the product's documentation; if it isn't in the docs, it isn't in the film.
- The mascot floats or drifts off its element → measure the DOM every frame, stand only on top edges.
- The mascot covers text or sits under a caption → reserve a text-free lane for it.
- Blur-filter "fake depth" on text you want read, or zooming out past the screen → rack focus only on panes not being read; zoom ≥ 1.
- A hand, arm or finger on screen → the cursor is the user.
- Motion blur applied to a transformed layer smears the pixel sprite wrong → blur an untransformed wrapper, and only on whips.
- A keypress or pop landing on a product name masks it → shift foley off word onsets; re-check with whisper on the final mix.
- TTS mispronounces the product name → try voices and spellings, verify with whisper.

## 10. Engine

In `demo/`: `film.js` (timeline: VO at fixed times, every visual beat hung on a spoken word with `W(id, word)`, camera moves, `Actor` mascot segments, `Cursor`, sound events), `ui.js` (state → HTML for each interface), `clawd.js` (sprite grid, poses, pixel props: replace the sprite with your own mascot), `main.js` (light/dark layers, DOM anchor measurement, motion blur, HUD: captions, keys, pixel wipes, spotlight), `sound.py` (score, foley and VO from `events.json`, with ducking). Build notes: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#build-notes).

## 11. Variation space

You decide the features and their order, the mascot (the product's own, or an original pixel character), the story, the opening, the ending, the camera path, the chapters and the music. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a bug hunt** (the mascot chases one error through logs, code and a fix, a single chapter); **a day of one user** (morning to evening in one app, the theme and music shifting with the hour); **a race** (two windows side by side, old way vs. new way, the mascot winning on the right).
- Openings: **mid-task** (a half-written document; the mascot is already pushing the cursor's selection); **the notification** (a system toast lands; the mascot is inside it); **empty state** (a blank app, a caret blinking; the mascot drops from the menu bar).
- Endings: **the mascot goes to sleep** on the finished item as the window dims; **the app closes** and the mascot is left standing on the dock; **a real share** (the result is sent and the mascot rides it out of frame).

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: Meet Pip — Mid-century Cartoon
author: lemomo-ai
prompt:
# Mid-century Cartoon — Style Prompt

> 1950s flat colour and limited animation for "follow along" films: colour printed a few pixels off its broken ink line, bodies that hold still while hands do the work, abstract colour-block rooms, a calm classroom narrator, and a cool-jazz combo.
> References (grammar only): UPA's early-1950s shorts (*Gerald McBoing-Boing*, *Rooty Toot Toot*): colour and line on separate cels, geometric people, colour-plane backgrounds, limited animation. 1950s classroom films (Coronet, Encyclopaedia Britannica): direct address, one sentence per picture, numbered cards. Charley Harper and Mary Blair: soft atomic-age complements, geometric figures. 1950s appliance manuals: numbered medallions, curved arrows, round call-outs, sunbursts. Copy none of their characters, drawings, lettering or music, and never name them in a film.

A **scene style**: it performs a real use (a set-up guide, a how-to, a recipe card, a safety card) rather than telling a story. The viewer should come away able to do the thing. See §11 for the jobs.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

Flat, printed-looking colour with a thin, breathing ink line that never quite closes. **Every fill is a separate "cel" printed a few px off its line**, re-rolled on twos, so the picture shimmers like hand-registered paint while the camera glides. Light dry-brush tooth, paper grain, warm vignette.

People and things are geometric: egg or bean heads with the nose part of the face outline, simple garments in two or three flat colours, four-finger cartoon gloves. **A presenter's body is a held drawing: only arms, hands, eyes and mouth animate.** Rooms are not drawn: a scene is one colour plane, a floor band, a horizon line with gaps, and one or two props.

Not the 1930s rubber-hose cartoon (no black-and-white, no bouncing world, no hot jazz). Not a whiteboard explainer: it shows *how to do*, not *why*. The pictures are printed, not written on.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Off-register cels**: fill drawn with a small offset (a few px, down-right) from its line; the offset jitters ±1–2 px on twos. Keep it on everything, text included; switch it off only for a crisp diagram.
- **Line**: 3–5 px ink ribbons with ±40 % width breathing and 12–25 % breaks. Characters ~4 px, props 3–4.5 px, walls in plans thicker and broken. Hands: one outline around the union of palm and fingers, thin finger separations.
- **Shading**: one flat darker plane clipped inside a shape, never a gradient. Drop shadows are a copy of the shape offset down-right in a paper shade at ~50 %.
- **Ornaments**: 4-point atomic sparkles, 8–18-point starbursts, sunburst rays (~30 wedges, semi-transparent), boomerang and kidney shapes, polka dots.
- **Grain**: light; print, not film.

## 3. Colour logic

- **A warm paper ground, a warm near-black ink, soft atomic-age complements.** Nothing pure or neon.
- **One ground colour per scene**: a lighter tint for walls, a darker shade for floors. Never place the product on its own colour, never the presenter on their own accent.
- **The product keeps one colour through the whole film**; the accent (a presenter's garment, stars, bullets) is a different hue. Step grounds rotate through the rest.
- Examples: *coral / mustard / turquoise* on cream; *tomato / olive / powder blue* on oatmeal; *plum / lime / sand* on off-white.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Roles: a 1950s script for a kicker (Oleo Script Bold); a slab serif (Alfa Slab One) for titles, numerals and headers, in ink over an offset colour plate; a geometric sans (Jost 500/600) for body, details, labels and captions.
- **Caption card**: a paper-coloured rounded slab with a thin ink border (its colour cel offset too), small turning stars at the ends, ~40 px sans, bottom-centre. Fades in quickly with a small rise. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s, chars/12 + 1 s).
- **Step header**: an ink disc with a paper numeral, a small letter-spaced "STEP n OF N", and the step title with a cream plate; it slides in on twos.
- **Detail tags**: a paper card with a star bullet, popping on the action beat next to the call-out. Data lands on the picture, never as a slide.

## 5. Motion quality

- **On twos:** poses, hand shapes and the cel jitter change at 12 fps. The camera, iris wipes, arrows, plan routes and rays move at 24 fps.
- **Held body, moving hands:** switch poses with a single in-between. A hand action has anticipation (pull back or lift), a fast action (0.15–0.25 s, eased out), a follow-through (recoil, settle, lift away) and lands exactly on a beat.
- **Pop-ins:** medallions, tags, labels and titles scale in with a back-ease (~0.25 s, strong overshoot).
- **Reaching the floor**: a kneel pose with 2-bone IK keeps the hands on the object while it moves; never stretch standing arms.
- **Lettering**: a script writes on left→right with a clip; headers slide in on twos.

## 6. Camera grammar

The camera is "the stand": never handheld. A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Slow push (a few %) | Collecting the eye | a product on its stage; a result settling |
| Iris through a medallion | The number *is* the door | a change of step; a change of rule |
| Round call-out with a leader line | Context and detail at once | a hand action; a screen; a small part |
| Tilt with a pointing finger | The finger leads the frame | the one action that matters most |
| Push into a device, pan along signal rings | Person → interface → device | pairing; connecting |
| Iris from a round object into a top view | Circle to circle, function to plan | a button starting a job; a lid opening; a dial |
| Pull-back with counter-rotation from a detail to a plan | One lane becomes a pattern | a route, a schedule, a garden, a floor plan |
| Colour-block wipe (side, bottom-up) | Turning the manual's page | a tip; a summary; a new card |
| Split frame in two colour blocks | Right vs wrong, before vs after | a safety rule; an upgrade |
| Dead still ≥ 3 s | "This is the frame to screenshot" | a summary; a CTA; a QR code |
| Iris-out onto one object | The last circle | a closing on the product, the logo, the result |

Key subjects ≥ 1/3 frame height and clear of the caption band. Transitions are circles, colour-block wipes and cuts on a beat; no dissolves.

## 7. Sound palette

Three layers, always:
- **Music**: an original West-Coast cool-jazz combo: flute or muted trumpet, vibraphone (chords, arpeggios, glissandi, tremolo), pizzicato walking bass, brushes (sticks on the ride for energy), celesta, bongos or finger snaps. Not ragtime, not a spy big band, not piano and strings. Options: give **every step its own vibraphone chord** and bring them back one per summary item; halve or double the feel instead of changing tempo; move up a step for a payoff.
- **Silence as a tool**: cut *everything*, ambience included, for the beat before the most important action, so the first sound after it (the click, the pour) is the step. Room tone alone before a summary.
- **Foley by material**: cardboard creaks and thumps, appliance plastic knocks and clicks, floor scrapes, glass and ceramic clinks, pours, damped rubber stamps for medallions, paper swishes for wipes, slide whistles for dimension arrows, rising pips for "connected", pen scratches for a route, an iris "shhk".
- **Ambience**: warm room tone (low-passed brown noise, very quiet), a mantel-clock tick on the grid; a device's motor hum can take over when it works.
- **Mix**: J/L cuts (lines start before their iris, tails ring on); narration compressed on top, music ducks ~8 dB, foley unducked, −14 LUFS.
- **Voice**: calm classroom authority, one clause per line ("Step one. Set it against a wall."). Whisper-check every line; accents can blur key nouns.

## 8. Native moves

Each move serves information. A menu: use the ones your film needs.

- **Off-register colour** makes an info card hand-made and warm. *Fits content like:* museum rules; a bank app screen; hotel check-in.
- **Limited animation points the eye**: the still body leaves the hand as the only mover, and the hand *is* the step (one hand action per step, on a beat). *Fits content like:* threading a sewing machine; changing a bike tyre; setting a thermostat.
- **The round call-out** is the close-up; the step's data lands inside or on it on the action beat. *Fits content like:* a dosage on a measuring cup; a torque value on a bolt; a PIN on a keypad.
- **The numbered medallion** marks hierarchy and opens the next step; it stamps onto the outgoing subject and the camera goes through it. *Fits content like:* a pool's five rules; a checklist for a flight; stages of a recycling sort.
- **The payoff turns function into ornament**: a real process (a route, a watering schedule, a seating plan) draws itself region by region and, seen whole, reads as an atomic-age textile. *Fits content like:* a sprinkler's coverage; a delivery round; a week of medication.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- A route that ignores obstacles → follow the product's real rules; flow streamlines bend around obstacles and never cross. Lay it one region per beat, not all at once.
- A separate nose wedge looks glued on → one open spline from the bridge round the skull, closed at the nose tip.
- Thin arms read as sticks from the neck → shoulders at the torso corners, sleeves as a thick ink ribbon with a colour ribbon on top.
- Fat-blob fingers turn the hand into a cloud → stroke every part first, fill second (one union outline), slender fingers with separation lines.
- Zooming the world triples the ink → close-ups in call-out circles drawn at native scale.
- Detail text without reading time → move the data into the detail, the context into the title and the voice; chars/12 + 1 s.
- A transition drawing the next scene before its start → clamp local time to just past the start.

## 10. Engine

`demo/engine/toon.js` (the style: `setClock`, `shape` for any shape in the style, `ink` ribbons, `plane`, two-plate `text`, `fit`, the manual `arrow`, ornaments, the global register `REG`), `demo/engine/chars.js` (presenter, glove hands, the demo product), `demo/engine/icons.js` (18 icons). `demo/film.js` has liftable helpers: `callout()`, `medallionAt()`, `tag()`, `stepHeader()`, the flow-route generator `laneY()` + `buildPath()`, and the transition block (medallion iris, button iris, colour-block wipe, iris-out). API table and a minimal example: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

## 11. Variation space

You decide the thing, the presenter (or none), which steps and in what order, the opening, the ending, the camera path, the colours, the pacing and the music. Use cases are **grammar for the order and duration of information**; build your own timeline from the user's facts.

| Use case | Information order | Hold per layer | Length |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Product set-up guide** | product name → title → step title → step detail on the action beat → payoff → tip → CTA | title ≥ 4 s; step title the whole step; detail ≥ chars/12 + 1 s; summary ≥ 3 s clean | 30–40 s, 2–5 steps |
| **Safety / rules card** | rule number → rule → one "why"; a held figure, a medallion, a gesture, a pictogram per rule | 3–4 s per rule | 20–40 s, 3–6 rules |
| **Recipe or ritual card** | step → quantity/time → result; side view, call-out on the hands, result as a top-view pattern | 3–5 s per step | 30–45 s |
| **Onboarding for an app or service** | screen action → setting value → confirmation stamp; the screen lives in the call-out | 3–4 s per action | 20–30 s |
| **Store or event notice** | headline → time/place → CTA; colour-block wipes between cards | ≥ 3 s per card | 15–25 s |

All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a rules card with no product**, one held figure and a medallion per rule; **a recipe on a tabletop**, seen from the side, ending in a top view; **a do / don't split**, each rule shown twice in two colour blocks.
- Openings: **the finished result first**, then "here's how"; **the problem in one gesture** (a hand fumbling a cable); **a numbered list** stamped on, then opened item by item.
- Endings: **a checklist ticking itself**; **the hands at rest** beside the finished thing; **a QR code** held dead still in a starburst.

Swapping `demo/content.json` and rebuilding is a technical check that the engine re-flows, not a way to make a film.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build, content fields): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

title: Humpback whale breach: a procedural fifteen-second ocean cinematic
author: aGim_asf
model: Claude Opus 5.5 / DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 / MiniMax M3.1 Flash
prompt:
Create a single self-contained HTML file using three.js (CDN import only, no external assets or textures, everything procedural) that plays a 15-second cinematic of a humpback whale breaching in the open ocean at golden hour. Autoplay full-screen at 1920x1080, no interaction.

Timeline:
0–3s: low camera skimming over a vast animated ocean (Gerstner wave shader with foam on crests, sun glint, Fresnel reflections, subsurface teal color), seabirds circling far away.
3–7s: a dark shape rises beneath the surface, the water bulges and whitens.
7–11s: the whale explodes out of the water nearly vertically (long pectoral fins, ventral grooves, barnacle bumps, a natural spine flex), twisting in slow motion while sheets of water and thousands of spray particles fall off it, catching the backlit sun.
11–15s: it crashes back on its side, producing a huge splash, a ring of foam and outward ripples, and lingering mist that drifts across the low sun. The camera slowly pulls back.

Requirements: the whale must look anatomically like a humpback (not a fish or a blob). Use procedural geometry with smooth shading and skeletal-style bending. Use ACES tone mapping, bloom, fog and a warm sky gradient. Water must displace and react where the whale exits and enters. It must run without errors in Chrome. Loop after 15 s.

title: Living orbital garden station above a colorful gas giant
author: loktar00
prompt:

title: Hands 2.0: first-person rigging, layered animation and dynamic grip correction
author: maxt3chno
model: Opus 5.5 / Astra (mentioned by author; exact demo model not established)
prompt:
TASK: Build production-grade first-person arms ("Hands 2.0") for a Three.js browser game, then fix them until every pose actually holds the object it should hold. Do the whole thing yourself with scripts, from generating the model to the in-game checks. I already did this once. Below is what works and the traps I fell into, so you don't repeat them.

━━━ PART 1 — THE MODEL (Blender + MPFB2, fully scripted) ━━━

1. Don't patch AI-generated "statue" arms (Meshy etc.). Chaotic topology with no edge loops at the joints and fingers baked into a pose will crease at every bend. Without clavicle and twist bones the wrist twists like a candy wrapper. Gluing separate generated parts together only adds seams to the same bad mesh. Start over with a real humanoid generator.

2. Use Blender (headless: `blender --background --python tools/hands/*.py`) + MPFB2 (MakeHuman, CC0) and its official asset packs. Put every step in a script so it can be rebuilt:
   - build_body.py: macro params (male, ~30 y/o, wiry and lean: muscle ~0.66, weight ~0.3) plus local arm targets.
   - build_arms.py: game skeleton with clavicle → shoulder → upperarm01/02 → lowerarm01/02 (twist bones!) → wrist → metacarpals → 3 phalanges per finger. Keep skin only from the elbow down and apply subdiv 1. Make the sleeve a separate mesh on the same bones, with real geometry for the rolled cuff. Accessories (watch, bracelet) are parented to forearm/wrist bones; watch hands are bones too.
   - build_tex.py: UVs, then bake veins, tendons and knuckles into geometry and normals. Author every detail in bone-local 3D space so it survives re-UVs, then bake in Cycles.
   - 
http://
export.py → pack script → hands_v2.glb. Budget ~25–40k tris for both arms incl. sleeves (they're huge on screen), 1–2 skin materials + sleeve + accessories. Textures 2048² on High, 1024² on Low, plus a tiling micro-normal for pores.
   - Generate a full body with pants, boots and the same shirt, and save it as a .blend for a future "player body" stage. Don't put it in the game yet.

3. Look: tanned back of hand and forearm, paler palm and inner side. Scars, calluses, short nails with natural cuticles. Flannel sleeves rolled just below the elbow, with a visible inside-out lining on the roll. Tactical watch on the left wrist, cord bracelet on the right.

4. Check skin weights on stress poses before you export: fist, pinch, spread fingers, 90° supination. Fix weights in a script, not by hand.

5. HARD STOP #1: render review shots in Blender (neutral light and warm daylight): front, back, palms, fist, pinch, cylinder grip, spread fingers, sleeve close-up, two plaid colour variants. Wait for my verbal OK. Iterate. Don't integrate anything into the game until I say yes.

6. glTF only gives you standard material slots, so use them as carriers. Example: MR = (R AO, G roughness, B subsurface thickness), emissive = masks (R hair, G dirt accumulation order), clearcoatNormal = pore tile. Document the mapping and read it back in the runtime.

━━━ PART 2 — SHADERS (MeshStandard/Physical + onBeforeCompile) ━━━

- Skin: wrap lighting, back-lit translucency in thin areas (fingers, webbing, knuckles go red against the sun), pore detail normal, micro-sheen, tan gradient by mask.
- Hair: 4 fur shells in ONE instanced draw, only on hairy triangles, visible on the silhouette against the sun. Disabled on Low.
- Dynamic state:
  · wet = max(world wetness, rain when not under a roof), with two layers of droplets. The sleeve goes darker when wet.
  · dirt builds up from game events (gather, pickup, log, fish_land, climb_out…), fingers and palms first through the mask, and washes off in water or rain.
- Arm lighting mirrors the world: shade under roofs, lamp light, lightning.
- Precompile every arm shader behind the loading screen. 
http://
renderer.info.programs.length must not grow during gameplay.
- Budget: the arm overlay may cost at most ~0.3 ms more GPU than before on High. Measure with a timer query before and after, not by feel.

━━━ PART 3 — THE ARM SYSTEM (data, not code) ━━━

Goal: a new item or action (axe, bow, paddle, steering wheel) should be a data entry plus a clip, never new logic.

1. Rig wrapper: bone map, wrist twist spread over the twist bones (e.g. 0.3 / 0.8 on lowerarm01/02). No candy-wrapper wrists.
2. Two-bone IK (shoulder–elbow–wrist) with pole vectors (elbows down and out) and joint limits.
3. grips.js: for each item, per hand: `at / axis / back / r / diag / gap / slide / fingers / thumb` in item space. One hand owns the item, the other IKs to its socket.
4. Fingers are always a joint table `[[mcp, pip, dip, spread, twist] × 5]` (absolute bend) and blend between poses. Autogrip closes the fingers until they touch the handle.
5. Animation layers, in this order: base pose → clip keyframes → IK → procedural (breath, bob, mouse-turn inertia, sway, recoil, fatigue tremor) → additive reactions. Smooth transitions between states.
6. Clips: JSON keyframes in code, plus importing .glb animations (with empty hand_R/hand_L) for future Blender-made actions. Clip events (strike frame, bow release) go onto the effects bus.
7. In-game pose editor (Shift+H, game keeps running, cursor free): sliders for item offset and rotation, sockets, every finger joint, elbow pole, shoulders, layer speeds. Show changes live. "Copy" puts JSON on the clipboard to paste into grips.js. I need to be able to tune a grip without Blender.
8. Keep the old public API as a facade (hands.anim, reach, lampInHand…) so fishing, boat, lamp, weapons, sleep and the seaplane don't need deep rewrites.
9. Port EVERY existing action: rifle (stance, ADS, fire, reload with mag, dry fire), knife (2 strikes), stone throw, fishing rod (cast, fight, reel, fish in hand), carried log, lamp, reach and pickup, plant gathering, inspect, crate, swimming (breaststroke and crawl), boat tiller, hands down while sleeping, hidden arms in vehicles. Each one must be at least as good as before. Delete the old arm code only after everything is ported (keep a backup).
10. HARD STOP #2: in-game screenshots for my approval (idle, rifle, rod, log, lamp at night, wet after swimming, dirty after firewood, under a roof and in full sun).

━━━ PART 4 — THE FIX PASS (bake this in from day one) ━━━

The first version shipped with these bugs. Every one of them came from old poses written for "stump" arms with no shoulder.

ROOT CAUSE: a real arm has a fixed length (shoulder→wrist ≈ 0.48 m in view space). Old poses put wrists at targets the arm can't reach. The solver then "cheated": it pushed the clavicle out (up to 0.32 m) and clamped the wrist rotation. The hand ended up somewhere else, while finger curls were cached for the ideal hand position, so the fingers squeezed thin air.
  - Rifle, left hand: handguard 0.516 m away with a 0.479 m arm → shoulder pushed out ~0.3 m and the fist still sat 3.8 cm below the handguard.
  - Rifle, right hand: wrist rotation clamped by ~21°, palm not seated on the grip.

FIXES, as SYSTEM features:
1. Shoulder stance as data: per item/pose, `stance: { L:[x,y,z], R:[x,y,z] }` with smooth blending, and the elbow pole moves with the shoulder. Rifle: left shoulder forward and in, right shoulder slightly back (a real shooter's torso rotation). The left elbow stays slightly bent and the clavicle doesn't stretch.
2. Elbow auto-swivel: give each forearm a pronation range (e.g. R −100°…+95°, 0 = thumb up). If the requested pole would over-twist the forearm or bend the wrist past its limit, rotate the elbow around the shoulder–wrist line to the nearest valid angle. The old poses were silently over-twisted (+101° on the rifle, +80° on the knife).
3. Grip by the REAL handle shape. A cylinder radius is wrong: the knife handle was a 2.6 × 4.2 cm oval, not Ø2.5 cm, so the knuckles sank 2–6 mm into it.
   - Handle = elliptical cylinder with end caps (`sec` [along back, across], `span`, `inset`).
   - measureSection(item, socket): take the cross-section automatically by slicing the item mesh around `at` along `axis`.
   - CPU-skin the hand (SkinnedMesh.getVertexPosition, palm and phalanx vertices with weights) and test real skin vertices, not phalanx tips.
   - gripFit, cached and computed at startup: first push the palm out until it leaves the handle. Then close each finger with all joints together until first contact, and after that only the joints past the touching phalanx. If the start pose already intersects, open it up.
   - Fingertip targets: `fingers: {1: {to:[x,y,z]}}` puts the index pad on the trigger.
4. Validator: hands.check(pose) and hands.checkAll(). Run every scenario × both hands + the live rod pose, print a console table, and show it live in the Shift+H editor with a "Check all poses" button. RED if wrist miss > 0.5 cm, rotation clamp > 3°, shoulder push > 0.5 cm, twist over the limit > 3°, or any skin vertex deeper than 1.5 mm inside the handle. Don't call the work done until it's all green (mine ended at 122/122).

DATA FIXES that came from my screenshots:
- Rifle: left hand on the WOODEN handguard, not the metal in front of it. Handguard runs diagonally across the palm, thumb along the left side, forearm coming in from the lower-left corner. Right hand fully on the pistol grip using the grip's real rake (axis (0, 0.95, −0.32), not a guessed 40°), index on the trigger. On reload the hand leads and the mag rides in the hand, and the shoulder dips to follow it. Check sprint, recoil, dry fire, and steering a boat while holding the rifle.
- Log: nobody carries a 44 × 7 cm log with two arms like a crate. One hand, an ordinary hammer grip like a bottle: knuckles up, thumb on top, held about a third from the back end, log pointing forward and up from the thumb side, riding in the fist. The throw is a one-handed wind-up and lunge. The left hand stays free, so the lamp stays in it.
- Swimming: fingers together and slightly cupped (no fan), hands in the bottom third of the frame. Crawl recovery comes in from the side, palm facing out. The sleeve never covers the middle of the screen and the palm never faces the camera.
- Fix every pose the validator flags: stone wind-up and throw, aim, lamp, lamp lowered, climbing, reach.

━━━ RULES ━━━
- Backup before each stage. Measure, don't guess: write every claim down as a number (cm, °, ms, tris, programs).
- No performance regression: grip fit is cached per socket, and the validator only runs in the editor or dev builds.
- Write down what's still unfinished honestly in the report (e.g. "right hand mostly below the frame on the rifle", "pinky sometimes curls without contact").
- DONE = I approved the renders and the screenshots, bends are clean on every grip, fingers wrap handles with zero penetrations, wet and dirt work, every old action works on the new system, a new item is one grips.js entry + one clip, and FPS is unchanged.

title: Opus delegates to Haiku: watercolour character motion short

- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
   - Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
   - Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
   - Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
   - Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file
- The key-art process with both image models
- Voice auditions
- Music and sound effects
- The timing map
- The reusable Remotion components
- Every verification loop

---

## Approval gates
1. `facts.json` and the chosen treatment
2. Style bible, character sheets and key poses → **wait for my approval**
3. Audio-only mix and `timing.json`
4. Final film, contact sheet and critique
5. Skill

Keep a task list throughout. At each gate, show me the work, not a description of it.

title: Build the Floor: magnetic-field kinetic spoken-word typography
author: Gdgtify
prompt:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”
Treat this as an original miniature speech staged inside a typographic field. Every line reorganizes the field of the frame. The final declaration must stand on a field that finally lies flat.
Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.
ART DIRECTION
Background #102820. Letterforms # F4E9D5. Field lines and filings # F2B544. A magnetic-monument world: streamlines, flux, stillness at the null. Typography stays crisp; particles are atmosphere only. High-contrast serif for the speech, heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, restrained monospace for flux gauges. No horseshoe magnets, lightning, electron diagrams, or sci-fi arcs.
ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER
“We were told to wait.”
“So we learned the weight of waiting.”
“Then one voice made room.”
“Then another.”
“Now the floor belongs to us.”
Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.
CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
Words have assigned field roles. WAIT is a repelling plate; letterforms lean away from it, kerning compressed. WAITING is field lines sagging under load while filings stream toward the low side. VOICE is one pole reversed; the field reorganizes and letters stand upright along it. ROOM is a null point, a still eye inside the field. FLOOR is the field flattened into a horizontal plane. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms responding to the field, not from illustrations.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00 — “We were told to wait.” The sentence leans away from the WAIT plate; streamlines compress against it. Available space pinches on the plate side; the sentence remains readable, pressed but intact.
3.00–6.50 — “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal in phrase groups. Field lines sag deeper with each phrase. Filings — deterministic, hash-seeded per id and time — drift along the streamlines toward the low side and gather. The WAITING glyph hangs tilted inside the field as a suspended load.
6.50–10.00 — “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters; one pole reverses. The field reorganizes: old streamlines retract by dash-offset while new ones draw in. Letters rotate upright along the new field — analytic rotation of whole glyphs, never path morphing. ROOM opens as a null point, a still eye; the counter of the O in ROOM is its center, and the next composition sits calm inside it.
10.00–12.50 — “Then another.” A second pole turns. The field becomes symmetric; every letter stands vertical. The baseline levels into the first perfect horizontal in the film. Hold absolute stillness for at least 400ms — even the filings pause.
12.50–16.00 — “Now the floor belongs to us.” The field flattens into a horizontal plane. The filings settle onto its surface as hairline grain. The final sentence locks in with the field; US aligns with the strongest flux line. Emphasis through alignment and scale only.
16.00–18.00 — Hold the complete declaration. One streamline pulses gently, then stills. No new text. No decorative motion.
18.00–20.00 — The camera travels along a flux line into the WAIT plate; filings rise as an occluding curtain filling the frame. Under full occlusion, return hidden elements to initial positions. Reveal the exact opening composition.
CHOREOGRAPHY
No dance beat; the field follows phrases, pauses, and emphasis. Phrase reveals follow reading order. Streamlines are precomputed curves revealed by dash-offset; filings are pure functions of (id, t), never simulated. Critically damped settling for the flattened plane. Available still space carries the emotional progression.

title: White Space: cathedral stained-glass light and falling typography blocks
author: AGIOyaZ
prompt:

【Experience】
Without showing a single human figure, let viewers physically feel how a life consumed by efficiency loses its light — and how a single empty space lets a richer light pour back in. The climax should make people hold their breath: a world-class stained glass image of the Virgin and two angels projected across a cathedral floor in blazing color.

【Setting】
- A dim Gothic cathedral interior with one lancet window, 15 m tall and 10 m wide.

【Stained glass quality bar】
Aim for the level of Chartres or Sainte-Chapelle:

- Grisaille painting on the glass: serene faces with painted eyelids, brows and lips; drapery folds with soft shading; every feather painted with a rachis and barbs
- Edge matting so each piece glows brighter at its center
- A deep blue diaper background with ruby rosettes, a jeweled border of alternating colors and pearls
- The Virgin in a ruby niche under a pointed Gothic arch with crockets, columns and capitals, gold rays radiating behind her halo

title: One pencil line: paper, blueprint and hologram showreel
author: heyiamnick
prompt:
<direction>
Build a 30-second looping motion design showreel that introduces CLAUDE, a motion designer.
Concept, in one line: one pencil line gets promoted three times (graphite on paper, wire on a blueprint, light on black) and never leaves the screen.

Every shot is made out of the previous one: shapes, type and colour transform into the next scene. No cuts, no fades.

Typeface: Geist only. Weight 900 for big words, 600 to 800 for small labels (24 to 28 px, tracked 0.14 to 0.3 em).
Palette: paper cream #EDE6D5, blueprint blue #1B3ED2, hologram cyan #45F0DD, plus black #07080A, graphite #16161A and white. Each stage's accent is the next stage's colour: blue pencil on paper, cyan on the blueprint, white on the hologram.
Camera: locked and front-on for the whole film, like a drafting table. Objects turn; the camera never moves.
Empty border: nothing at rest within 150 px of the sides or 90 px of the top and bottom. Things travelling through may cross it.

Three inks. The same geometry is drawn in whichever ink is on screen:
- PAPER: a cream paper background (use my paper image if I give one, otherwise flat cream with fine drawn grain) with a 60 px blue grid at about 13% and every fifth line at 26%. Lines are pencil: resampled and pushed off true by slow sine waves whose phase changes 8 times a second, stroked twice (full width at 90%, half width at 40% with more wobble), with paper tooth knocked out of the strokes, then multiplied onto the paper. Fills are diagonal hatching drawn on one line at a time. Big type is hatching cut to the letter shapes, with a doubled outline.
- BLUEPRINT: flat blue with the same grid in white. Clean white lines 3 to 4 px, hidden edges dashed and thinner, fills are fine clean hatching.
- HOLOGRAM: black with the same grid in cyan. Cyan lines with a white core 30% of the line width. Fills are horizontal scan lines on an 8 px pitch whose thickness follows how lit the surface is. No blur halo anywhere: it reads as light through line density only.

Banned: particle bursts, glows, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split, crossfades, generic gradients, bouncy easing, holds longer than half a second, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 60 beats, 15 bars of 2 seconds. Something happens on every beat. Moves start 0.05 s before their beat so they land on it.
Easing: a critically damped spring, 1 - (1 + w t) e^(-w t) with w between 12 and 40, so nothing ever passes its target; exponential ease-in and ease-out for wipes, presses and exits.
Scene changes: paper to blueprint by a shape that floods the frame with a hard edge; blueprint to hologram and hologram to paper by one horizontal scan line.
The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Two corner labels stay on all film: top left "FIG. 07 — GEAR" (bar number and name), bottom right "BEAT 27 / 60". Bar names: DRAFT, TYPE, CURVE, MORPH, TILE, SOLID, GEAR, PANEL, DATA, LIGHT, WAVE, GLOBE, DRUM, FORM, END.
</structure>
<mascot>

The creative director: a small box character. Body 76 x 54 units with rounded corners, two short arm stubs (24 x 16) at mid height, four straight legs (11 x 33), two tall rounded-rectangle eyes (8 x 14). Draw it about 250 px wide. Its right arm is raised 58 degrees holding a pencil.
On paper: graphite outline with sparse blue hatching and graphite eyes. In the hologram: cyan outline with scan-line fill and white eyes. It is never a fourth colour.
It runs with alternate leg pairs lifting, six steps a second, leaning 7 degrees into the run.
</mascot>
<storyboard>

Bar 1, HOOK, 0-2 s, paper.
Frame 0: CLAUDE in Geist 900, fitted to 1500 px wide, centred, pencil-hatched. INTRODUCING small above it, A MOTION DESIGNER small below. A pencil rail 1620 px wide sits 96 px above the letters. The mascot stands on the rail at x = 1560 with CREATIVE DIRECTOR lettered to its left.

0.0: the small lines un-type; the mascot runs off the right edge, accelerating.

0.36 to 0.5: the rail drops, accelerating, to 26 px below the baseline and presses the letters flat into itself.

1.0: the line rises to the middle, shortens to 1320 px and splits into two rails 140 px apart; 41 blue ruler ticks sweep along the top rail.

1.5: the rails open to 300 px; a blue height dimension draws at the right with a live number.

Bar 2, KINETIC TYPE, 2-4 s, paper. Words sit between the rails and are clipped to that slot; the rails move to fit each word.

2.0: INTRODUCING rises through the baseline letter by letter, then lifts out through the top.

2.5: A MOTION whips in from the left (1400 px in 0.2 s).

3.0: the rails clap shut on it and reopen, stretching DESIGNER out of the line; its letters then fly out sideways.

3.5: CLAUDE in blue pencil, letters dropping from above one every 0.05 s. At 4.0 the rails close and crush it into one line 1476 px long.

Bar 3, CURVES, 4-6 s, paper.

4.1: the line gets pen-tool handles (430 px long at 58 degrees, small squares at the ends, circles on the handle tips, the label EASE) and bends into an S.

4.5: the handles swing to the mirror angle; eight blue copies fan out 34 px apart, joined at both ends like a leaf.

5.0: handles retract; the ribbon becomes travelling sine waves (amplitude 92 px, 2.75 cycles, each line a little out of phase).

5.5: it gathers back into one flat line.

Bar 4, SHAPE MORPH, 6-8 s, paper.

6.1: the line curls into a circle of radius 235 (curvature grows, length stays). 6.5: triangle, turning 120 degrees as it changes. 7.0: square. 7.5: hexagon, point up, radius 270. Blue hatching builds inside, then cross-hatching.

Bar 5, TILING, 8-10 s, paper.

8.0: the hexagon shrinks to radius 96 and six more slide out around it. 8.5: twelve more, a honeycomb of

19. 9.0: dense hatching sweeps across until every cell is solid blue. 9.6 to 10.0: the centre cell's shape grows past the frame with a hard edge; inside it is the blueprint, with the honeycomb in white line.

Bar 6, 2D TO 3D, 10-12 s, blueprint.

10.0: three lines draw inside every hexagon, plus three dashed hidden ones: each is a cube seen corner-on. 

10.5: the eighteen outer cubes slide into the centre one, which grows to radius 270. 11.0: it turns a quarter and perspective switches on. 11.5: it faces front.

Bar 7, MECHANISM, 12-14 s, blueprint.

12.0: the cube flattens and its front square grows teeth: a 16-tooth gear, pitch radius 208. From 12.25 the train steps 45 degrees on every eighth note. 12.5: a 10-tooth gear grows out to the upper right, meshing. 13.0: a 12-tooth gear to the upper left. Each has a dashed pitch circle, a hub and a label (16T, 10T, 12T). 13.5: the small gears retract; the gear becomes a square again and the cube gets its depth back.
Bar 8, UNFOLD, 14-16 s, blueprint.

14.0: the cube unfolds on its hinges into a cross of six squares. 14.5: the squares slide and stretch into six panels: a header strip, a tall sidebar, a wide chart, two tiles, a timeline strip.

15.0: they fill in. Header: "CLAUDE — MOTION REEL", a BARS / RING switch, a LIGHT toggle. Chart: 30 bars, one per second of this film, heights 42 30 36 44 50 46 52 62 50 56 62 72 60 66 58 76 56 62 68 74 70 78 86 94 100 93 97 90 80 50. Timeline: the 15 bar names, a keyframe diamond on each.
15.5: counters roll up: 120 BPM, 60 BEATS, 1800 FRAMES, 0 CUTS.
Bar 9, DATA, 16-18 s, blueprint.

16.0: a graph line draws across the bar tops; a cyan playhead lands on the timeline at the real time. The current second's bar is solid cyan, earlier ones hatched, later ones outlined. A cursor arrives.
16.5: it clicks RING: the chart's baseline bends round into a circle of radius 110 with the bars pointing outward and the beat number in the middle. 17.0: the ring turns once. 17.5: it clicks BARS, the ring straightens, and the cursor goes to LIGHT.
Bar 10, LIGHT ON, 18-20 s, hologram.

18.0: click; the toggle flips and a scan line sweeps top to bottom in half a second, turning blue to black and white to cyan.
18.5: the side panels fold shut; the chart frame falls back as a floor while the bars stay upright and gain depth. 19.0: the floor turns and the columns sort into a rising staircase. 19.5: one ridge line draws across their tops and the columns sink away.
Bar 11, WAVES, 20-22 s, hologram.

20.0: the ridge line multiplies into twelve rows going back, each hiding what is behind it. 20.5: a wave runs across the rows. 21.0: the floor turns and the wave becomes rings from the centre. 21.5: the field closes up into one cube (side 180) rising from the floor, seen corner-on.
Bar 12, GLOBE, 22-24 s, hologram.

22.0: the cube's faces, each a 6 x 6 grid, push out into a globe of radius 205. 22.5: a ripple runs down it. 23.0: it splits into two halves that turn against each other a quarter turn. 23.5: they rejoin and stretch into a long drum, 900 x 220 x 220, facing front and tipped 9 degrees.
Bar 13, DRUM TYPE, 24-26 s, hologram.

The drum carries one word per face in solid cyan: MOTION, DESIGNER, IN CODE. It rolls a quarter turn at 24.5, 25.0 and 25.5. On the last roll it is squeezed back into a cube, turns to a corner view and shrinks by a quarter just before 26.0.
Bar 14, PEAK, 26-28 s, hologram. The strongest moment.

26.0: the cube bursts to side 320, spinning; a ring of type reading "CLAUDE ·" orbits it (radius 430; the far half is mirrored outline, the near half solid).
26.5: it splits into eight cubes; a second ring, "A MOTION DESIGNER ·", crosses the first at radius 520. 27.0: the top layer twists a quarter turn. 27.25: the right layer. 27.5: everything is pressed flat into one line of light.
Bar 15, END TITLE, 28-30 s, hologram to paper.

27.7: the line fans into horizontal scan lines (10 px pitch, 8 px thick). 27.9: the parts outside the letters thin to nothing, leaving CLAUDE. A white band sweeps down through it twice a second.
28.0: INTRODUCING types above. 28.5: the lines swell solid for a moment, A MOTION DESIGNER types below, and the rail draws across above the name.
28.7: the mascot runs in along the rail from the right. 29.0: it stops, raises the pencil, CREATIVE DIRECTOR types beside it; it blinks.
29.5: a scan line runs bottom to top and prints all of it in pencil on paper: frame 0.
</storyboard>
<sound>

Write the soundtrack in code with the Web Audio API (OfflineAudioContext, 48 kHz stereo) and render it to WAV:
- a kick on all 60 beats (sine falling from 165 to 46 Hz);
- a low hit on every bar line, the biggest at 26 s, with a crash at 26 and 28;

http://

title: Continuous product UI loop: chat, music player, rubber-band slider and chart

<direction>
A 22 second square loop, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take. Nothing ever cuts: every scene grows out of the last, and every gesture physically carries the camera into the next world. Every morph glides for 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve, so shapes change so smoothly you barely notice. Content dissolves in the back half of each glide. One gesture per scene.

Banned: hard cuts, bouncy springs, particles, glows, zooming in and straight back out, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's, and the press lands on its drop.
Generate: the cursor clicks, the pill glides into a spinner, then a check.
Chat: the check splits into three typing dots (goo). The left dot flies up into the question bubble and types it, the right one flies down into the reply. Both contract back into dots while gliding in and pour into the middle one.
Play: the middle dot bends into a play triangle, point by point. The cursor presses it on the drop: a white button pops in under the click and the dark app floods out around it, so the leftover white becomes the play button. The camera pulls back to reveal the full now-playing screen: big cover, title, heart (liked, fills green), progress, controls, volume.

Chart: the line lands and bends up into a green chart while the number counts up. The volume knob becomes its last point.
Dive: the cursor clicks that point and the camera dives into it until the light stage fills the frame.
Ending: an "Ask [my product]" button grows out of the light, thins into a line, and the line fans out into my logo (default: the Claude spark, six copies rotating into twelve rays in Claude orange). It folds back into the line, which thickens into Generate. Last frame = first frame.

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. A camera with position and log-space zoom. Scenes live side by side in one world, so a pan really travels.
3. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merges.
4. Floods are circles that grow from whatever caused them to the farthest corner in about 0.4s, and the colour switch happens underneath them.
5. Sound: before the press the song plays through a low-pass filter, like it's in the next room, and opens up to full on the drop. A downloaded Mixkit SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes, 12 on the fast pan. Then scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

A handoff between two drawings only works once the first one has fully landed, or it pops. The cursor must stay on whatever it drags, even while it stretches. A counter or tooltip that changes every frame smears under motion blur, so swap whole values.

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (chat, play, app, drag, chart, logo) before you render.
