title: Interactive Lamborghini FL3 tractor diesel engine
author: exploraX_
prompt:
Build an interactive 3D web page: a live "bench study" of the **Lamborghini FL3**, the air-cooled three-cylinder diesel that powered the Lamborghini 2R tractor (1961 to 1967), from the years before Lamborghini built cars. Visitors should be able to start the engine, rev it, load it, cut it open, watch the cooling air, and take it apart. The page should feel like a beautifully printed technical plate that happens to be alive.

## Hard rules

- **Everything procedural.** No 3D models, no Blender, no textures, no image files, no audio files. Geometry, materials, drawings and sound are all generated in code.
- **three.js (WebGL)**, vendored locally, ES modules with an importmap, no build step. It must run from a plain static server.
- **60 fps** on a recent laptop at 1440x900 and on a retina display.
- **Desktop:** the whole sheet fits a 1440x900 viewport with no scrolling.
- **Phone width:** the sheet becomes a vertical scroll with nothing cut off. On touch, horizontal drags turn the engine and vertical swipes scroll the page.
- **No em dashes** anywhere in the copy.

## The engine: facts

Only these figures are published. Use them exactly:

- 3 cylinders, inline, air-cooled, direct-injection diesel, Lamborghini type FL3
- bore 92 mm, stroke 110 mm, 2,193 cc
- 39 hp (29.1 kW) at 2,200 rpm
- electric starter, Bosch injection
- about 2,000 2Rs sold between 1961 and 1967
- factory colours: orange and light blue ("celeste")

The external layout, from photographs of a restored 1962 2R:

- the engine block painted celeste
- an axial cooling blower in a round housing at the front, belt-driven from the crank, with a wire guard
- a sheet-metal air cowl along the cold side
- individual finned cylinder barrels and finned heads, held down by long studs
- a silver inline injection pump on the hot side, with three copper high-pressure lines up to the injectors
- twin fuel filters
- a black vertical exhaust stack with a silencer and a flapper rain cap
- an oil-bath air cleaner
- a dynamo, a starter motor, and a flywheel with a ring gear

Everything else is an assumption and must be labelled **modelled** on the page:

- compression ratio (about 17:1), rod length, valve timing
- idle (about 700 rpm) and high idle (about 2,350 rpm)
- torque curve, friction, airflow, temperatures, fuel use

Never dimension an assumed size in the drawings.

## Art direction: a 1960s Italian two-ink print

It must not look like a Victorian parchment plate or a generic blueprint. Think of a page from an Italian factory manual or a mid-century industrial catalogue, printed in the tractor's own two inks.

- **Paper:** ivory offset stock (about #EEE9DC) with fine paper grain and soft, uneven ink absorption.
- **Inks:** arancio (#E0561C), celeste (#58AED6 for the print, a deeper #3F9DD0 for the painted engine) and near-black (#1C1B19).
- **Type:**
- Bodoni Moda for display: a huge "FL3" with the 3 in arancio, and an italic "Lamborghini" above it.
- Archivo for labels (wide, letter-spaced small caps).
- IBM Plex Mono for numbers.
- Every label carries its Italian term in small italic Bodoni (for example: Hand throttle *acceleratore*).
- **Print details:**
- registration marks in the four corners and a colour bar in the margin
- a thin double frame and a running head across the top: "Bench study · *banco prova*", "Air-cooled diesel · three cylinders · direct injection", "Sheet 03"
- a giant celeste numeral "3" printed faintly behind the engine, slightly out of register
- **Layout at 1440x900:**
- left column: title, deck, lede and the controls
- centre: the 3D engine
- right column: four live instruments
- bottom strip: four live drawings and a readings card

Copy:
- Kicker: "Lamborghini Trattori · 1961–1967"
- Deck: "Three cylinders. No radiator."
- Lede: "Before the supercars, Lamborghini built tractors. The 2R of 1961 carried this engine: 2,193 cc of direct-injection diesel and no radiator, cooled by a belt-driven blower and cast fins. About 2,000 were sold by 1967, and tractor money paid for the move into cars in 1963."

## The 3D model

Build the FL3 to its real proportions: 92 mm bore, 110 mm stroke, cylinders about 150 mm apart, crank axis as the origin.

Exterior parts:

- crankcase with main-bearing ribs and mounting feet, oil sump, timing case, flywheel plate
- three separate finned barrels, with the fins flattened where neighbours meet
- three finned heads with rocker covers and long studs
- blower with a spinning rotor, stator vanes and a guard
- V-belt around the crank, dynamo and blower pulleys
- air cowl with a stencilled "FL3 · raffreddato ad aria"
- intake runners into the oil-bath air cleaner with a glass pre-cleaner bowl
- exhaust manifold, silencer and a flapper cap that lifts on each exhaust pulse at idle
- injection pump with a governor housing whose throttle lever follows the hand throttle
- copper injector lines and a leak-off line, injectors, twin fuel filters
- starter motor whose pinion slides into the ring gear while cranking
- a small name plate reading "MOTORE DIESEL · FL3 · CV 39 · 2200 g/min" (no company logo anywhere)

Moving internals:

- crankshaft with counterweights, pins 120 degrees apart, turning clockwise seen from the blower end
- connecting rods, pistons with rings and a combustion bowl
- camshaft at half speed with lobes timed to the valve events
- tappets, pushrods, rockers, valves and springs that compress, all driven by the same valve-lift curves the simulation uses

Materials and setting:

- **Materials:** glossy celeste enamel with subtle procedural grain, rougher on castings than on sheet metal. Steel, alloy, copper and heat-darkened exhaust.
- **Stand:** the engine sits on an **arancio test stand**.
- **Lighting and floor:** a soft cast shadow and a contact shadow lands on the paper itself (a transparent canvas over the page).
- **Life at rest:** the engine rocks slightly on its mounts against the gas torque.

## The simulation

Write it as a pure, testable module.

- **Kinematics:**
- exact slider-crank piston motion and rod angle
- four-stroke cycle over 720 degrees, firing order 1-2-3, one firing every 240 degrees
- **In-cylinder pressure:**
- polytropic compression and expansion with a double-Wiebe heat release (fast premixed burn plus a slower diffusion burn), tabulated by fuel level
- calibrate the heat release so that full fuel at 2,200 rpm gives exactly 29.1 kW at the flywheel
- peak pressure lands around 70 to 75 bar at full load
- **Crank dynamics:**
- integrate with sub-steps of about 2 degrees of crank, so the instantaneous gas torque gives real speed ripple at idle and real compression pulses while cranking
- flywheel inertia about 0.8 kg·m²
- **Governor and load:**
- an all-speed mechanical governor with about 120 rpm of droop and a little fuel-rack lag
- the hand throttle sets the governed speed between idle and high idle
- the PTO brake applies a load that rises with the square of speed, so 100% load at 2,200 rpm needs exactly full fuel
- **Starting:**
- the starter cranks at about 250 rpm
- the charge needs a few compressions before it lights, the first cycles misfire and burn rich, and that black smoke leaves the stack
- the engine catches in about 1 second and the starter disengages
- **Stopping:**
- friction rises with speed, plus blower drag rising with the square of speed
- an unfired cylinder gives back less than it took to compress (heat lost to the fins), so the engine stops about 2 seconds after the fuel is cut at idle
- **Temperatures:**
- head temperatures come from about a quarter of the fuel's heat going into the metal, removed by blower air that rises with engine speed
- full load settles around 160 to 175 °C
- run thermal time 30 times faster than real time and say so

The simulation emits events with timestamps: crank, fire, misfire, exhaust valve opening, caught, stop, stalled. Events raised between steps (the key) must not be lost.

## Interaction

- **Ignition key:** a round bakelite-and-steel switch. Click (or Space) to start and stop. It shows Start, Cranking or Stop.
- **Two levers:** the hand throttle shows the governed rpm, and the PTO brake shows a percentage. Style them as notched quadrants with orange lever knobs.
- **Four views** (keys 1 to 4), each with a smooth scripted camera move:
- **Painted.**
- **Cutaway:**
- a section plane through the cylinder axes, with cut faces printed as a light arancio hatch
- parts lying wholly in the removed half (pump, filters, exhaust, starter, pushrods, cam) disappear
- pistons, rods and crank stay whole
- a combustion glow fills each chamber as it fires
- **Airflow:**
- everything except the barrels and heads fades to a paper-grey ghost
- barrels and heads show a temperature ramp from deep celeste to arancio
- particles are drawn in through the blower guard, run along the cowl, cross the fins and leave warm on the pump side
- particles are drawn through the metal like the flow arrows of a technical illustration
- **Exploded:**
- waits until the engine has stopped, then separates the parts along sensible axes and holds the crank still
- each part gets a callout: English name in small caps, Italian term in italic, and a leader line to an orange dot
- labels sit on a paper backing and never overlap
- **Other controls:**
- Slow motion (S) eases time to 1/25
- a Sound toggle
- Reset view
- drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- **Narration line:** a single italic line in the console that reacts to what is happening. Examples:
- "Key turned. The starter pinion meshes with the flywheel and spins the engine at about 250 rpm."
- "Squeezed about 17 to 1, the air gets hot enough to light the diesel. No spark plugs."
- "It caught."
- "Idling near 700 rpm: three power strokes every two turns, one every 240 degrees."
- "The hand throttle sets the governor, which opens the rack until the engine holds that speed."
- "Full PTO load at 2,200 rpm: the rack is wide open and the FL3 makes its rated 39 hp."
- "No water anywhere. The blower pushes air down the cowl, across the fins, and out warm on the pump side."
- "Fuel cut. It runs down and rocks back on its last compression."
- Each view also gets a line of its own.

## Live instruments (Canvas 2D, ink on paper)

1. **Tachometer:** a period Italian dial, 0 to 25 x100 rpm, with an arancio arc above rated speed and an hour meter whose tenths drum rolls.
2. **The cycle:** a 720-degree wheel with three rings (one per cylinder, offset 240 degrees). Power is arancio, exhaust grey, intake celeste, compression hatched. A pointer follows the crank and a dot flashes at each firing.
3. **Indicator diagram:** the live P-V loop for cylinder 1, with the full-load loop dashed for reference, a dot at the current state and the peak pressure labelled.
4. **Chart recorder:** scrolling chart paper with an rpm pen in black and a power pen in arancio.

Below the drawings, a **readings card**:

- live values: speed, power, torque, fuel (l/h), cooling air (m³/min) and head temperature
- marked "live, modelled"
- a footnote listing what is published and stating that the page is an independent study, not affiliated with Lamborghini

Power and torque are measured at the flywheel, so they never overshoot the rated 39 hp during transients.

## Live drawings: blueline prints of the running engine

Front, Right side, Plan and **Section A-A** are real orthographic renders of the same running model, not illustrations. Ink them in a shader like 1960s diazo prints:

- render normals and depth, then draw blue outlines from silhouette, crease and depth edges
- shade with a celeste 45-degree screentone
- print an arancio hatch wherever the section plane cuts metal
- the diazo paper and its faint grid are printed by the shader itself
- add centre lines and numbered cylinders
- Section A-A cuts through cylinder 1 so you see the piston moving. It dimensions only the published bore (Ø 92) and stroke (110), with TDC and BDC lines marked PMS and PMI.

## Sound (Web Audio, synthesised)

- **Exhaust:** each pop is scheduled from the simulation's own exhaust-valve events at the correct sub-frame time. It is not a looped sample.
- **Layers:**
- diesel knock at each injection
- blower roar and a blade-pass tone tracking speed
- valve-gear whirr
- a starter whine that strains on each compression
- a solenoid clunk on start and stop
- the flapper cap ticking at idle
- a soft metallic cue when the engine comes apart and a seating clunk when it goes back together
- **Slow motion** spaces the pops out and deepens them.
- **Mix:** run everything through a compressor. It must never clip.
- **Autoplay:** audio starts on the first user gesture.

## Deliverables

- the page: `index.html`, `css/`, `js/`, with three.js vendored in `vendor/`
- a tiny no-cache static server (`https://serve.py/`)
- a README that separates published facts from modelled ones
- a headless Node check of the simulation that asserts:
- 29.1 kW at 2,200 rpm
- peak pressure 60 to 85 bar
- catches within 3 s
- idles between 650 and 750 rpm
- full load holds about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp
- heads pass 120 °C under load
- it stops after the fuel is cut
- optional: a frame-exact video capture script (virtual time at 60 fps, a drawn cursor with click rings, the sound rendered offline from the simulation's event log so it stays in sync)

## Done means

1. The sheet loads with no console errors and holds 60 fps.
2. Turning the key cranks, catches with a dark puff and settles near 700 rpm.
3. Full throttle plus full PTO load reads about 2,200 rpm and 39 hp, and the P-V loop peaks around 73 bar.
4. Every view works, including Section A-A cutting through the moving piston.
5. The exploded view waits for the engine to stop, and its labels are all readable.
6. Every figure that is not published is labelled as modelled.
7. At 1440x900 nothing overflows, and at phone width nothing is cut off.

title: Alpine lake scene built in code
author: LexnLin
prompt:
Recreate the environment in these 10 reference images in 3D, using only code. No assets, no textures. It's a big environment: a lake with mountains and forest around it.

The task has two parts:
1. Build the 3D environment.
2. Make a cinematic one minute video that showcases the world, and render it.

The environment:
- Make it look 99.9% like the reference images. Don't stop early because you think it's good enough. Iterate until you reach 99.9% similarity. It might take days, I know. There's a lot to do.
- Colors: 100% clean, the best colors. Compare your colors with the colors in the images. Most of the time the colors come out wrong and a bit too grey, and coloring is one of the most important things. Light and shadows have to match too.
- Water: get the water right. The colors, the physics, everything should look perfect.
- Trees: they can't look fake. Give them much better textures and make the forest denser.
- Mountains: better textures and a better vibe.
- Rocks and terrain: good rock textures and a lot more detail in the small stones and the terrain.
- Distance: render everything. Don't render the trees only half of the distance. Trees far away need detail too, also in the half-wide shots.
- In the end it should look like a real place to the human eye.

The video:
- Cinematic, like a drone-filmed movie. That's only a comparison: no drone UI, no drone noises, just a clean video.
- Start with a really good scene and show the best stuff first. Then slowly show more and more: for example, you're behind a rock and can only see a bit, then the camera flies up and you see a really nice view.
- Every six or seven seconds, switch to a different place. Sometimes fast, sometimes slow.
- Sound: calm nature sounds and epic background music. The music has to be really good.
- Output: high resolution and ultra-wide, so you can see the trees on the other side as well. Clean and not buggy. Keep full quality, even if it takes longer.

How to work:
- I don't have a strong GPU, so keep that in mind. You can use my GPU, on CPU it would take a lot of time.
- Work in rounds and send me screenshots after each round, without pausing. If it still needs improvement to reach 99%, start the next round right away.
- Don't start the final video before everything is really good. Send me the screenshots first, wait for my approval, and only then render.
- Don't stop until it's really done and really good.

If you have questions, ask me now. Otherwise, build as long as you can and make it awesome. Go and cook.

title: Code-only three.js temple at dusk
author: leo_xiaolei
prompt:
【段落 1：开工 ＋ 平面图】
我想用 three.js 做一座黄昏时刻的寺庙，最后输出成 70 秒的视频。
规则：不准用任何 3D 模型、贴图或照片，所有东西全用代码生成。
先不要渲染画面，先输出一份场景平面图 ⁠layout.js⁠：定义好主殿、五重塔、拱桥、莲花池、山门的位置和尺寸，单位用“米”。之后所有的代码都只能从这个文件里读取坐标。
太阳定在西南偏西方向、地平线上方约 7 度，打暖色光。
【段落 2：分身施工】
平面图确定后，开启 6 个 Sub-agent（子智能体）并行施工，每个 Agent 负责一个区域：地形、池塘（莲花、锦鲤）、主殿、五重塔、拱桥、树木。
每个 Agent 只能修改自己的文件。
全局材质（朱漆、金箔、青铜、屋瓦、木头）统一写在 ⁠materials.js⁠ 里供大家调用。
随机数一律使用固定种子（固定 Seed），保证每次打开渲染出来的样子一模一样。
（注：这一步记得附上几张高清的寺庙照片，给 AI 作为参考）
【段落 3：镜头调度】
安排 10 个镜头，每个镜头 7 秒。
每个镜头都从一个小物件的特写开始（灯笼、莲花、风铃、佛像面部等），再慢慢拉远露出整个场景。镜头开头先在特写停留片刻，中间加速拉远，结尾放慢缓动。
最后一个镜头，从逆光的枫叶拉远，最后过渡到整座寺庙的全景俯拍（航拍视角）。

title: Explainer video of 9 football rules
author: lukasersil
prompt:
Postav mi video, které vysvětluje pravidla sportu stylem televizní analýzy s AR grafikou. Bez AI video modelů a bez stahování assetů: 3D scénu, postavy, textury, grafiku i zvuk vytvoř kódem. Pracuj samostatně a průběžně mi ukazuj kontrolní snímky.

## Parametry (pro jiný sport změň tuhle sekci a sekci Scénář)
- Sport: fotbal
- Pravidla (9): ofsajd, faul, pokutový kop, vhazování, rohový kop + kop od branky, hra rukou, přímý volný kop, žlutá a červená karta, gól (celý míč za čarou)
- Jazyk všech textů: čeština (plná diakritika, desetinná čárka)
- Délka: cca 68 s (úvod ~4,5 s, každé pravidlo 6 až 8 s, závěr ~4 s)
- Formát: 1920×1080, 30 fps, MP4 (H.264 + AAC)
- Styl postav: PS2 éra ve stylu GTA San Andreas (low-poly tvarované tělo, ručně malované textury)
- Týmy: Červení (červený dres s bílými lemy, bílé trenky), Modří (královsky modrý dres, tmavě modré trenky), rozhodčí černý s limetkovými lemy, brankáři zelený a fialový

## Technologie a pipeline
- Three.js (npm). index.html obsahuje WebGL canvas 1920×1080 a nad ním DOM vrstvu pro HUD.
- Deterministická funkce `window.renderFrame(t)`: stav scény i HUD je čistá funkce času, žádný stav mezi snímky.
- `render.mjs`: lokální statický HTTP server + puppeteer-core se systémovým Chrome (headless, na Macu `--use-angle=metal`). Pro každý snímek zavolej renderFrame(t), počkej 2× requestAnimationFrame, udělej JPEG screenshot a pošli ho rourou do ffmpeg (libx264, CRF 18, yuv420p). Režimy: `stills t1 t2 …` (PNG na kontrolu), `video`, `info` (zapíše časovou osu do out/timeline.json).
- Cesty řeš přes fileURLToPath (složky s mezerami v názvu).
- WebGLRenderer s `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`, ACES tone mapping, PCF soft shadows. EffectComposer s MSAA (samples 4, HalfFloat): RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, vlastní grade pass (vinětace, jemné zrno, chromatická aberace, záblesk, whip blur, VHS efekt), OutputPass.
- Zvuk: Python (numpy + scipy) syntetizuje celý soundtrack do WAV, ffmpeg ho přimíchá (AAC 192k).
- Výstupy: plná kvalita + webová verze (CRF 23 až 24, maxrate 10M).

## Struktura projektu
src/util.js (easing, tmap pro freeze a zpomalení, track() pro pohyb hráčů po časovaných waypointech s fází běhu podle uražené vzdálenosti, seeded rng), src/world.js, src/player.js, src/ar.js, src/hud.js, src/grade.js, src/segments.js, src/main.js, render.mjs, https://audio.py/, PROGRESS.md (průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jak se to pouští, ať se dá navázat po přerušení).

## Svět
- Hřiště 105×68 m. Tráva jako canvas textura (pruhy po 5,25 m, šum, skvrny) + dlaždicová detail textura přes onBeforeCompile. Čáry jako ostrá geometrie, ne textura. Vnější hrana čar = hranice hřiště.
- Branky se sítí (LineSegments), rohové praporky.
- Stadion: dvoupatrová mísa podle superelipsy, dav jako canvas textura lidí v řadách, LED pás mezi patry, střecha s žebry, řady reflektorů na hraně střechy (emisivní, bloom), vnější fasáda s osvětlenými okny, noční obloha, světla města kolem, tmavá zem.
- LED mantinely kolem hřiště s českými nápisy (PRAVIDLA FOTBALU, RESPEKT, FAIR PLAY, ZNEJ PRAVIDLA, #PRAVIDLAFOTBALU), pomalu se posouvají.
- Světla: 4 směrová světla z rohů střechy se stíny (shadow kamera zaostřená na akci daného segmentu), hemisférické světlo, jemná mlha.
- Analytický grade: do všech materiálů světa vlož přes onBeforeCompile sdílený uniform uFreeze (odbarvení do chladné šedozelené + ztmavení). AR materiály ho nemají, takže při zastaveném obrazu zůstanou syté.

## Postavy (styl GTA San Andreas)
- Hierarchický rig: root → body (pánev) → trup → hlava a ramena → lokty, kyčle → kolena → kotníky. Póza = sada úhlů (náklon a rotace trupu, flexe a abdukce ramen, lokty, kyčle, kolena, kotníky, náklon těla, výskok).
- Geometrie: trup jako LatheGeometry (široká ramena, užší pas), zúžené končetiny, klouby jako koule, dlaň s palcem, kopačka s podrážkou a zúženou špičkou, tvarovaná hlava (užší brada), nos, uši, vlasy jako slupka (krátké, objemné, ježek, holá hlava).
- Ručně malované canvas textury: obličej (oči s duhovkou a odleskem, obočí, stín nosu, rty, tváře, strniště nebo vousy, vlasová linie), dres (V-výstřih, boční pruhy, znak, sponzor, jméno a velké číslo na zádech, vrásky látky), rukávy, trenky s číslem, štulpny s pruhy.
- Každý hráč jiný: pleť, vlasy, účes, oči, vousy, barva kopaček, postava. Česká jména na zádech (NOVÁK, DVOŘÁK, RŮŽIČKA…).
- Procedurální běh (fáze z uražené vzdálenosti, ať nohy nekloužou) + knihovna póz: kop (nápřah, úder, dokopnutí), skluz, zakopnutí a pád, vhazování, výskok s paží nad hlavou, zvednutá karta, postoj ve zdi, výskok zdi, robinzonáda brankáře, hlava dolů.
- Zvýraznění: obrysová slupka (inverted hull, tloušťka podle vzdálenosti od kamery), průsvitný hologram „ducha“ pro naznačení restartu, rozsvícení paže.

## AR grafika (additive blending, depthWrite false, kreslí se postupně přes progress)
GroundLine (zářící čára na zemi), Curtain (svislá rovina: ofsajd, branková a postranní čára), GroundRing (prstenec nebo disk s pulzem, čárkováním a výsečí, třeba kruh 9,15 m), Area (vyplněné území s okrajem a skenem), Trail (trubice trajektorie míče), GroundArrow (šipka s běžícími chevrony), Marker (zaměřovač kontaktu), Beam (světelný sloup), ScanGrid (skenovací mřížka), Segment3D (měřicí úsečky), Silhouette (válec obrysu těla).
Barvy: tyrkysová = měření, červená = přestupek, jantarová = míč a území, zelená = platné rozhodnutí.
DŮLEŽITÉ: shadery musí být NaN-safe (clamp UV, žádné pow ze záporného čísla). MSAA na hranách extrapoluje UV a NaN se v bloomu rozleje do černých bloků přes půl obrazu.

## HUD (DOM, styl sportovního přenosu)
- Logo vlevo nahoře „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU / AR ANALÝZA ZÁPASU“ + počítadlo „01 / 09“.
- Vpravo nahoře stav (ŽIVĚ, ZÁZNAM, ZPOMALENĚ ×0,6, STOP · AR, PŘETÁČENÍ ◀◀, KONEC ZÁPASU) a herní čas.
- Lower third vlevo dole: číslo pravidla, název, jednověté vysvětlení, ukazatel postupu z 9 dílků.
- Panel rozhodnutí vpravo dole v barvě rozhodnutí (OFSAJD, PENALTA, GÓL…) s podtitulkem.
- Při zastavení obrazu: záblesk, rohové závorky, štítek „ZASTAVENÝ OBRAZ · AR ANALÝZA“, krátký technický řádek dole.
- AR štítky ukotvené na 3D bod (projekce kamerou) s odkazovou čarou. Drž je v bezpečné zóně (ne pod spodní grafikou, ne pod logem) a nesmí se překrývat.
- Velká grafika karty (žlutá a červená) s důvody, úvodní titulek, závěr „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ s mřížkou 9 pravidel, stinger přechod (šikmé pruhy navy, tyrkysová, bílá + logo) na každém střihu.
- Čitelnost: minimální velikosti (název pravidla 66 px, popis 29 px, štítek 33 px + podtitulek 21 px, technický řádek 22 px). Text vždy na tmavém podkladu, krátké texty. Line-height aspoň 1,05, aby diakritika (Ž, Č, Ř) nebyla oříznutá. Titulky neodhaluj maskou, vypadá to jako ořez: použij fade + rozostření + lehký zoom.
- Fonty: systémové s českou diakritikou (na macOS DIN Condensed + Avenir Next Condensed). Pokrytí znaků ověř předem přes fc-query.

## Scénář (vnitřní časy segmentů, natažení na čtení viz další sekce)
Úvod (3,5 s): dron sjíždí z noční oblohy přes střechu do stadionu na široký záběr středu hřiště. Skenovací mřížka přejede hřiště, pod hráči naskočí kroužky, štítek „MÍČ SLEDOVÁN“. Titulek „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU“, nad ním „TV ANALÝZA PRAVIDEL“, pod ním „9 KLÍČOVÝCH PRAVIDEL · AR ANALÝZA“.
1. Ofsajd: televizní kamera, Červený #8 přihrává, zastavení v okamžiku přihrávky. Kamera se přesune do osy ofsajdové linie. Tyrkysová rovina u nejzazší části těla předposledního obránce (Modrý #4), červená u předsunutého kolena útočníka (Červený #9), měření „+1,59 m“ (spočítej z kloubů, paže se nepočítají). Rozhodnutí OFSAJD: nepřímý volný kop, Modří.
2. Faul: záznam ×0,6 nízko u trávníku. Modrý #10 vede míč, Červený #6 jde skluzem zezadu do kotníku. Zastavení v okamžiku kontaktu: zaměřovač „KONTAKT“, „MÍSTO FAULU“ (kruh + sloup), šipka dráhy skluzu, červený obrys. Kamera obkrouží, pak pád. FAUL: přímý volný kop.
3. Penalta: Červený #9 ve vápně, Modrý #3 ho podrazí. Zastavení, jeřáb nahoru. Zvýraznění pokutového území, oblouk z místa faulu na pokutovou značku s drátěným míčem, „11 m“. PENALTA.
4. Vhazování: přihrávka Červeného #2 přejede postranní čáru (trajektorie se kreslí živě). Zastavení až ve chvíli, kdy je celý míč venku, střih na kameru za čarou. Červená rovina, „+15 cm“, „CELÝ MÍČ VENKU“, „POSLEDNÍ DOTEK · ČERVENÝ #2“, modrá šipka do hřiště a hologram modrého hráče s míčem nad hlavou. VHAZOVÁNÍ (Modří).
5. Roh + kop od branky: střela Červeného #10 tečovaná Modrým #4 za brankovou čáru → ROHOVÝ KOP. Pak efekt přetáčení (VHS) a stejná střela bez teče → KOP OD BRANKY (zvýrazněné brankové území).
6. Hra rukou: střela, Modrý #5 ve výskoku s paží nad ramenem, míč do předloktí. Paže zčervená, ramenní linie, čára paže „ÚHEL PAŽE 135°“, průsvitný válec „OBRYS TĚLA“. RUKA: přímý volný kop.
7. Volný kop: zeď na 8,00 m „ZEĎ MOC BLÍZKO“, nakreslí se kruh 9,15 m, zeď ustoupí, číslo naběhne na 9,15 m a zezelená. Kamera za exekutora, zahraný oblouk přes zeď zpomaleně, zastavení „PŘES ZEĎ“. PŘÍMÝ VOLNÝ KOP.
8. Karty: detail rozhodčího se žlutou kartou proti hráči se svěšenou hlavou + velká grafika ŽLUTÁ KARTA / NAPOMENUTÍ se 3 důvody. Střih, červená karta, vyloučený odchází + ČERVENÁ KARTA / VYLOUČENÍ.
9. Gól: střela, brankář vyrazí, míč padá na čáru. Kamera u brankové čáry. První zastavení: polovina míče na čáře, červená rovina, „−11 cm“, „ZATÍM NENÍ GÓL“. Míč se dokutálí. Druhé zastavení: celý míč za čarou, rovina zezelená, „+3 cm“, blesky foťáků v hledišti. GÓL.
Závěr (2,5 s): kamera stoupá nad hřiště (návrat k úvodnímu záběru), mřížka, „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ + mřížka 9 pravidel, stmívačka.

Každé zastavení obrazu: krátký záblesk, odbarvení scény, kamera se dál pomalu hýbe kolem zmrazených hráčů, AR prvky naskakují postupně. Mezi segmenty vždy stinger.

## Čas na čtení
Akce (běh, kopy, skluzy) běží ve skutečné rychlosti. Analytické části každého segmentu natáhni 1,5× až 2,1× přes warp funkci (výstupní čas → vnitřní čas segmentu), aby každé pravidlo bylo na obrazovce 6 až 8 s a všechny texty se daly v klidu přečíst. `node render.mjs info` exportuje výslednou časovou osu do out/timeline.json.

## Zvuk (procedurální, https://audio.py/)
120 BPM broadcast groove (kopák, virbl, hi-haty, basa se sidechainem, arpeggio, pad), riser v úvodu, závěrečný akord. Při zastaveném obrazu hudba ztlumená low-passem. Dav (filtrovaný šum s vlněním, řev při gólu), whoosh + boom na každém střihu, kovový úder na každém zastavení, krátké „razítko“ při rozhodnutí, píšťalka, kopy do míče, zvuk přetáčení. Časy všech zvuků načti z out/timeline.json, ať sedí na obraz i po změně délky. Cílová hlasitost kolem −14 LUFS.

## Postup práce a kontrola
1. Nejdřív rozjeď pipeline (server, render, ffmpeg) s jednou scénou a ověř, že WebGL v headless Chrome běží.
2. Po každé změně vyrenderuj kontrolní snímky v klíčových časech a prohlédni je, včetně výřezů na 100 % kvůli textu a diakritice.
3. Celé video kontroluj přes kontaktní listy (ffmpeg filtr tile) a snímky kolem přechodů.
4. Hotové video ověř dekódováním (`ffmpeg -v error -i video.mp4 -f null -`) a délku a stopy přes ffprobe.
5. Do PROGRESS.md průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jakými příkazy se to pouští.

title: Kinetic Lyric Video
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second kinetic lyric video for an original song, every word landing on a 120 BPM beat.

<inputs>
Artist: Odile Varga. Song: "A World Asleep". Lyrics, one line per bar: "Hold the city lights" / "like they're ours to keep" / "we were wide awake" / "in a world asleep". Hero word per line: LIGHTS, OURS, AWAKE, ASLEEP. Tempo: 120 BPM. Duration: 10s. If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Beat grid: a beat is 0.5s and a bar 2.0s; after a half-second pickup, bar n starts at 0.5 + (n − 1) × 2.0s. Every word lands exactly on a beat or an eighth. Default word times, in beats from the start of the line's bar: line 1: Hold 0, the 0.5, city 1, LIGHTS 2. Line 2: like 0, they're 0.5, OURS 1, to 2.5, keep 3. Line 3: we 0, were 0.5, wide 1, AWAKE 2. Line 4: in 0, a 0.5, world 1, ASLEEP 2.
Palette: ground #17111D, type #F4EEE4, and one accent per line, used only on its hero word: amber #FFB020, coral #FF5A5F, aqua #2FD9C9, lilac #B49BFF. During each line the ground mixes in 7% of that line's accent, switching on the downbeat.
Type: two families in hard contrast. Content words in Anybody (variable, wdth 50–150, wght 100–900), uppercase: hero words at weight 900 and width 150, sized 1100–1500px wide and at most 300px tall, leading 0.86; other content words at weight 700, width 90, 120–160px. Small words (the, they're, to, we, were, in, a) in Fraunces italic 400, 72px, lowercase, tucked onto a content word's baseline or cap line.
Layout: each line builds as a flush-left stack from x 200, kept vertically centered; nothing within 120px of an edge.
Motion: scale, stack, slide. A word lands by scaling from 1.35 to 1.0 in 0.18s on cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.9, 0.1, 1). Each new row pushes the rows above it up over 0.2s on cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1). A hero word also sweeps its width from 50 to 150 over 0.3s as it lands. On every beat the current hero word kicks to scale 1.03 and back in 0.12s. On the next bar's downbeat the whole stack slides up and off in 0.25s on cubic-bezier(0.7, 0, 0.84, 0) as the next line's first word lands: no crossfades. Behind each hero word, a copy at 3× scale and 6% opacity, cropped by the frame, drifts at half speed for depth.
Premium is every word on the beat and a hierarchy that tells you which word to sing loudest. Cheap is every word popping the same way, centered, in one weight.
Banned: centered stacks, equalizer bars, waveforms, particles, glow, gradient text, typewriter reveals, elastic or bounce easing, emoji, flashing more than 3 times per second.
</direction>

<structure>
0.0–0.5s: pickup: the ground fades up from black; nothing else.
0.5–2.5s: line 1 builds on its beats; LIGHTS lands in amber at 1.5s.
2.5–4.5s: line 2 takes over on the downbeat; OURS lands in coral at 3.0s.
4.5–6.5s: line 3; AWAKE lands in aqua at 5.5s.
6.5–8.5s: line 4; ASLEEP lands in lilac at 7.5s.
8.5–8.8s: outro on the downbeat: the line-4 stack slides up 140px and the beat kick stops; beneath it the song title rises 16px into place in Fraunces italic 44px, with "ODILE VARGA" in Anybody 700, width 100, 28px, tracked 0.12em.
8.8–10.0s: hold, still.
For other durations or tempos, recompute every time from the BPM, fit whole bars, and keep at least 1.2s of final hold.
</structure>

<build>
One self-contained index.html, CSS and JS inline. The stage is 1920×1080 (16:9), scaled to fit the window. Design for 60fps. window.seek(t), t in seconds, must compute every visual from t alone, clamping past the end to the last frame: no CSS transitions or animations, no setTimeout or setInterval, no state carried between frames, and randomness only from a seeded PRNG. Anything cumulative is precomputed once at load at a fixed step or solved analytically, so seek can jump to any time. Load Google Fonts via <link> and await document.fonts.load() for each face before defining window.seek. Without ?render in the URL, drive seek from requestAnimationFrame so it plays in a browser (loop after a 1s end hold); with ?render, don't start that loop.
Engine: HTML/CSS. DOM text with transform, font-size and font-variation-settings set in seek; request Anybody's wdth and wght axis ranges in the css2 URL. No canvas or three.js.
</build>

<check>
Before showing me, step through one frame per second (0–10s): screenshot each and look at it. Fix overlaps, clipped or cramped text, accidental edge collisions, and anything off-style or Banned. Check that each word's landing frame matches its beat time, hero words stay within 1500px and clear of the edges, small words sit on a shared baseline or cap line, and each accent appears only on its line's hero word. Confirm seek(10) and seek(11) match, so the final frame holds.
</check>

title: Podcast Audiogram
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second podcast audiogram: cover art, a live waveform and word-by-word captions.

<inputs>
Show: Kettle Hours. Episode: "Ep. 42 · Why bread takes its time". Guest: Hana Ostrow, baker. Quote, in three phrases: "Most of baking is waiting." / "You mix it, then you leave it alone," / "and the dough does the work." Clip position: 12:41 of 48:03. Duration: 10s. If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Palette: ground forest #14271F, card #1B3329, cream #F3EAD8, apricot #F2A65A, sage #8FAF97 for secondary text.
Type: Young Serif 400 for the show name (54px) and on the cover; Figtree for everything else: captions 64px 700, line height 1.15; episode line 28px 500; guest line 24px 500 in sage. Timestamps in IBM Plex Mono 500, 22px.
Layout: a 1680×840 card, radius 28px, centered on the ground (x 120–1800, y 120–960). Left, the cover: 600×600 at x 200, y 240, radius 16px. Right column, x 880–1720: the show name at y 210 with the episode and guest lines beneath; captions in a two-line block at y 400–560; the waveform strip at y 620–780; at y 860 a 44px round play-pause button, then the progress track to x 1720, with timestamps under its ends.
Cover art, drawn in code: an apricot ground, a big cream circle like a loaf seen from above with three diagonal score cuts in forest green, a faint seeded flour speckle, and "KETTLE HOURS" in Young Serif at its lower left.
The signal: a synthetic speech envelope built from the quote. Phrase windows: 0.90–2.60s, 2.95–5.40s, 5.75–8.20s. Inside each, words get time in proportion to their syllables, with 0.06s gaps and 0.22s after the comma. Each syllable is a raised-cosine bump of seeded height 0.55–1.0 over a 0.05 breath floor, with fine texture from seeded value noise at 30Hz. Captions and waveform read the same timing table, so peaks sit under spoken words and pauses show as low bars.
Waveform: 84 bars, 6px wide with 4px gaps and rounded caps, mirrored about the strip's centerline. It scrolls left at 100px/s with "now" at the right end: bar positions shift by (100t mod 10)px and each bar's height is the envelope at its own moment. Bars are cream; the newest 12 are apricot.
Captions: one phrase at a time, flush left. Spoken words in cream, upcoming words in cream at 35%, and the current word on an apricot pill (radius 10px, 8px side padding) in forest. title: 30-second AI-made short drama
author: AI_DVD6
prompt:
你现在不是普通小说作者。

你是一名同时懂：

* 中文短剧编剧
* 短视频留存机制
* AI 视频制作
* 低成本内容生产
* 商业化内容设计

的短剧主创。

我要做一个公开实验：

**挑战：一个人能不能依靠 Opus 5.5 + AI 视频工具，把一句故事创意做成一部真正有人愿意看完的 30～40 秒短剧。**

这个实验最终会公开：

* 完整制作过程
* 最终成片
* 总耗时
* AI 工具成本
* 人工参与程度

所以你的任务不是展示文学水平，而是帮我设计一个：

**好看、低成本、容易用 AI 做出来、适合中文社交媒体传播的商业短剧 Demo。**

## 一、制作硬限制

请严格遵守：

* 成片目标：30～40 秒
* 最佳目标：约 35 秒
* 主要人物：最多 2 人
* 次要人物：尽量没有
* 场景：优先 1 个，最多 2 个
* 总镜头：6～8 个
* 单镜头尽量 3～6 秒
* 开头 3 秒必须出现冲突、异常或强信息
* 避免复杂群众场面
* 避免追车、打斗、大规模动作戏
* 避免大量需要精准口型的长对白
* 避免频繁换服装、年龄、发型
* 避免复杂手部动作和物体交互
* 避免需要大量环境变化的剧情
* 尽量让主要人物在大部分镜头中保持同一套服装
* 尽量让大部分剧情发生在同一空间
* 故事必须适合 AI 图片 / AI 视频生成
* 优先提高人物、服装、场景的一致性
* 最终必须可以由一个人完成

## 二、内容目标

目标观众是中文互联网普通成年人。

故事必须同时满足：

1. 前 3 秒就出现明显冲突、异常或利益损失；
2. 8 秒内让观众明白“为什么我要继续看”；
3. 中途至少有一次信息升级；
4. 最后 8～10 秒出现明显反转、揭晓或情绪释放；
5. 不需要复杂背景知识也能看懂；
6. 看完以后最好会让人产生评论欲；
7. 题材优先靠近成年人真实欲望：

* 钱
* 工作
* 阶层
* 婚恋
* 面子
* 逆袭
* 欺骗
* 省钱
* 人性反转
8. 不要写成 AI 科技故事。AI 只是幕后制作工具，不是剧情主题。
9. 不要依赖旁白解释剧情，尽量让人物行为和短对白推动故事。
10. 不要为了反转故意写得不合常理。

## 三、特别考虑“商业短剧”

这不是文学比赛。

请优先考虑这种结构：

**一个非常容易理解的人物处境**
→
**迅速制造不公平、误会、羞辱、损失或欲望**
→
**冲突进一步升级**
→
**最后反转**

例如可以借鉴但不要机械照搬：

* 大家以为最穷的人其实……
* 看起来占便宜的人最后……
* 一个不起眼的决定让局面完全逆转
* 被轻视的人掌握了其他人不知道的信息
* 一个人为了省一笔小钱，最后付出更大代价
* 看似普通的陌生人，真实身份完全不同

不要使用已经被拍烂的：

* 霸道总裁亮身份
* 富豪装穷打脸
* 服务员其实是老板
* 穷小子突然继承百亿资产

除非你能给出明显不同的新意。

## 四、特别考虑 AI 制作成本

每个故事都要主动压低后期生成成本。

优先选择：

* 1 个固定室内场景
* 2 个固定人物
* 少走动
* 少复杂动作
* 少道具
* 少换镜头环境
* 少大幅度表情变化
* 少精准口型要求
* 可以通过特写、反应镜头、手机画面、账单、短信、文件等低成本视觉信息推动剧情

如果一个创意虽然好看，但需要很多人物、地点、动作或复杂镜头，请主动淘汰。

## 五、你第一阶段只做“选故事”

先不要写完整剧本，也不要写分镜 Prompt。

请先提出 **5 个完全不同的短剧创意**。

每个创意必须包含：

### 1. 一句话故事

用 20～40 字说清楚。

### 2. 开头 3 秒

具体发生什么。

### 3. 核心冲突

为什么观众会继续看。

### 4. 中途升级

大约在第 12～20 秒发生什么新信息。

### 5. 最终反转

最后 8～10 秒揭晓什么。

### 6. 为什么适合 AI 制作

从以下角度说明：

* 人物数量
* 场景数量
* 动作复杂度
* 人物一致性
* 背景一致性
* 口型难度

### 7. 商业潜力

这个题材以后可以延伸成什么：

* 短剧账号
* 剧情广告
* 小说改编
* 商业客户 Demo
* 系列内容
* 低成本样片
等。

### 8. 制作难度

1～5 星。

### 9. 预计 AI 视频镜头数

目标控制在 6～8 个。

### 10. 最大制作风险

例如：

* 人物一致性
* 动作生成
* 口型
* 道具交互
* 反转难以视觉化
等。

## 六、最后帮我做选择

在 5 个方案之后，请从以下 5 个角度比较：

* 最容易让普通观众看完
* 最容易用 AI 做好
* 最容易压低制作成本
* 最容易在 30～40 秒内讲清楚
* 最适合拿来证明“一人短剧工作流”

然后选出你认为最适合作为第一次实验的 **1 个方案**。

不要只告诉我“它最好”。

请明确说明：

* 为什么它比另外 4 个更适合第一次实验
* 它最大的剧情风险是什么
* 它最大的 AI 制作风险是什么
* 如果成片失败，最可能失败在哪一步

如果五个方案都不够好，请直接推翻重做，不要为了完成任务硬选。

## 七、输出文件

请在当前项目中创建：

`01_story_candidates.md`

把全部内容写进去。

先停在这里。

不要继续写：

* 完整剧本
* 分镜
* 图片 Prompt
* 视频 Prompt
* 配音方案

等我审核故事以后，再进入下一阶段。

title: Beat-synced manga-style music edit
author: aimikoda
prompt:
Turn the attached footage into a beat-synced, manga-style music edit and send me the finished MP4.

INPUTS (fill in or leave blank; if blank, choose sensibly and tell me what you chose)
- Source footage: [attached]
- Music: [attached track / use the source audio]
- Aspect ratio: [default 4:3 1440x1080; 9:16 1080x1920 for vertical], 24 fps
- On-screen text / credit: [optional]
- Palette: [default: paper #f8f2ea, ink #141012, main accent red #d0141e (shadow #7c0a12), highlight yellow #ffd60a (shadow #f29a00)]

GOAL
The edit should feel like a living manga page: ink lines, screentone, flat accent colours, bold graphic backgrounds, and hard cuts locked to the music. It must look designed, not like a filter over video.

1. STUDY THE MATERIAL
- Go through the footage frame by frame using contact sheets. Catalogue every usable moment: framing, pose, motion peaks, internal cuts, and strong details (eyes, hands, silhouettes, close-ups, crash zooms).
- Analyse the music: BPM, beat grid, downbeats, phrases, sections, energy curve, accents, fills, ending.

2. LOCK THE LOOK (applies to every shot)
- Mask the subject on every frame (rembg isnet-anime for anime or illustration, a human-segmentation model for live action). Check mask quality before relying on it.
- Ink lines via XDoG/DoG, with thickness scaled to the framing.
- Paper base. Mid-tones become halftone dots: fixed screen angle, area-correct radius. The deepest shadows become solid ink.
- Strict palette: paper + ink + one main accent + one highlight.
- Map the subject's most distinctive colour to the flat main accent.
- Map glowing or brightest elements to the highlight.
- Everything else stays monochrome.
- Tune tones per shot so faces read clean (mostly paper, light screentone).
- Give subject cut-outs a thin ink outline when composited over graphics.

3. DESIGN YOUR OWN SHOT VOCABULARY
Based on what this footage does well and what this music needs, define 6-10 recurring shot types. Each type pairs a kind of source framing with a graphic treatment. Draw from this palette or invent your own:
- extreme close-up of a detail with impact shake
- silhouette over a bold graphic (concentric rings, rays, burst)
- clean black-and-white manga panel with a lightened background
- subject cut-out over a graphic ground (halftone texture, printed-page texture, blobs, speed lines, flat colour)
- typographic panel (large vertical CJK or bold type, plus small secondary lines; all text original)
- impact marks (!!, stars, sparkles)
- black or flash frames
- glitch frames (channel split, slice offset, magenta/yellow)
- tinted frames (pink, red, mono)
- halftone-dissolve transitions
- punch-ins and crash zooms
Rules:
- Every type must use something the footage genuinely does well.
- Save the strongest images for the strongest musical moments.
- Briefly justify each type.

4. PLAN A FRAME-ACCURATE EDL BEFORE RENDERING
List start/end frame, shot type, source frames, framing, motion, transition and text for every shot. Rhythm rules:
- Cut 1-2 frames before the beat.
- Mix durations: 3-6 frame hits against 1-2 beat holds, with at least one breathing moment per phrase.
- Build a recognisable 8-beat (or phrase-length) pattern and repeat it, using different source footage each time.
- Let the energy follow the music:
- a calm intro (for example desaturated, with only the highlight in colour)
- dense peaks
- an outro where colour drains, glitches escalate, and the edit fades with the music
- Land gestures and motion peaks in the footage on musical accents.

5. MOTION AND FINISH
- Animate the subject on twos. Keep camera moves (zoom, drift, rotation) smooth on every frame.
- Use shake and scale bumps on hits, with subtle film grain.
- An optional small HUD element (for example a timecode box) is fine.

6. PREVIEW, FIX, RENDER, VERIFY
- Before the full render, render one frame per shot as a preview sheet. Fix composition, mask errors, text cut-offs and palette breaks.
- Render, then review the whole output on contact sheets, fix problems and re-render the affected frames.
- Encode H.264 at CRF ~20-22 with AAC 192k, synced to the music at the same length.

QUALITY BAR
- Every frame could pass as a printed panel.
- No muddy greys, no unmasked background smears, and no accidentally cropped text.
- Dot size stays consistent.
- Outside glitch frames, no more than two colours appear besides paper and ink.

DELIVER
The MP4, plus a short summary of the shot types you invented and where they land in the edit.

title: Vault Street pixel-art bank heist diorama
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single-file, original pixel-art diorama called "Vault Street": a toy-like bank job on a floating isometric town block, rendered with three.js (r160) at low resolution and upscaled with a post shader (depth outlines, OKLab quantisation to a fixed 64-colour palette, optional Bayer dither, a "Raw 3D" toggle). Orthographic camera, drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, whole-pixel snapping. No weapons anywhere: cartoon robbers in striped shirts, beanies and eye masks.

World: a two-lane loop road (Main St / South St) with curbs, sidewalks, zebra crossings and a parking bay cut into the far side of South St. Inside the block: a columned bank ("ACORN SAVINGS") with a dome, a counter with three teller windows behind glass, a rope line, a manager's desk and a round vault door that rolls aside on a track; everything above knee height is one lid that lifts off while the gang are inside (Auto / Off / On). Also a diner and a park with a fountain. North of Main St: a police station with a beacon, a radio mast, a flag and a three-bay lot (two black-and-white cruisers with red/blue light bars, one impound bay), plus a donut shop with a giant donut on the roof and a hardware store. Street lamps with real lights at night, an alarm bell on a post by the bank, trees, a bus shelter. Day / dusk / night; rain with puddle reflections.

Story loop: a brown sedan waits in the bay → two robbers cross and go in → staff and customers put their hands up → one goes behind the counter and opens the vault → a teller trips the alarm (bell rings, station beacon turns) → four officers run to the cruisers; Car 21 heads for the bank, Car 22 goes the other way and turns across both lanes of Main St → robbers run out with "$" sacks, the sedan pulls out and flees round the block with banknotes fluttering from the boot, Car 21 in pursuit → the sedan stops at the roadblock; hands up, or one runs for the park and gets a flying tackle → cuffs, escorted to the station, the loot carried back through the bank's back door → the cruisers back into the lot, the sedan towed into the impound bay → later the gang make bail and drive back to the bay.

Traffic and people: civilian cars keep their distance (people crossing included), pull over for sirens and give up after a while if nothing passes; cruisers go out over the line to pass. Cars wait at a line while anyone reverses out of or pulls into the lot, and lot moves wait for an empty street. Passers-by walk the sidewalks, step round lamps, wait for cars crossing and sometimes use the bank. No deadlocks, no overlapping vehicles.

UI (English): a lit scoreboard (HEISTS · clock + status · ARRESTS, "LOOT RECOVERED $"), a rail with Time & weather, Bank roof, Units (Car 21, Car 22, Brown sedan, the bank with live status; "Start a heist", Pause, "Heists happen on their own"), a Radio log, View controls; click the bank to start a heist; a "How it's drawn" note. title: Animated robot story across 12 art styles
author: pradeepXkapoor
prompt:
[Y]ou are the director, animator, rigger, compositor, sound designer and render engineer for a 45–50 second animated short made entirely in code. The bar is "this looks like a real studio short and goes viral on X." Treat this as a multi-session production. Do not rush to a final render. Work in milestones, render stills constantly, look at them, criticize them honestly, and fix them.

0. The film in one line

Pip, a tiny, curious scrap-built robot, is happily rolling through his world when it starts regenerating around him. He slowly realizes someone is prompting his reality. The prompts get more absurd, he finally climbs onto the floating prompt box and types "let me out", and the camera pulls back to reveal his whole universe is a video playing on a phone propped up on a cluttered workbench, being watched by another Pip, who is about to get prompted too. Perfect loop.

The joke must land with zero dialogue. Pip communicates only through his eyes, antenna, body language and little robot chirps. Every 3–5 seconds there must be a new visual payoff.

1. The character (non-negotiable)

Study ./reference/pip_sheet.png carefully before writing any code. Open it, describe it back to yourself in detail, and write your findings into docs/character_bible.md:

Size: about 28 cm tall. He is small. The whole film should feel his scale.
Head: a wide, rounded-rectangle helmet in cream with a soft-yellow rim band framing a black glossy visor screen. His eyes live on that screen: two large glowing warm-cream eyes with dark pupils and a bright highlight. Small graphite ear-caps on each side. Wear, scratches and dusty-brown dirt around the edges.
Antenna: a thin graphite stalk on the top-right of the head with a small muted-orange signal flag. It is his "tail": it perks, droops, wiggles and vibrates with emotion.
Body: a boxy cream torso with yellow trim, warning-triangle decals, rivets and grime. A small chest compartment with a hatch that opens to show a tiny green sprout glowing softly. Back: panels, a vent grille, an orange panel, a small leaf decal.
Side decal: "PIP" lettering with orange diagonal stripes.
Arms: thin segmented graphite arms with yellow joint sleeves and three-finger claw grips. Very expressive.
Wheels: four chunky rubber wheels with yellow hubs and independent suspension, rugged and compact.
Personality: curious, kind, scrappy, expressive, always exploring. "Small bot, big feelings." He is never mean, even when furious; his anger is cute and determined.
Extract the exact palette from the sheet's swatches (sample the image with Python/PIL) into src/theme/palette.ts: Cream (body), Soft Yellow (primary), Muted Orange (accents), Graphite (metal/tech), Dusty Brown (wear & dirt), Mint Blue (lights/UI).

Identity lock rule: in every world, his helmet-and-visor silhouette, antenna flag, yellow trim, claw arms and four wheels must stay instantly recognizable. Worlds change his rendering style, never his design. The only intentional design change is the "more adorable" gag in Act 3, and even there his helmet shape, antenna and wheels stay.

2. Technical stack
Remotion (React + TypeScript) for frame-accurate, deterministic rendering. Output 1920×1080, 30 fps, H.264, high bitrate (CRF ~14). Landscape.
SVG for the character rig and most artwork. Canvas/WebGL (via @remotion/three or raw canvas) only where needed for particles, water, explosions, glow and noise effects.
SVG filters (feTurbulence, feDisplacementMap, feMorphology, feGaussianBlur) and custom canvas shaders for style "materials," scratches and grime.
@remotion/motion-blur (or your own sub-frame accumulation) for motion blur on fast action.
Python (numpy/scipy/PIL) for palette extraction, procedural audio synthesis and QA contact sheets. ffmpeg for muxing, loop checks and contact sheets.
Everything seeded and deterministic. No Math.random() without a seed.
No external copyrighted assets, no real brand logos or product names anywhere. The prompt box UI must be a generic, original design. Fonts only from Google Fonts (e.g., Inter for UI text, a rounded hand-lettered font for any handwritten notes).
Target hardware: MacBook Pro M4, 24 GB RAM. Keep render concurrency sensible.
3. The character rig (build this first, it's the whole film)

Build src/character/ as a proper 2D cutout rig:

Hierarchy: root → chassis (with suspension) → torso → neck joint → head (helmet + visor + ear-caps) → antenna → flag. Torso → shoulder → upper arm → forearm → claw (with swappable claw poses: open, closed, pinch-holding, pointing, poking/typing, gripping an edge, waving). Chassis → four wheels, each with its own suspension spring and rotation driven by distance travelled.
The visor face system (most important part): the eyes are shapes drawn on the black screen, so treat them as a fully procedural face. Parameters for eye size, roundness, top-lid cut, bottom-lid cut, pupil size and position, highlight position, glow intensity, squash/stretch, and special shapes (sparkle stars, happy arcs ^ ^, flat unimpressed lines, spirals, tiny hearts). Add a faint scanline and screen reflection over the eyes so it reads as a screen. Blink by squashing eyes vertically in 3–4 frames.
Expression targets: match the six on the sheet exactly: curious (with the "?" pop), shy (eyes low, looking away, blush marks), excited (happy arcs with little burst lines), worried (small eyes, sweat droplet), determined (angled top-lid cut), delighted (star sparkles with a heart pop). Also add: deadpan-to-camera (flat half-lidded eyes, antenna limp), horrified (tiny shaking pupils, eyes wide), furious-but-cute (determined + screen glow flickers orange), and three "glow-up" stages (see Act 3).
Secondary motion: antenna and flag on damped springs (this is his main expressive tool, use it constantly), suspension bounce on every stop and bump, arm sway, a tiny head lag when the body accelerates or brakes, dust puffs from wheels.
Turnaround: front, 3/4, side, back views matching the sheet, with clean view switching for turns.
Cycles: rolling forward (with speed lines and dust puffs as on the sheet), idle hum (gentle suspension breathing + occasional antenna twitch + blinks), recoil-in-fear, looking-up-in-wonder, holding a tiny object, reaching up, climbing, poke-typing.
Chest hatch: animatable open/close, with the sprout's soft green glow spilling out.
Style skin interface: the rig takes a style prop that changes line weight, fill treatment, texture, grime, outline boil, shading model and filters without changing geometry. This is how he stays himself across worlds.
Milestone 1 gate: render a "lineup" still: Pip in all four turnaround views + all six expressions, placed next to the reference sheet. Compare side by side. Iterate until someone who saw the sheet would say "that's Pip." Do not move on until this passes.
4. The worlds (style materials)

Each world is a full environment component with foreground, midground, background parallax layers and its own style skin for Pip. Build a shared WorldLayer system so all worlds share camera and depth logic.

Scale rule: the camera lives low, near Pip's eye level (about 20 cm off the ground). Everything is huge. People appear as giant legs and shoes, a curb is a cliff, a puddle is a lake. This is what makes a small robot cinematic.

Base world: golden-hour overgrown city. Match the header illustration of the sheet: warm sunset light, weathered stone and brick, moss and little plants, hazy tall buildings in the distance. Painterly, cozy, lived-in. This is "real life." Also used for the reveal.

Anime Tokyo. Crisp cel shading, bold outlines, glowing signs with invented (non-brand) shop names, speed lines, cherry petals drifting past him like giant pink snowflakes. His visor gets anime sparkle highlights.

Clay village. Soft rounded shapes, fingerprint/smudge noise texture, stop-motion stepping (render him "on twos"), warm tungsten lighting. He looks sculpted in plasticine.
Medieval battlefield. Muddy field, banners, distant catapults, smoke. Armored boots thunder past him. He rolls calmly between them, antenna ducking.
Toy-brick city. Everything built from generic stud-topped plastic bricks (no real brand styling or logos), glossy plastic highlights. Pip rendered with plastic sheen and slightly blockier wheels.
Underwater. Seabed street with coral lampposts, fish swimming past his visor, caustic light patterns, bubbles from his vents, his antenna flag waving slowly like seaweed.
Pencil sketch. Paper texture, graphite hatching, construction lines, eraser smudges, his lines boiling as if being redrawn every frame (match the sketch vignettes at the bottom of the sheet).
Running gag: the sprout. Pip starts the film carefully holding his tiny green sprout in one claw (the "holding a tiny object" pose). It survives every world and transforms with it: cel-shaded anime sprout with sparkles, clay sprout, sprout in a tiny battered helmet-pot, brick-built sprout, sprout releasing a bubble underwater, sketched sprout. He protects it every time the world changes. It is the emotional anchor of the film.
5. The signature transition: "regeneration"

World changes must look like an AI image re-generating, not like normal wipes. Build RegenTransition:

The frame breaks into drifting diffusion-style noise from the edges inward (not over his body at first), holds a few frames of structured noise, then the new world denoises in from coarse blobs to fine detail.

Pip's body lags one beat behind the world, briefly showing half-old / half-new style, then snaps to the new style skin. His visor glitches for 2 frames (scanline tear) during the snap. This half-state is the visual proof that he persists.

Subtle audio "whoosh-crackle" per regen, plus a tiny startled chirp from Pip on some of them.
Duration 8–12 frames each. Vary the direction and noise seed so it never feels repetitive.
6. Beat sheet (≈48 seconds at 30 fps)
Timing is a guide; adjust if a beat reads better slightly longer. The first 2 seconds must hook.
ACT 1: A GOOD MORNING (0:00–0:03)

Low tracking shot, base world. Pip rolls left-to-right along a mossy ledge, holding his sprout, eyes curious, antenna bobbing. Start mid-roll (needed for the loop).

At 0:02 the first regen hits without warning.

ACT 2: THE CASCADE (0:03–0:14)
Rapid world changes, about 1.4 s each: Anime Tokyo → Clay village → Medieval battlefield → Toy-brick city → Underwater → Pencil sketch.

Emotional progression: delighted at first (star eyes, he thinks it's wonderful), then curious ("?" pops), then worried (sweat drop, antenna droops), then he brakes hard in the sketch world with a suspension bounce and a skid mark.

Camera stays on a locked tracking framing so the only thing changing is the world, which makes the joke readable.
ACT 3: THE PROMPTS (0:14–0:30)
Base world returns. Pip looks up in wonder (pose from the sheet). In the sky, a giant floating prompt box fades in, glowing mint blue, glassy and rounded, with a soft original UI. Text types itself with a blinking cursor: "make it more cinematic" → enter key click sound.Letterbox bars slam in, the sun becomes absurd: enormous anamorphic lens flares, god rays, orange-and-teal grade, slow-motion dust, a single dramatic leaf drifting past his visor. His eyes squint into the flare. His antenna flag flaps heroically in wind he didn't ask for.

"add explosions"Huge cartoon-orange explosions bloom behind him in sequence with debris chunks. He does not turn around. His eyes go flat and half-lidded. He slowly rotates his head to look straight into the camera. Deadpan. Hold 1 full second. Then an explosion lands close and he snaps into the "recoiling in fear" pose from the sheet, the "!!" popping above him, shielding the sprout with his body.

"make the protagonist more adorable"Glow-up stage 1: his eyes grow bigger and shinier, blush marks appear, a tiny bow sprouts on his antenna. He sees his reflection in a puddle and his eyes turn horrified.

"more.": Stage 2: pastel repaint, eyes take over the whole visor with triple highlights, floating hearts and sparkles, his wheels become fluffy.
"MORE." (bigger font, screen shake): Stage 3: comically maximum cute. Plushie fur texture over his whole body, giant anime eyes, rainbow halo, a choir "aah" sting, heart confetti. His helmet shape, antenna and wheels stay so he's still clearly Pip. His eyes are still tiny and horrified inside the giant cute eyes, which is the joke.
ACT 4: HE SNAPS (0:30–0:38)
Pip vibrates, then the cute stages shatter off him like glass. He's back to normal, scuffed and furious (determined expression, screen flickering orange).
He opens his chest hatch and gently tucks the sprout inside for safety. Hatch closes with a click. This is the one quiet, kind beat in the chaos and it matters.
He races forward, launches off a rock, grabs the edge of the floating prompt box with both claws and hauls himself up, wheels spinning against the edge (match the "reaching toward a floating prompt box" pose). The camera tilts up with him.
On top of the box he holds backspace with one claw; the old prompt deletes letter by letter with fast clicks, and his visor reflects the vanishing text.

He poke-types with one claw, slowly and deliberately: "let me out". Winds up and smashes enter.

ACT 5: FREEZE AND REVEAL (0:38–0:47)
Everything freezes: debris mid-air, confetti mid-fall, dust suspended, Pip mid-pose on the box. All audio cuts to total silence for about 1 second.
Camera begins a smooth pull-back. The frame's edges reveal a rounded rectangle: his universe is a video on a phone screen. Keep pulling back: the phone is propped against a chipped mug on a cluttered workbench full of spare parts, wires, screws and scraps ("built from tomorrow's leftovers"). Sitting in front of it, tiny next to the giant phone, is another Pip, same scuffs, same antenna, watching.
The second Pip's eyes blink slowly. His antenna droops a little. A small quiet chirp.
ACT 6: THE LOOP (0:47–0:50)

Above the second Pip's head, the same mint-blue prompt box fades in and types: "make it more cinematic."

His eyes slowly slide upward toward it. His antenna flag goes stiff. On the enter key sound, hard cut to frame 1 of the film.
Loop engineering: the final shot's framing, lighting, and the start of a regen flicker must make the cut back to frame 1 feel intentional. The music must loop seamlessly across the cut. Verify by concatenating the video with itself (ffmpeg) and watching the seam.
7. Camera and cinematography

Virtual camera system: position, zoom, rotation, handheld micro-shake (seeded noise), shake impulses for explosions, tilt for the climb, dolly pull-back for the reveal.

Low camera height by default to sell his scale. Shallow depth-of-field feel: blurred foreground grass/pebbles and soft background, like a macro lens.
Depth: minimum 4 parallax layers per world. Atmospheric perspective (haze, desaturation with distance).
Motion blur on fast moves, debris, the jump and the climb.
Lighting per world: key/fill/rim implemented as gradient overlays and multiplied shadow layers on the rig. The visor glow should cast a faint warm light on nearby surfaces and on his own claws. Rim light on his helmet in every world.
Film finish pass on the whole frame: subtle grain, gentle vignette, very slight chromatic aberration only in the "cinematic" beat.
Composition: keep him on a clear third. His eyes must be readable at phone size, since most people will watch this on a phone.
8. Text and typography
Sky prompts: clean UI font, lowercase, typed at a natural human rhythm (not constant speed; tiny pauses, one small typo-and-backspace somewhere for realism).
The text must be readable in under a second on a phone. Test at 360 px wide.
No subtitles, no titles. The film opens cold.
9. Sound (procedural, original)
Create all audio in code (Python synthesis or offline Web Audio) and mix with ffmpeg:
Pip's voice: original synthesized chirps, boops and warbles built from sine/FM tones with pitch bends. Design a small emotional vocabulary: curious rising chirp, happy trill, worried wobble, startled squeak, grumpy low buzz, tiny sigh. He never speaks words.
Pip's body: servo whirs matched to arm and head moves, wheel crunch on gravel/stone, suspension creaks, hatch click, soft electrical hum on idle.
Score: a light, loopable, warm score whose instrumentation changes per world (koto/synth for anime, wooden marimba for clay, drums/horn for medieval, plastic clicks for bricks, muffled underwater filter, pencil scratch rhythm for sketch).
SFX: regen whoosh-crackle, keyboard typing clicks, enter "thunk", explosions with low-end, choir "aah" sting, glass shatter, total silence at the freeze, then quiet workshop ambience (a ticking clock, distant hum) in the reveal.

Loudness normalized to about −14 LUFS. Put stems in audio/stems/ so they can be swapped for a licensed track later.

10. Production workflow and self-improvement loop
Work in this order and don't skip gates:
Plan: write docs/character_bible.md, docs/shotlist.md (every shot with frame ranges, camera, expression, antenna state, world, SFX) and docs/style_guide.md. Show me the shot list before building.
Rig: build Pip, pass the lineup gate (section 3).
Worlds: build each world as a standalone still with Pip in it. Render all 7 as a single contact sheet. Check the identity lock and the scale feel.
Transitions: build RegenTransition, render a 5-second test.

Animatic: assemble the whole film at 960×540 with rough motion and placeholder audio. Watch it. Fix pacing first.

Full animation pass, then polish pass (secondary motion, easing, timing, antenna acting), then finish pass (lighting, grain, blur, grime).
Audio pass and mix.
Final render.
For every shot, run this critique loop at least 3 times:
Render 3–5 stills at key frames with npx remotion still, open them and look at them properly.
Score each 1–10 on: Pip matches the reference, emotion reads instantly from eyes + antenna, joke is clear without sound, composition, sense of scale, depth, lighting, polish, readability at phone size.
Write the scores and the three biggest problems into docs/review_log.md, fix them, re-render, re-score. Continue until every category is at least 8, then move on.
After each full preview render, make an ffmpeg contact sheet (one frame every 0.5 s) and review the whole film's flow in one image.

Be honest in reviews. If something looks cheap, say it and fix it. Usual failures to hunt for: stiff or dead antenna, wheels sliding instead of rolling, eyes that feel like stickers instead of a glowing screen, missing suspension weight, identical-looking transitions, muddy text, and off-model proportions.

11. Deliverables
out/pip_final_1080p.mp4: the film.
out/pip_loop_check.mp4: the film played twice back to back, to prove the loop.
out/poster_frame.png: the best single frame for the X post thumbnail (probably Pip deadpanning at camera with explosions behind him).

out/lineup.png: Pip across all worlds.

Clean, commented source with a README explaining how to re-render.
Start with step 1. Ask me anything essential before building, otherwise make strong creative decisions yourself.

title: Interactive jelly dam simulation
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Dam Jelly", a new piece in my "Material Studies" series: a single-file, self-contained interactive WebGPU diorama (one HTML file, all JS/CSS/WGSL inline, no network requests, no libraries). A mountain valley with a concrete gravity dam is cut out as a wobbly block of jelly sitting on a pale studio table, seen from above at three-quarters.

SCENE (block-local coords, origin at base centre, y up, block ~5.2 × 5.2 units):
- A river valley running back to front: steep rocky slopes with crags, scree and boulders, conifer and broadleaf woods, grassy shoulders. Where the block is cut, the side faces show layered grey bedrock in tilted beds with joints, a weathered brown band and dark topsoil at the top, and gravel and silt under the water. At the very bottom are thin coloured "jelly" strata in the current flavour.
- A long reservoir behind the dam, with a bare drawdown ring of rock round its shore, a floating log boom of orange and yellow floats in front of the spillway, and a small patrol boat lapping the lake.
- A concrete gravity dam across the valley, its ends let into rock abutments: a battered downstream face with lift lines, a crest road with railings and lamps, an intake tower with trash racks and three penstocks down the face.
- A central stepped spillway with three bays between piers. Each bay has a radial (Tainter) gate: a curved skin plate on arms that swing about trunnions on the piers, with hoist houses on top. Below is an ogee crest, a stepped chute, training walls and a plunge pool scoured into the riverbed.
- A powerhouse at the right toe: a concrete base in the river, a hall of siding and tall windows, tailrace mouths. Above it, a switchyard on a terrace with transformers and gantries, and lattice pylons climbing the right slope with sagging lines.
- A fish ladder up the left bank: 14 stepped concrete pools with weirs between them from the river up to the lake, an exit gate and a counting hut at the top.
- A visitor centre on the left abutment, roads with hairpins, a suspension footbridge over the river downstream, rocks, weed and gravel bars in the river.

SIMULATION:
- Shallow-water heightfield (about 168×168), split into two bodies by the dam (reservoir and river), each with its own still level, separated by flood-fill classification. Sources, sinks and current jets make visible flow: inflow at the back of the lake, a draw toward open gates and the intake, boiling outflow in the plunge pool and tailrace, and drainage at the front edge. Foam advects on the currents.
- Reservoir level ODE: dL/dt = (Qin − Qspill − Qturbines − Qover) / AREA, where Qspill ∝ gateOpening · (L − sill)^1.5 and Qover ∝ (L − crest)^1.5. The river level rises with total outflow.
- Head-based power: 3 units × 120 MW, scaled by head.
- An automatic dam keeper opens the gates (siren first) when the lake nears the crest or a flood is coming, and shuts them again once the water is back down.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, can be tipped by dragging its side, and settles back.

INTERACTIONS (right-hand glass panel, "The dam"):
- Open spillway: a 3.5 s siren, then the gates swing up over ~9 s, and white water streams down the steps with spray and mist. Press again to shut them.
- Turbines on/off: the units spin up or down, power rises or falls, the tailrace boils or goes still, and the powerhouse windows glow while running.
- Salmon run: salmon gather below the dam, try leaping at the falls, then climb the ladder pool by pool (a leap per pool, waiting their turn) and swim out into the lake. A counter tallies fish through. Runs also arrive on their own every few minutes.
- Flood: a storm builds, blows and eases (rain, darkening, lightning hitting pylons, ridges or the lake). A big inflow surge comes down the valley: the keeper pre-releases, the lake still rises over the crest, and a white overflow sheet pours across the whole dam face. The water turns muddy brown and clears slowly afterwards.
- Tap a gate, the powerhouse or the ladder to trigger the same actions. Tap the patrol boat for its horn. Space sounds the siren.
- Tallies: Power (MW), Head (m), Salmon. Status lines: Spillway, Powerhouse, Reservoir (Rising/Falling/Steady/Flood coming in/Over the crest, with level relative to the crest in metres).
- Drag on water makes waves, drag the block's side tips it, drag empty space or right-drag orbits, wheel or pinch zooms.
- Flavour swatches (Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant) tint the jelly and water. Sliders for Firmness, Wave damping and Wind. Reset, Pause, Sound on/off and View buttons.

LIFE: rainbow trout in the river and lake, salmon, mallards (drakes and hens) paddling and taking off, herons wading and stalking, ospreys circling and plunge-diving for fish, people walking the crest (who pause at the siren), the powerhouse yard, the visitor centre and the footbridge, and a fisherman on the bank. Animals startle at the siren, lightning and splashes.

SOUND (synthesised with WebAudio, events only, no constant ambience): motor siren, gate-hoist clunk and drone, the spillway's rush as the gates lift, turbine spin-up and spin-down whine, a rumble of overtopping, salmon leaps, a chime for each fish counted, osprey splashes, the boat horn, thunder, and wind and rain only while a storm blows.

RENDERING: WebGPU with MSAA, a sun shadow map, caustics on the riverbed, refraction and absorption through the water and the jelly, Fresnel reflections, translucent premultiplied passes for spray and mist puffs, white-water sheets, ladder pools and rain, and a muddy-water tint during floods.

UI and layout: editorial look with an italic serif masthead ("Material Studies" eyebrow, "Dam Jelly." title, a one-line description) and a "How to play" footer at bottom left. On mobile the controls panel becomes a bottom sheet. If WebGPU is unavailable, show a clear fallback card. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. No page scroll.

QUALITY: keep the sim around 2 ms/frame, no NaNs over long soaks, everything stays inside the block, the boat always afloat. Verify with headless Playwright screenshots (SwiftShader WebGPU) and an end-to-end test that drives every button, tap target, slider and the mobile sheet, and checks for zero console errors.

title: Interactive pixel art swimming club
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Make a pixel-art 3D diorama of an open-air lido on a floating island, the same series and engine as my other pixel dioramas (three.js, orthographic isometric camera turned in quarter steps, small render target with no anti-aliasing snapped to whole pixels, depth-based outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, hard sun shadows, day/dusk/night, rain with puddles). Call it "Deep End".

The lido: a 25 m four-lane lap pool (shallow end roped off for children, lane ropes whose floats ride the waves, backstroke flags, starting blocks) and a 5 m deep diving pool, with 1 m and 3 m springboards that bend and a 1930s concrete tower with platforms at 5, 7.5 and 10 m and an open stair. Around them: striped changing cabins with a clock, a kiosk, the judges' table, the lifeguard's high chair, loungers, parasols and umbrella pines.

Real water: each pool is a height field run with the wave equation, so dives, strokes, raindrops and clicks make rings that reflect off the walls. The surface shades from its normals, with sun glints and a mirrored render of the scene; the tiled floor gets caustics.

Dives are flown, not animated. The diver takes off with an upward speed and an angular momentum chosen to land the somersaults, the momentum is conserved through tuck, pike and straight shapes, and the body rotates about its real centre of mass, with twists about the spine. Kick-out timing errors tip the entry angle, which sets the splash and five judges' cards; drop the highest and lowest and multiply by DD. Run a six-diver, five-round meet on the 10 m platform or the 3 m springboard (with the approach and hurdle), with standings, then a medal moment, then free swim with pencil jumps, cannonballs and belly flops.

Also: lap swimmers doing freestyle, breaststroke and backstroke with flip turns; divers who swim to a ladder, shower, sit in the hot tub and climb again; children who get whistled at for running; wet footprints on the deck that dry; pool lights glowing at night. Click the water to make a splash. English UI; must work on phones.

title: Electric motor 3D animation comparison
author: rubenssoto_ai
prompt:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

Field: vertical stripes edge to edge, 32px period, half black. Warp them by displacing each stripe's x with a Gaussian lens bulge (a sphere swelling from the surface) and a slow sine wave. Draw stripes as filled polygons sampled every 8px for crisp edges. For the type, mask a horizontal-stripe layer with text drawn to an offscreen canvas (destination-in). No stripe may get thinner than 10px, or the 1280×720 preview will moiré.

Motion is slow and hypnotic: warp amplitudes move on cubic-bezier(0.45, 0, 0.55, 1) over 2–3s. Real op art is precise, binary and mathematical; the cheap version is a spinning spiral or a strobing checkerboard.
Banned: color, gradients, blur, glow, flashing, spirals, rotating fields, inversion, stripes under 10px, gray blending.
</direction>
