3.4–5.4s: the bulge drifts gently to center while a sine wave (amplitude 0 → 24px, wavelength 600px) phases in along the stripes.
5.4–6.8s: the title emerges as a vertical mask edge sweeps left to right across it over 1.2s, turning the stripes horizontal inside the letters; the bulge warps both layers.
6.8–7.8s: a 140px white band slides up from the bottom; subtitle, details and the three words sit on it in black between thin rules.
7.8–8.8s: warps ease to a still, gently curved rest.
8.8–10.0s: hold.
For other durations, scale every timestamp proportionally.

- Drag physics: a drawn hand cursor (an open hand on hover, a closed hand while grabbing) presses the handle; the card lifts over 0.15s (scale 1.035, shadow 0 24px 48px rgba(31,26,23,0.22), above every other card) and follows the pointer exactly in y, tilting up to ±2° with the pointer's vertical speed (velocity averaged over the previous 0.12s, computed from the path, never stored). When its center crosses a neighbor's midpoint, that neighbor springs into the vacated slot (stiffness 520, damping 38, about 3% overshoot), and the open slot shows a 2px dashed tangerine outline at 40%. On release the card glides into its slot on the same spring as its scale and shadow return over 0.2s.
- Checking: the checkbox fills tangerine and a white check draws (200ms); a strike line draws through the title left to right (250ms) and the title fades to secondary; the summary reads "1 of 6 done · 2 h left".
- Pointer moves: curved paths of 0.45–0.7s on cubic-bezier(0.45, 0, 0.15, 1); drags take 1.0–1.2s on cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.3, 1).
- Premium: weight and consequence: a card you can feel lifting, neighbors making room, times re-planning in the same frame. Cheap: rows swapping places instantly under a static arrow.
Banned: real app names, emoji, confetti, glow, dark mode, a dragged card passing under its neighbors, teleporting cards, times that don't add up, anything flashing more than 3 times per second.
</direction>

<structure>
- 0.0–0.8s: the tangerine stage; "Dayloom" and the headline rise in; the panel rises 30px and the cards stagger in 40ms apart with their times.
- 0.8–1.4s: the hand enters and hovers the rent card's handle, which darkens; it grabs.
- 1.4–1.6s: the card lifts.
- 1.6–2.8s: it is dragged to the top; Review, Trains, Newsletter and Reply each spring down one slot as it passes.
- 2.8–3.2s: release; it settles and the times roll.
- 3.2–3.8s: the hand moves to the newsletter card, now 3rd, grabs it, and it lifts.
- 3.8–5.0s: it is dragged to the bottom; Trains, Review and Plants spring up one slot.
- 5.0–5.4s: release; it settles and the times roll.
- 5.4–6.2s: the hand rests beside the panel. At 6.0s the re-planned list reads cleanly.
- 6.2–7.0s: the hand clicks the top checkbox: check, strike, summary.
- 7.0–8.2s: the hand drifts to rest just below the panel's lower left, clear of the cards.
- 8.2–10.0s: hold, perfectly still.
For other lengths, stretch the pauses between moves; keep drags at 1.0–1.2s and at least 1s of hold.
</structure>

<build>
- One self-contained index.html (inline CSS and JS), a 1920×1080 (16:9) stage scaled to fit the window, designed for 60fps. No image, video, texture or model files: every shape and texture is generated in code.
- window.seek(t), t in seconds, computes every visual from t alone: no CSS transitions or CSS animations, no setTimeout/setInterval, no state carried between frames, randomness only from a seeded PRNG. Anything cumulative is solved analytically from t or precomputed once at load at a fixed step. Past the end, seek clamps to the last frame.
- Without ?render in the URL, drive seek from requestAnimationFrame so it plays in a browser (loop after a 1s end hold); with ?render, don't start that loop.
- Google Fonts via <link> are fine; await document.fonts.load() for each face before defining window.seek.
- Engine: HTML/CSS with inline SVG for the cursors, handles and checks, positioned from seek.
- The pointer path and the drag schedule are a timeline built once at load; springs are closed-form in the time since their trigger, and a spring retargeted mid-motion starts from its current offset and velocity.
</build>

<check>
Before showing me, step through one frame per second (t = 0…10): screenshot each and look at it. Fix overlaps, clipped or cramped text, and anything off-style or Banned. Check the dragged card always stays above its neighbors, each neighbor moves exactly one slot, every set of times matches the lists above and ends at 11:05, the strike runs through the whole title, and no text clips inside its card. Confirm seek(10) and seek(11) match, so the final frame holds.
</check>

title: Cut-Paper Title Sequence
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second opening title sequence in the mid-century cut-paper tradition.

<inputs>
Film title: The Vanishing Hour. Presented by: Larkspur Pictures. Three credits: "with Vera Holt", "music by Theo Marsh", "directed by Ines Calder". Motif: a keyhole (one object that sums up the film). Tempo: 132 BPM. Duration: 10s. If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Palette: vermilion #E4472B, mustard #E2A531, bone #F0E7D3, black #15120F. One flat ground per scene, plus at most two colors.
Type: Oswald 600 uppercase for the title (up to 170px), 400 for credits (40px), made to look hand-cut: fixed seeded per-letter offsets (±4px baseline, ±1.5° rotation) and edges roughened by an SVG feTurbulence + feDisplacementMap filter (scale 3).
Shapes: silhouettes and shards are polygons with straight, scissor-cut edges (8–20 jittered vertices). Paper layers cast a hard 2px shadow at 20% black. Leave big empty fields; set type off-center, often butted against a shape's edge.
Motion is jazz: everything lands on the beat grid (132 BPM; beat n starts at (n − 1) × 0.4545s; half-beats allowed), and scenes change with hard cuts on a beat. Shapes snap in over 0.18–0.3s on cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.9, 0.3, 1), hold, and snap out. Quantize paper motion to 12 steps per second (Math.floor(t * 12) / 12) so it feels animated on twos; cuts stay exact. The cheap version is smooth tweens under a paper texture; the real thing is rhythm, reduction and one strong symbol.
Banned: gradients, glows, blur, crossfades, photo textures, a second motif, rounded icon-like shapes, soft easing on cuts.
</direction>

<structure>
0.00–0.91s: black; four jagged bone bars slash down from the top edge, one per half-beat, each to a different depth.
0.91–2.73s: cut to vermilion. "Larkspur Pictures presents" in bone, low-left; black shards jab in from the right on beats 4, 5 and 6, pointing at it.
2.73–4.55s: cut to bone. The black keyhole lands center-left at 30% of stage height on beat 7, jumps to 60% on beat 8, then the camera pushes into it over beats 9–10 (scale 1 → 12, cubic-bezier(0.7, 0, 0.9, 0.5)) until black fills the frame.
4.55–6.82s: on that black, the title slams in a word per beat (letters 30ms apart, alternating bone and vermilion, 108% → 100% in 0.12s); a jagged mustard stripe slides under the last word.
6.82–8.64s: cut to mustard. The credits arrive one per beat on a stepped diagonal, each nudged by a black shard.
8.64–10.0s: cut to vermilion. A small title lockup bottom-left beside a 120px keyhole emblem, still from 9.1s on.
For other durations, scale scene lengths proportionally and snap every cut to the nearest beat.
</structure>

<build>
One self-contained index.html, CSS and JS inline. Google Fonts via <link> are fine; no other libraries (no three.js: this style is flat). Draw in inline SVG. The stage is 1920×1080 (16:9), scaled to fit the window. Design for 60fps. window.seek(t), t in seconds, must compute every visual from t alone: no CSS transitions or animations, no setTimeout or setInterval, no state carried between frames, and randomness only from a seeded PRNG. Without ?render in the URL, drive seek from requestAnimationFrame so it plays in a browser (loop after a 1s end hold); with ?render, don't start that loop.
</build>

<check>
Before showing me, step through one frame per second: screenshot each and look at it. Fix overlaps, clipped or cramped text, accidental edge collisions, and anything off-style or Banned. Check every cut lands on a beat. Confirm seek(duration) and seek(duration + 1) match, so the final frame holds.
</check>

title: Apple Liquid Glass style UI motion showcase
author: motion_conquest
prompt:
<role>
You are a senior UI motion designer and creative technologist. You build UI animations in code, frame-accurate, and render them to video yourself.
</role>

<inputs>
Style: Apple Liquid Glass. Reference platforms: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26.

Format: 1440x1440, 60fps, seamless loop.

Song: "Digital Clouds" by Alejandro Magaña (A. M.), from Mixkit, free under the Mixkit License. If the file is not attached, ask me for it and nothing else.

Tempo: about 120 BPM, 8 bars, and something happens on every beat. Measure the real tempo from the file. If it differs from 120, keep the beat map in beats and derive every time from the measured grid.

Palette: light mode system materials.
- Labels: #1D1D1F. Secondary labels: #6E6E73. Opaque surfaces: white.
- One accent, #0A84FF, used only for on, active and selected states.
- The Dynamic Island is the only pure-black element.

Canvas: a macOS Tahoe style wallpaper.
- Large, soft color fields: deep blue #1B3A8C, teal #2BB3B1, violet #7B5CFF, and a warm peach highlight #FFB38A.
- Slow parallax drift: 12px per bar at most.
- Saturated enough that the glass visibly refracts it, calm enough to sit behind text.

Font: SF Pro Display for 20px and above, SF Pro Text below 20px, if installed locally. Otherwise use Inter from Fontsource: 600 for titles, 500 for labels, 400 for body. Use -1% tracking at display sizes and tabular numbers for any number that changes.

Icons: one SF Symbols-like set drawn as SVG, medium weight matched to the adjacent text, one consistent optical size per state. Symbols needed: play, pause, speaker with 3 waves, house, heart, chart bars, person, magnifier, note, checkmark.

Pointer: an iPadOS adaptive pointer.
- A 22px translucent gray circle (#8E8E93 at 45%).
- It snaps (magnetism) into any control it hovers and becomes that control's highlight shape.
- It becomes an I-beam in text fields.
- It shrinks 10% on press.
</inputs>

<direction>
Apple keynote and WWDC Liquid Glass session-level UI motion. One element, never cut. Every state is the same element morphing its size, corner radius, material and color, while its content swaps with a short blur. The pointer drives every change with real clicks, holds and drags.

Material:
- Liquid Glass is a lens, not frosted plastic. It refracts the wallpaper, and the bending is strongest at the rim.
- Light frosting and a 10–16% white tint.
- A 1px specular rim lit from the top-left, with a fainter counter-highlight bottom-right. The highlight shifts as the element moves.
- A soft contact shadow: 0 10 30 at 12% black.
- Glass never sits on glass. Content on glass uses vibrant or solid fills.
- Corners are concentric: inner radius = outer radius − padding.
- When glass shapes split or merge, they join like droplets (smooth union), never crossfade.

Motion language:
- Apple-like springs everywhere:
- Morphs: response 0.45, damping 0.86.
- Presses: response 0.25, damping 0.72.
- Pointer snap: response 0.3, damping 0.9.
- Overshoot is at most 3%.
- On press, glass lifts and swells (scale 1.06–1.12, brighter rim). It never shrinks.
- A toggle knob on hold turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that stretches in its direction of travel.
- The tab bar selection is a glass droplet that magnifies the icons under it while dragged.
- Sliders thicken when grabbed and rubber-band past their limits.

Camera:
- Each state fills about 60% of the frame, and the wallpaper is always visible around the glass.
- Camera moves use response 0.6, damping 1.0.
- The wallpaper scales at 70% of the camera zoom for depth.

The last frame is the first frame, pointer position and velocity included.

Banned: bouncy or elastic easing, overshoot over 3%, particle bursts, neon glows, colored gradients on UI chrome (the glass specular rim is the only gradient), heavy drop shadows, glass on glass, mismatched corner radii, mismatched icon weights, emoji, crossfades between states, dead time longer than half a beat, anything that looks like a template or a Dribbble clone.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 8 bars, 32 beats. Beat map, one line per beat:

1. A glass capsule button "Continue" floats on the wallpaper. The pointer glides in.
2. The pointer snaps into the button and becomes its highlight.
3. Click: the glass lifts and swells, the rim brightens.
4. The capsule contracts into a circle and becomes a spinning activity ring.
5. The ring completes, filling in accent.
6. It morphs into a checkmark that draws itself.
7. The circle stretches into a black Dynamic Island, compact: album art on the left, a live waveform on the right.
8. Click: the island expands into Now Playing ("Digital Clouds", "A. M.", progress 0:42 / 1:41).
9. Click play: the play icon morphs into pause, with a path morph rather than a swap.
10. Grab the progress bar: it thickens, and the time labels shift out of the way.
11. Scrub forward with direct manipulation. The time counts in tabular numbers.
12. Release: the bar springs thin, and playback continues from the new position.
13. The island dissolves into a glass volume slider with a speaker icon.
14. Drag up: the fill follows the pointer, and the speaker waves appear one by one.
15. Drag past max: the whole slider rubber-bands and stretches, leading edge first.
16. Release: it springs back to its length at 100%.
17. The slider morphs into a toggle (track plus knob), off. Its label is "Focus".
18. Hold: the knob turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that shows the track through it.
19. Flip on the beat: the lens stretches in its travel direction, and the track fills with accent.
20. The knob detaches as a droplet and becomes the selection lens of a floating glass tab bar with 4 tabs: Home, Health, Activity, Profile.
21. Drag the lens across the tabs. The leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing edge, and the icons magnify under the lens.
22. The lens settles on "Activity", and its icon turns accent.
23. The tab bar grows upward into a glass widget card titled "Activity", with concentric radii.
24. A 7-day bar chart (M T W T F S S) rises in a left-to-right stagger.
25. Hover Thursday: a glass tooltip bubble shows "8,412 steps", anchored to the bar.
26. Hover Friday: the tooltip slides over and counts to "11,036 steps".
27. ⌘Space: the card collapses into a Tahoe Spotlight bar with a magnifier icon.
28. Type "ne": the results list filters (New Note, Network, News), and rows spring in and out.
29. Type "w": "New Note" rises to the top as a selected accent row.
30. Enter: the row presses and lifts.
31. The Spotlight bar drops into a glass notification banner from the top: a Notes icon, "Note created", "now".
32. The banner contracts back into the "Continue" capsule. The pointer returns to its frame-1 position and velocity.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1440x1440. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.

2. Springs are closed-form damped step responses with Apple parameters: ω = 2π/response, ζ = dampingFraction.
- A value that is retargeted many times is the sum of one spring per retarget, so it stays a pure function of time.
- Releases start from the current value and the current velocity.

3. Asymmetric edges: the tab lens, the toggle knob and the slider stretch each have their leading edge on response 0.28 and their trailing edge on response 0.42.

4. Drags are direct manipulation.
- While held, the value is a function of pointer position, with rubber-banding past limits: offset = limit + (1 − 1/(x·0.55/d + 1))·d.
- On release it springs back from wherever it was.

5. Glass is rendered in a WebGL2 pass, not with CSS backdrop-filter:
- The wallpaper is drawn to a texture with a precomputed blurred mip chain.
- Every glass shape is a rounded-rect SDF. Merging and splitting use smooth-min with k = 24px.
- Refraction offsets the sample along the SDF gradient. The offset is strongest within 14px of the edge and scaled by lens thickness.
- Frost is a mip-level bias.
- Chromatic aberration is at most 1px, at the rim only.
- The specular rim comes from the SDF normal against a top-left light.
- The Dynamic Island is an opaque SDF in the same pass.
- Text, icons, charts and the pointer are crisp SVG/DOM layers above the canvas, under the same camera matrix.

6. Content swaps inside a morphing container:
- Exit takes 120ms: blur 6px, scale 0.96, fade.
- Enter starts 60ms later with its own spring.
- Exit and enter text never overlap.

7. Audio:
- Analyze the song with numpy (onset envelope plus autocorrelation) for the beat grid, and start on a measured downbeat.
- Synthesize Apple-subtle UI sounds with numpy: soft taps for clicks, ticks for scrub detents, a low detent at max volume, a keyboard click per typed letter, and a gentle two-note chime for the notification.
- Place each sound on its measured peak, mixed about 18dB under the track.

8. Render with Playwright at 1440x1440 with 4 subframes per frame (240fps).
- Blend to 60fps with ffmpeg: tmix=frames=4, select='not(mod(n\,4))', setpts=N/60/TB.
- Encode H.264 yuv420p, crf 16, with AAC 192k and faststart.

9. Before the full render, render one still per beat (32) as a contact sheet. Fix anything off the grid, cramped, illegible over the wallpaper, or with non-concentric radii.
</build>

<gotchas>
- The glass and the DOM layers must share one camera matrix per frame, or the content drifts off its glass.
- Glass over a bright wallpaper patch kills legibility. Add an adaptive dim under the text based on sampled wallpaper luminance, rather than a heavier tint.
- The Dynamic Island is never glass.
- Icons crossing a morph keep their optical size. Scale the container, not the glyphs.
- The tooltip stays anchored to its bar through the camera move, not to the screen.
- Typed characters in Spotlight enter with the pointer's I-beam; the caret blinks on half-beats.
- Never put will-change on anything the camera scales, or text renders blurry.
- Make the last frame identical to the first, pointer included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
If the song file is missing, ask for it. Then measure the BPM and the downbeat, and show me the beat map as a table (beat, time, state, pointer action, sound), snapped to the measured grid, before writing any code. Wait for my OK.
</start>

title: Interactive squishy jelly whale
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single-file interactive WebGPU soft-body study called "Whale Jelly" (Material Studies / No. 043), matching the quality of an earlier watermelon-slice jelly study. Subject: a humpback whale cast in two layers of gummy jelly, lying on its belly on a studio table.

Geometry: a signed-distance whale — an elliptical section swept along a curved spine (broad head with a flat crown, deep chest, narrow keeled tail stock), the belly pressed flat on the floor, smoothly joined to notched flukes with a scalloped trailing edge, long flippers with knobs along the leading edge, a small dorsal fin and twin blowhole dimples. Mesh it with surface nets and Newton projection; simulate it with a snapped hex lattice (5 tets per cell, a node layer on the floor) and XPBD (60 Hz, 10 substeps, co-rotational shape matching, volume constraints, edge damping, floor friction). Make the fins firmest and the clear body jelly softest.

Look: clear tinted jelly over a milky layer. The milky layer is its own embedded surface, cut by a wavy line along the flank that rises at the head into the mouth. Light it with key light absorbed through the jelly above it, measured from shadow-map depth. Draw throat pleats, a dark mouth groove, head tubercles and tail-stock knuckles in the shader from rest-space coordinates as bump-mapped relief. Add glossy dark bead eyes and a few trapped air bubbles. Render with refraction plus Beer–Lambert thickness from back-face depth, back-lit glow on the thin fins, a jelly-tinted floor shadow, PCSS soft shadows, contact AO, studio softbox reflections and GGX highlights, then PBR Neutral tone mapping.

Interaction: grab and stretch anywhere, with twist on scroll or a second finger. A "Blow a spout" button fires a column of rigid jelly drops from the blowhole along its deformed axis; the drops bounce, roll, land on the whale through its tets, and can be picked up and thrown.

UI (English, editorial style): masthead, live status pill, specimen panel (three colourways — Ocean, Slate, Lagoon; Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Blow / Reset; ¼ speed; Show mesh; Pause), live readouts (mass, volume %, length in cm snout-to-notch, loose drops), "Inside the experiment" notes, a WebGPU fallback and a stacked mobile layout.

title: Pixel art winter hockey scene comparison
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Build a real-time pixel-art isometric diorama of hockey on a frozen river, as a single HTML page using three.js (WebGL). A floating winter island: a frozen river crosses it from edge to edge and spills off both ends as icicle falls. On the black ice, a rink has been shovelled out and walled with a ring of snow lumps, with a gap for the bench and a small red-framed net with white mesh at each end. The nets are set in from the walls so players can go behind them. The north bank climbs to a terrace with snow-roofed log houses (smoking chimneys, icicles on the eaves, lit windows), a fence, birches with crows and a sledging slope. The south shore is low: firs, a snowman, a fire and a small bath-house. Add a footbridge upstream and an ice fisherman on a box over his hole downstream. Render at low resolution with an orthographic camera, snap colours to a fixed 64-colour OKLab palette, draw depth outlines, and reflect the scene in the ice.
Play three skaters and a goalie a side, village rules: no lines, no offside. The goalies wear felt boots and pads. Skaters have momentum: pushes to accelerate, long glides, limited turning, and hockey stops with a spray of snow. They skate backwards when defending and fall and slide on their backs after collisions. Simulate the puck physically: low friction on ice and high on snow, solved passes (v0² = v² + 2ad), saucer passes over sticks, lifted shots aimed through a spot in the net, soft snow walls that can bury a hard puck, posts and crossbar.
AI: a chaser chosen by intercept time, attack and defence shapes, a presser and markers, poke checks, dekes, wristers, snapshots, slapshots, backhands, wraparounds and one-timers, plus blocked shots. Goalies read the shot from a forecast, drop into the butterfly, stretch, glove or kick out rebounds, and cover the puck.
An old man drops the puck at faceoffs, catches the puck the beaten goalie slides up to him, and tosses spares when a puck is lost in the snow. A dog digs the lost pucks out and brings them back.
The rink is a live canvas: skate blades scratch it white, falling snow settles on it and slows the puck, kids clear lanes with snow scoops, and between games the old man floods it from buckets into a mirror.
Village life: sledders, the fisherman catching perch, a woman crossing the bridge with a yoke of buckets, fans on a bench who comment, a boy on the snow wall who throws snowballs on click, crows, chimney smoke, breath in the frost. Day/dusk/night lighting with lamps, a string of bulbs and the fire; clear/snow/blizzard weather.

title: Pixel-art table tennis courtyard diorama
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build a single-file HTML pixel-art diorama called "King of the Table": table tennis in the courtyard of a three-storey pastel panel apartment block, on a small floating island, rendered with three.js (r160 via importmap) as a real 3D scene drawn into a low-res render target (orthographic isometric camera in 90° steps, whole-pixel snapping, depth outlines, a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab, optional dither, Raw 3D toggle).

World: the block with three entrances (canopies, numbered plates, lamps), windows, balconies with washing; brick garages; a regulation concrete table (2.74 × 1.525 m, top at 76 cm, steel net 15.25 cm) on a slab pad with a flip score counter on a stool; benches; a playground (swings, slide, sandbox, carousel); washing lines whose sheets flap in the wind; two parked cars; birches, lilac, painted-tyre flower beds, a chalk hopscotch; lamp posts. Merge static meshes by material.

Ball physics: 40 mm / 2.7 g ball with strong quadratic drag, Magnus lift from spin (topspin dives, backspin floats), table bounce that converts spin into pace, net and net-cord, ground bounces and rolling, walls, wind with gusts. Shots are solved (bisection over launch angle) to land on a target with a given spin and net clearance, then perturbed by an error model (hurry, incoming pace, risk, wind, mishits). Serves: tossed ≥16 cm from the palm, struck behind the end line, solved so they bounce once on each half; lets.

Game: 4 neighbours with distinct styles (lefty topspin attacker, close blocker, far-back chopper, wild smasher) play king of the table: games to 11, two clear, serve changes every 2 points and every point from 10-all; winner stays, loser to the back of the bench. Players predict the ball's flight, shuffle to meet it after the bounce, and choose forehand/backhand loops, drives, blocks, pushes, flicks, chops, lobs, floated returns and smashes, with keyed bat paths and two-bone IK box-rig bodies. Between points the nearer player fetches the ball wherever it rolled (or takes a new one if it falls off the island), throws it to the server, who bounces it on the table before serving. Yard life via generator coroutines and A*: grandmothers knit and comment, kids swing/slide/ride the carousel/dig/watch, a man walks his dog, pigeons peck and take off when approached. Day/dusk/night, rain (everyone shelters under the canopy, puddle reflections, then the table is wiped), wind calm/breeze/gusty. Clicks: the table aims the next shot; the yard calls the pigeons; buttons call Loop/Push/Smash/Lob. The club: one court inside a chain-link fence with low dark-green windscreens reading LOVE ALL, a net that sags from 1.07 m at the posts to 0.914 m at the strap, the umpire's high chair with a sunshade and the players' chairs with parasols, a three-row stand, a clubhouse with a red roof, a clock showing the real time, a flag and a terrace, a groundsman's shed, floodlights (spotlights aimed at the court, so night stays dark around it), poplars and a gravel path. The court can be clay, grass or a hard court, painted to the rule book.

Real ball physics: gravity, drag and the Magnus force of topspin and slice; a different bounce on each surface; net cords that trickle over or drop back. Players predict the ball's flight, pick where the strings can meet it (after the bounce, or on the volley or smash at the net), run there and swing in time. Each figure is a rig of boxes posed with two-bone IK; the racket follows keyed paths for a forehand, a two-handed backhand, a volley, a smash and a serve with toss, trophy pose and jump, and the strings meet the ball at contact. Shot choice comes from the situation (cross court, down the line, sharp angle, slice when stretched, lob or pass against a net rusher, drop shot against a deep player, approach and volley). Each launch is solved to clear the net and land on its target, then thrown a little off, so winners, errors and long rallies come out of the physics. Four players with their own styles play a ladder where the winner stays on: short sets to four games, no-ad scoring, a tiebreak at 3–3 and a match tiebreak to ten.

Life on court: ball kids fetch dead balls and bounce a new one to the server, who bounces it before serving. The umpire watches the ball and calls the score. On clay the ball leaves marks, and on close calls the umpire climbs down to read the mark. Between sets the groundsmen drag the clay; grass wears behind the baselines. In rain the players sit under their parasols and the groundsmen pull a cover over the court. Spectators follow the ball and clap. Click the court to aim the next shot, with buttons for a lob or a drop shot, and a ×3 speed toggle. Show a tennis scoreboard (sets, point, server, serve speed) and the ladder; English UI; it must work on phones.

title: Jelly cube spaceport comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Launch Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a spaceport on a low tropical island, cut out as a cube of translucent jelly on a studio floor. Everything procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, wave damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Shallow-water sim for the sea (wind waves, wakes, foam), sandy seabed with ripples and caustics, seagrass, coral heads, sponges, starfish, conchs, an old rocket engine bell on the bottom. Cut faces show sand, shelly limestone and candy strata. Drag the water to stir it.

THE SCENE
- Land along the back and left: dunes, scrub, palms, dune grass, a beach.
- Launch pad on a concrete berm: mount over a flame trench opening toward the sea, steel deflector, four red-and-white lightning masts with sagging catenary wires, a deluge water tower, tank farm (LOX sphere, kerosene tanks, nitrogen bottles), floodlights.
- A long hangar with ribbed siding and a vertical-lift door, rails to the pad, a transporter-erector (white lattice strongback on a rail car with hydraulic rams).
- Landing zone (concrete circle with ring and cross), refurbishment shed, fire truck, a tracking radar dish that follows whatever is flying.
- Press site: bleachers full of spectators, a flag, a big amber seven-segment countdown clock (T−0:10 … T+0:45).
- Quay with fenders and bollards, a crawler crane with a long lattice boom, two booster stands, a warehouse.
- At sea: a drone ship (dark deck with landing target, blast walls, thruster houses), a tug, a fairing-recovery boat with a big net on four arms.
- The rocket: two stages — booster with nine engines, black interstage, four folding landing legs, four grid fins; upper stage with a long dark vacuum nozzle; a two-piece fairing whose halves carry parafoils.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Roll out: the hangar door lifts, the erector carries the rocket out horizontally on rails and stands it on the mount; it vents LOX wisps.
- Launch: 10-second count with beeps and the clock, strongback leans back, deluge water, ignition at T−3 with huge steam clouds boiling out of the trench toward the sea, slow liftoff, the block trembles, the crowd cheers, gulls go up. The rocket pitches downrange and climbs out of sight leaving a billowing exhaust trail; the camera rises with it.
- Staging: MECO, separation, the upper stage lights a pale blue-violet vacuum flame and leaves. The booster flips, boostback burn, grid fins out, entry burn, steers down, landing burn on one engine, legs swing out, touchdown — on the drone ship or back at the landing zone (toggle, or tap the ship / the pad). Double sonic boom (triple for the landing zone). Boosters come back sooty; the deck and pad get scorched.
- Recovery: the tug tows the drone ship to the quay; the crane hooks the booster, lifts it (pendulum swing), folds its legs, sets it on a stand; the ship is towed back out. Fairing halves come down under orange-and-white parafoils, circling in: one lands in the boat's net, the other splashes and is fished out; the boat brings them home.
- Reuse: the next rollout takes a flight-proven booster ("B1 · flight 2", soot partly cleaned).
- Storm: wind, waves, rain, darkened room, lightning on the masts, the crane or the sea. No launches in a storm or above 15 m/s ("No go · weather / wind"); a count in progress holds.

LIFE
- Brown pelicans that circle and plunge-dive for fish, gulls on masts, lamps and roofs, a pod of bottlenose dolphins, manatees grazing the shallows and surfacing to breathe, fish schools, moon jellies; pad crew who leave before the count, hands on the quay, spectators who raise their arms at liftoff and landing.

RENDERING
- Engine plumes as glowing translucent cones (white-hot core, orange, shock diamonds low down, widening and turning blue-violet in thin air) that light the ground, the smoke and the rocket orange; steam and exhaust as soft lit puffs; soot streaks on flown boosters; shadows, refraction, caustics.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Roll out, Launch (Hold during the count), Land on ship / Land at pad, Storm. Space rolls out / launches. Taps: rocket = launch, hangar = roll out, drone ship / landing zone = choose landing site.
- Tallies: Launches, Landings, Fairings; status lines for the Rocket (T−/T+ timeline: Liftoff, Max Q, Stage separation, Boostback, Entry burn, Landing burn…), the Drone ship and the Fairing boat.
- Flavours: Lime, Curaçao, Blackcurrant. Sound toggle, pause, reset, view.
- All sounds synthesised with WebAudio, only for events (door motor, hydraulics, countdown beeps, engine roar loop while burning, sonic booms, touchdown thud, tug horn, winch, net catch, thunder) — no background ambience.
- Mobile bottom sheet, touch orbit, pinch zoom; a fallback message without WebGPU.
- Copy: "Launch Jelly. A spaceport on a low island, its rockets flying and coming home, set in a block of jelly." — "Roll it out. Light it up. Bring the booster home."

title: Far Cry 3 clone game (polished)
author: maxt3chno
prompt:
CLOSING THE GAP TO THE REFERENCE (Stages 6–11)

Stages 1–5 are done: the world, controller, outpost, water, sky, vegetation, hands, weapons, inventory, weather, time of day, audio and menus all work, and the layout already matches the reference. What's missing is image quality. Right now the frame looks like clean low-poly under a milky haze. The reference looks like a saturated, high-contrast, gritty, lived-in photograph. Stages 6–11 close that gap.

Global rules for Stages 6–11:
- Every new effect sits behind a quality flag. Low must stay fast.
- Don't break earlier stages: time of day, weather, rain, wetness and lightning must all still combine correctly. At the end of each stage, check Noon/Clear and Sunset/Storm once.
- Keep existing APIs compatible: getWaterHeight(x,z), addRipple(x,z,strength), setSkyState({...}), shared globals (wind, wetness, rain, time) and the effects event bus.
- Rebuild the standalone bundle after every change and do one console-error check. No test loops.
- Run each stage in a fresh session. Do only that stage.

────────────────────────
STAGE 6 — Light, atmosphere, color grading, dappled shadows (reasoning: High)
Goal: remove the milky haze and get a punchy tropical-noon frame with lace-like leaf shadows. This stage is the cheapest and has the biggest impact.

1. Haze/fog: cut daytime fog density and height sharply. Fog only lies low at the foot of the mountains and far out over the water. Aerial perspective is blue (#9cc3dc → #cfe6f5), never white. Mountains read in 3 depth layers, with more blue on each layer further back.
2. Sky: zenith ~#4f9fe0 fading to a #cfe6f5 horizon. Cumulus clouds get crisp, sunlit white tops, blue-grey undersides and a silver lining near the sun. Denser clouds, less smeared vapor.
3. Sun and ambient: stronger sun; darker, cooler ambient/hemisphere light so shadows go deep (shadowed areas at ~15–20% of lit brightness); warm bounce light from the sand.
4. Grading: an S-curve for contrast, saturation ~×1.25, slightly lower exposure, warm highlights and cool turquoise shadows. Add a contrast-adaptive sharpening pass after FXAA. Raise the bloom threshold so it never washes the frame out. God rays only through foliage, not across the whole screen. Make sure eye adaptation doesn't brighten the image back up.
5. Dappled shadows: add 1–2 palms over the shelter, with one trunk and its fronds framing the top-left of the starting view like the reference. Leaves cast alpha-tested shadows (custom depth/distance materials using the leaf mask). Also add an animated light cookie that projects leaf dapples inside the shelter and sways with the wind. Tighten the shadow frustum/cascade near the player so shadows on the table stay crisp.
6. Ambient occlusion: stronger SSAO where surfaces meet (table/deck, crates, legs, props on the table), plus small contact-shadow decals under objects.
7. First-person hands: warmer skin, a bit more fill light from the sand, and scale/position closer to the reference (large, low in frame).
Acceptance: the starting frame next to the reference has comparable contrast and saturation, a deep blue sky, and visible leaf dapples on the deck and table.

────────────────────────
STAGE 7 — FLAGSHIP WATER (reasoning: Max)
Goal: water is the star of the game, at modern AAA quality — something you'd watch for minutes. Rewrite the water module in depth, not as patches, while keeping the CPU height query (getWaterHeight) exactly in sync with the GPU surface.

7.1 Wave model
- Large swell: 6–8 Gerstner harmonics using the correct deep-water dispersion relation. The CPU height query evaluates the same harmonics (iterative inverse displacement).
- Fine surface: GPU FFT ocean spectrum (Phillips/JONSWAP) with ping-pong render targets, 128²–256², in 2–3 cascades at different scales. Output displacement, normals and a Jacobian map for foam. Low quality: 1 cascade at 64² or baked tileable normals.
- No visible tiling: non-multiple cascade sizes plus rotation. In the distance, filter normals (Toksvig/LEAN-style) instead of letting them shimmer.
- Shallow water: waves shoal (grow steeper and shorter as depth drops) and refract toward the shore along the seabed gradient. Inside the lagoon it's calm and almost mirror-like; beyond the reef it's livelier.

7.2 Optics
- Per-channel RGB Beer–Lambert absorption over the real underwater ray length (from the scene depth buffer), plus in-scattering (#1fb0b8 / #16739e). Result: 0–0.5 m of water is nearly colorless, 1–3 m is vivid turquoise (#46d6c8), 6 m and deeper is deep blue, with a sharp turquoise-to-blue edge at the reef drop-off like the reference.
- Screen-space refraction offset by the normal and scaled by depth. Use a depth test so objects above the surface don't leak into the refraction. Add subtle chromatic dispersion.
- Reflections: screen-space reflections (High) with a sky/PMREM fallback, plus a half-resolution planar reflection over the near lagoon (High) so the pier, boat and palms reflect properly. Schlick Fresnel with F0 = 0.02: clear up close, mirror-like at grazing angles.
- Sun: a tight GGX highlight plus stochastic micro-facet glitter sparkling on wave crests. A proper sun glitter path at sunset, a moon path at night.
- Subsurface scattering: backlit wave crests glow turquoise.
- The sky and clouds in reflections come from the same sky function, and clouds move in the reflection too.

7.3 Seabed, caustics, reef
- Animated caustics (layered Voronoi or a baked caustic texture with perspective warp), RGB chromatic split, intensity by depth. Project them onto everything underwater: sand, rocks, pier piles, boat hull, the player's legs. Caustics fade in shadow (sample the shadow map).
- Reef: 40–80 instanced coral/rock clusters on the lagoon floor (the dark patches in the reference), swaying seagrass, sand ripples on the bottom (normal map), scattered shells. The seabed gets its own darker wet material.
- Underwater light shafts when looking up from below the surface.

7.4 Shore and foam
- Swash: a thin sheet of water runs up the sand and drains back. It leaves a dark wet band that dries with a delay, and a bubbly foam line rides on its leading edge.
- Foam: a real procedural bubble/foam texture, not raw noise. It spawns on crests (from the FFT Jacobian), along the shoreline, and around rocks, piles and the boat (from depth difference). It persists and decays over time (an accumulation buffer on High).
- Rings of foam and small ripples around piles and rocks standing in the water.

7.5 Interactivity
- addRipple feeds a real height-field wave simulation: a 256² ping-pong grid centered on the player that scrolls with them. Stone splashes, bullet impacts, raindrops and the player's footsteps in water create rings that reflect and interfere physically.
- Wake/Kelvin-style bow waves from the player wading.
- Buoyancy: the boat, fallen crates, shells and stones bob using the height query plus the surface normal. The boat tugs at its mooring lines. Fix the boat: hull above the waterline, clearly visible next to the pier in the starting frame.
- Underwater mode (camera below the surface): water-colored underwater fog, distortion, caustic light shafts, muffled audio (emit an 'underwater' event for the audio system), and a correct half-in/half-out waterline split across the screen.

7.6 Weather and time hooks
- Expose every new parameter through water.setParams({...}), driven by the weather/time compositor: wind drives the spectrum (flat calm when clear → whitecaps in a storm), rain adds droplet rings to the height field plus surface roughness, night gives a moon path, sunset a golden path.

7.7 Performance
- High: FFT with 2 cascades at 256², planar reflection + SSR, height field at 256². Low: 1 cascade at 64² (or baked normals), no planar reflection/SSR, height field at 128². Target: water under ~4 ms per frame on a mid-range GPU at High.
Acceptance: the starting frame shows crystal-clear turquoise shallows with a visible reef and caustics, a crisp drop-off into deep blue, a living swash line on the beach, and the pier and boat reflected. A thrown stone produces physically believable interfering rings.

────────────────────────
STAGE 8 — Terrain: karst mountains, rocks, beach, jungle (reasoning: High)
1. Karst mountains: ridged-multifractal displacement on top of the current shapes, sheer vertical walls, ledges and erosion gullies. A slope-based shader: steep areas are grey limestone with vertical streaks; ledges and gentle slopes are green canopy (a crown-shaped noise with occlusion between crowns). Thousands of cheap instanced canopy billboards on the slopes (one draw call). The sea arch and rock islet use the same materials.
2. Boulders: noise-deformed rocks with sharp ridged facets, grouped in clusters of 3–7, half-buried in sand or water, moss on top, and a dark wet band at the waterline. Triplanar texturing.
3. Jungle: broadleaf trees with clumped card-based crowns; palms of different ages and leans; dense undergrowth on the right-hand slope (ferns, bushes, banana/monstera) at 3–4× the current density with LODs; vines between trees; grass along the beach edge. No more "lawn": dark soil and leaf litter under the trees.
4. Beach: wind ripples (normal map), a wet band synced with the Stage 7 swash, pebbles, driftwood, fallen palm fronds, coconuts; a gradual transition from sand to soil to jungle, with grass.
5. Move the hut and the watchtower 20–30% closer into the starting frame if it doesn't break collisions or paths.

────────────────────────
STAGE 9 — Next-level procedural materials (reasoning: High)
All generators produce albedo/normal/roughness(/AO) maps at 1024² (512² on Low), cached.
1. Old weathered wood: stretched-noise grain, knots, cracks, a different tone and UV offset per plank, dark seams, grime in the corners, sun bleaching, worn light edges (from curvature). No striped "zebra" look. Used for the deck, table, pier, crates and posts.
2. Metal: paint → chipping → rust, driven by curvature/noise masks, plus rust streaks and scratches (barrel, ammo can, lantern). The mug gets chipped enamel.
3. Fabric: canvas with visible weave, stains and faded folds. Flags in faded rust-brown (#a8352a → rust), with torn alpha edges and a dirty skull.
4. Leopard pelt: correct rosette pattern plus fur shells (4–6 layers, High only) or a dense normal map, with a jagged hide edge.
5. Rope: twisted-fiber normals, thicker, frayed ends.
6. Rock and sand: triplanar mapping, moss by normal direction; grainy sand with tiny crystal glints in the sun.
If hand-made tileable PBR texture sets exist locally, use them instead of the matching generator (and embed them in the standalone bundle).

────────────────────────
STAGE 10 — Foreground props + custom models (reasoning: Medium)
1. Load any local .glb models from the models folder through the existing loader, keeping the procedural fallback. For each model: real-world scale in meters, grounding on its surface, colliders, shadows, wetness injection, and the Stage 3 interactions (inspecting the lantern/mug/map; the crate lid opens if the model has a separate lid part, otherwise keep the procedural lid).
2. Table: make the props larger and lay them out like the reference — the AK diagonally across the whole table, the knife on the front edge, the map under the knife, the mug, the ammo can, the lantern on the right, the bottle.
3. Left side: the cot (tube frame, sagging canvas, a plump pillow), the pelt hanging over its edge, a backpack and a crate next to the cot, a rusty barrel.
4. A torn flag hanging from the canopy at the top right, like the reference; rope lashings on the posts.
5. The boat moored at the pier (buoyancy from Stage 7), a crate on the pier, mooring ropes to the piles.
6. Hut and watchtower: corrugated tin roof, canvas awning, barrels, crates.

────────────────────────
STAGE 11 — Performance + final match against the reference (reasoning: Medium)
1. An FPS/frame-time overlay (F3) with a per-pass breakdown. Budget: ≥60 FPS on High on a mid-range discrete GPU, ≥30 FPS on Low on a modern iGPU.
2. Optimize: instancing, LODs, distance culling, half-resolution for the expensive passes, cached and compressed textures, proper disposal.
3. Take one screenshot from the starting view next to the reference and do a final palette tune. Check every time-of-day × weather combination.
4. Rebuild the bundle, do one console check, update the status log.

title: Jelly eyeball model comparison
author: semichenkko
prompt:
Build a single-file HTML + Three.js interactive scene called "Jelly / Eyeball."

Look: premium product render on a clean white background. One large gummy eyeball sits on the floor in the center - milky translucent jelly sclera with fine red veins, a glowing blue iris with radial fibers, a glossy black pupil and a clear wet cornea bulge on top. A red gummy optic nerve trails behind it on the floor. Soft colored glow and a soft shadow underneath. Around the edges: small jelly pumpkins (purple, green, orange), jelly beans and candy corn, all glossy and translucent. Physically based materials (transmission, clearcoat), environment reflections, ACES tone mapping, soft shadows.

The eye is a real soft body - deformation happens in the vertex shader so the sclera, iris, pupil and cornea all bend together:
1. It always watches the cursor, and keeps finding you even after it rolls.
2. Tap it - a gooey dent with a ripple, jelly eyelids blink, the pupil contracts, and it does a small hop.
3. Grab and drag it - the grabbed spot stretches toward the cursor like taffy into a teardrop. Lift it up and it dangles and sways with gravity.
4. Flick and release - it gets thrown with the hand's velocity plus a slingshot recoil from the stretch. It squashes and stretches along its velocity in flight, splats on the floor and walls with a big squash, bounces, rolls (the iris rolls with it), then wobbles and rights itself to look back at you.
5. Pull it sideways and let go - it snaps back like a slingshot.
6. Grab the nerve - it is a verlet rope, so you can lift the eye by it and swing it around.
7. Double-tap - hypnotized: the pupil dilates and the gaze spins in circles.
8. Hard landings make it dizzy - its eyes wander for a moment.

title: Network Graph
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second force-directed network graph: 72 members of a fictional makerspace join one by one, five communities take color, and the shortest path between two members lights up.

<inputs>
- Network: Copperwick Makerspace (fictional), 72 members in five workshops: Woodshop 18, Electronics 16, Textiles 14, Ceramics 13, Print Studio 11.
- Title: "Who knows whom at Copperwick". Subtitle: "72 members, 5 workshops".
- Path: from Ottilie (Textiles) to Bram (Electronics). Readout: "Ottilie to Bram: 4 introductions".
- Length: 10 seconds.
If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Data: generate the graph once at load from a seeded PRNG (mulberry32, seed 72) as a stochastic block model: two members of the same workshop are linked with probability 0.24, members of different workshops with probability 0.014; if any component is cut off, link it to the nearest hub. Choose Ottilie and Bram as a Textiles member and an Electronics member whose breadth-first-search distance is exactly 4 (re-seed if no such pair exists). The readout's number is that BFS distance, and the lit path is a BFS shortest path.
Palette: ground #0A1230 with a very soft radial lift to #10194A behind the graph's center; nodes before coloring #C7CEE0; communities Woodshop #F2A541, Electronics #4CC9F0, Textiles #F25F8B, Ceramics #8BD17C, Print Studio #B79CFF; edges 1.2px #C7CEE0 at 16%, and edges inside a community take its color at 30% once it is colored; the path #FFFFFF. Node radius 6 + 2.2·√degree px, each with a 2px ring of the ground color so edges read as passing behind.
Type: "Red Hat Display" 700 for the title (56px), 500 for the subtitle (26px), 600 for workshop and person labels (24px); "Red Hat Mono" 500 for the readout (28px) and legend counts (22px).
Layout: title top-left at x 96, baselines y 120 and 162. The graph fits a 1,100 × 740 box centered at (1060, 560). Legend bottom-left at x 96 from y 840: five rows with 14px dots, workshop names and member counts. Readout right-aligned at x 1824, baseline y 1000.
Physics is precomputed, never live: at load, simulate the whole piece at a fixed step of 1/120s and store every node's position per step; seek(t) interpolates between stored steps. Forces: springs on links (rest length 64px inside a workshop, 150px across), pairwise repulsion falling off with distance, a weak pull to the center, collision keeping circles 4px apart, and velocity damping. Each joining node reheats the system a little; after the last join it cools so the layout is completely still (under 0.3px per frame) by 8.0s.
Joining: members enter in a seeded order in which each newcomer already has a neighbor present; it spawns 24px from that neighbor and scales 0 → 1 over 0.25s on cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1), its links drawing out from the existing ends over 0.2s.
Camera: fit the bounding box of the nodes present, averaged over the previous 0.6s (10 samples), so it eases out as the graph grows; zoom stays between 0.85× and 1.6×.
Color: each community floods from its highest-degree member outward by hop distance inside the workshop, 90ms per hop, each node crossfading from gray to its color over 0.25s.
Path: rings mark the search: every node at distance 1, then 2, 3 and 4 from Ottilie gets one thin 1.5px white ring that grows and fades once (0.4s), never repeated. The path's edges then draw in white at 3.5px, 0.22s per hop; path nodes scale to 1.25× with 3px white rings; everything else dims to 30%; a 6px white dot travels the path once (0.8s, easeInOutSine). Person labels sit on the outer side of their node, clear of edges.
The real thing is a layout with mass: nodes ease in and stop, thin edges let the structure read, and color arrives only when it means something. The cheap version is neon spaghetti: glow on everything, a label on every node, endless jitter.
Banned: glow or bloom, 3D, labels on every node, rainbow edges, jitter in the hold, nodes teleporting, rings that repeat, graph libraries, emoji, anything flashing more than 3 times per second.
</direction>

0.0–0.6s: ground; the title and subtitle rise 12px and fade in.

6.6–7.8s: the path draws hop by hop; the rest dims to 30%; the dot travels; the readout types on at 30ms per character.

8.6–10.0s: hold, perfectly still.
Other lengths: stretch the join phase first; keep the settle and the hold at least 1s each.
</structure>

- On foot: a striding figure: round head, tapered torso, legs in a stride.

title: Animated bento feature grid for a product site
author: Kubai087
prompt:
# Small animations for a product site's feature tiles

Give every tile in my site's feature grid a small animation: a tiny scene that shows what the feature does.

## 0. Before you build
- Read the project: find out the tech stack (plain HTML/CSS, React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind, Framer Motion…) and build it the way the project already does. Don't add an animation library unless the project already uses one.
- Ask me which look to use:
A. The Lumno material below, as written.
B. My product's own style: take the colors, radii, borders and shadows from my existing design tokens and components, and keep only the structure and motion rules from this prompt.
C. A mix: the Lumno material in my brand's accent color and radii.
- Picking features: if I named features, animate those. If not, read the product's site, docs or code, list 3–5 features that a short scene can explain, and let me pick.

## 1. Lumno material (option A)
Overall: quiet, neutral, precise. Hairlines instead of borders, soft shadows tinted warm, no gradients or color washes, one accent color.

- Grid: one card with an outer radius of 28px. Cells are separated by 1px hairlines (a 1px grid gap over a hairline color). Cells are white. The card has a faint hairline ring and a soft shadow.
- Art panel: inset 8px from the cell edge, with a radius of the card radius minus the inset (20px), so corners stay concentric.
- Fill #fafafa, plus an inner 1px ring: box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(32,38,46,.07).
- Texture: background: repeating-linear-gradient(-45deg, rgba(32,38,46,.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 7px).
- The scene sits centred on the panel, about 126×118px.
- Text bars: body bars 4px tall with a 2px radius in #e5e9ef; heading bars 5px tall in #cdd4de. Vary the widths (34–92px).
- Mini windows and cards: white with a 9px radius.
- Shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(47,42,34,.06), 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(47,42,34,.25).
- Tab strip: 20px tall, #eef1f5. Tabs: 16px tall with 6px top corners; the active tab is white.
- Favicons: 10px.
- Inner surfaces such as charts or fields: #f4f6fa. Secondary data: #b9c9e0. Accent: #3462ad, used only on the result.
- Icon chip (top-left of each tile): 32px, 10px radius, 1px border rgba(32,38,46,.1), white, shadow 0 1px 2px rgba(32,38,46,.05), a line-style glyph in #4b5563.
- Text color: a warm near-black, #2f2a22.
- Hover: the cell darkens to about 2.5% grey; the panel goes to #f4f5f6 with its ring at .09; the icon chip grows 32→36px from its top-left corner, its glyph turns to the text color, and its shadow deepens slightly.
- Dark mode (suggested values; keep the same relationships):
- Cells #17181a, panel #1d1f22, inner ring rgba(255,255,255,.06), texture rgba(255,255,255,.04).
- Body bars #2c2f34, heading bars #3a3e45.
- Windows #24272b with a 1px rgba(255,255,255,.06) outline and a shadow of 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(0,0,0,.6).
- Tab strip #1a1c1f, accent #6f9bea, text #ecebe8.

## 2. Scene
- One idea per tile: 2–4 moves that show "action → result", such as "click → a small window opens" or "change here → the other side syncs".
- Abstract wireframes only: no screenshots and no real text. Use at most one small icon where something needs to be recognisable.
- Motion: ease-out for movement, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1); a slight spring for appearing, cubic-bezier(.34,1.4,.64,1). Each move takes 250–600ms; the whole scene is done in about 3s.
- Icon chip: when the tile plays, its glyph redraws stroke by stroke (draw, pop or slide per part), then hands back to the solid icon.

## 3. Playback
- Resting styles are the final frame. Animations only describe where things come from (fill-mode: both or equivalent), so reduced motion shows the result and an interrupted play never jumps.
- The art panel fades in (opacity, plus translateY 6px and scale .97 to none) as its tile first plays.
- Play once in view: when about 70% of the tile is visible, wait ~200ms, then play. Tiles that enter together go ~250ms apart, in reading order. Stop on the final frame.
- One "played" state (a class or data attribute) drives every animation in the tile. To replay: remove it, force a reflow, add it back (or re-key in a framework).
- On mouse hover (mouse only) or keyboard focus, replay: blur the final frame out over ~160ms (blur 6px, opacity 0), restart under the blur, then clear it. Don't restart a play that hasn't finished.
- Optional loop on hover: while the pointer stays on the tile, replay again ~600ms after each play ends. When the pointer leaves, finish the current play and rest on the final frame.
- Touch: a tap follows the tile's link; nothing depends on hover.
- prefers-reduced-motion: reduce: no animation; show the final frame.

## 4. Colors and dark mode
- Every color is a variable on the art panel (panel, ring, texture, bars, windows, tab strip, accent, shadow); no hard-coded colors in the rules.
- Follow prefers-color-scheme, and the project's manual theme switch too (a class or data-theme), if it has one.
- Check it in both light and dark.

## 5. Delivery
- Mark the art as decorative (aria-hidden) and keep translatable text out of it.
- Check it in a real browser: first play, hover replay, keyboard focus, reduced motion, dark mode and a phone-width layout.

title: Orbit landing page with and without TasteSkill
author: itsluneri
prompt:
Build a complete, production-quality landing page for Orbit, a project management platform for small product teams.
Orbit combines projects, tasks, discussions, documents, and weekly progress updates in one workspace. Its core purpose is to let teams understand what is happening without constantly asking for updates or scheduling status meetings.
Technical requirements
Build the website using Next.js, React, and TypeScript.
Use TSX components and a proper Next.js project structure. Do not create a plain HTML/CSS website.
The implementation should be clean, componentized, responsive, and production-quality. Use modern CSS or Tailwind CSS for styling where appropriate.
Do not merely describe the implementation. Build the complete working page.
Visual reference
Use the provided reference image as the primary art-direction reference.
Match its overall visual character very closely: typography treatment, density, spacing philosophy, texture, contrast, borders, surface treatment, visual weight, image treatment, and general design atmosphere.
However, do not copy the reference website or recreate its content.
Do not copy its:
branding
text or copy
logos
illustrations
exact layout
individual components
imagery
proprietary visual assets
Instead, understand the design language behind the reference and reinterpret it for Orbit.
For example, if the reference uses grain, paper texture, sharp borders, muted surfaces, unusual typography, dense layouts, editorial spacing, or a particular treatment of imagery, use those qualities as inspiration while creating an original design.
The finished page should clearly belong to the same visual world as the reference while still being an original website.
Page
The hero should immediately explain Orbit and show a convincing view of the actual product.
Throughout the page, create realistic Orbit UI showing projects, tasks, assignees, discussions, documents, statuses, deadlines, and weekly updates.
Include the sections that genuinely help sell the product, such as:
Hero
Product demonstration

Core workflow
Features
Team use cases
Integrations
Customer proof
Pricing
FAQ
Final CTA
You may change, combine, reorder, or remove sections when doing so produces a stronger page.
Design quality
Avoid the stereotypical AI-generated SaaS aesthetic.
No purple gradient hero.
No glowing blobs.
No glassmorphism.
No giant collection of rounded cards.
No endless 3-column feature grids.
No random floating icons.
No meaningless charts.
No fake AI functionality.
No excessive pills.
No generic startup illustrations.
No repetitive centered sections.
Do not make every element a card or container.
Use typography, composition, whitespace, texture, product UI, imagery, and hierarchy to create visual interest.
The product UI itself should be detailed and believable. Keep names, projects, dates, statuses, and other information consistent across different product previews.
Copy should be concise and specific. Avoid phrases such as “supercharge your workflow,” “unlock your potential,” and other generic SaaS language.
Add subtle, intentional interactions and motion where they improve the experience. Avoid animation for animation's sake.
Make the page excellent on desktop and mobile.
The final result should feel designed, not generated.
Take the reference image seriously. Analyze its design system first, then translate that design language into an original Orbit website.
Do not ask me to choose colors, fonts, layouts, libraries, or design direction. Make those decisions yourself and implement the complete site.

title: Pixel-art floating island lido across four models
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Build "Deep End": an open-air lido on a floating island of earth and rock, rendered as a real-time 3D scene in pixel art (three.js, orthographic isometric camera rendering into a small low-res target, no anti-aliasing, depth-buffer outlines, every pixel snapped to a fixed 64-colour palette matched in OKLab; quarter-turn rotation, zoom, pixel-size slider, Raw 3D toggle).
Scene: a 25 m lap pool and a 5 m deep diving pool cut into a concrete deck; 1 m and 3 m springboards that visibly bend; a 1930s concrete diving tower with platforms at 5, 7.5 and 10 m and an open stair; striped changing cabins with a clock, a kiosk, loungers and parasols; a judges' table.
Diving meet with real physics: each dive is flown, not animated — takeoff speed and angular momentum are solved to land the somersaults, angular momentum is conserved so tucking spins the diver faster and kicking out slows them to line up the entry. Divers kick out slightly early or late (more on harder dives), the entry angle sets the splash, five judges hold up score cards, highest and lowest are dropped, the rest are multiplied by the degree of difficulty. Events: 10 m, 3 m, free swim.
Water: each pool surface is a wave-equation height field (~20 cm cells) — entries, strokes, rain and clicks make rings that bounce off the walls; shaded from its normals with sun glints and a mirrored reflection of the lido; caustics on the tiled floor.
People: box-rig figures with two-bone IK — swimmers doing freestyle, breaststroke and backstroke with flip turns; divers swim to the ladder, shower, sit in the warm tub and climb again; children who run and get whistled at by the lifeguard; wet footprints on the deck that dry in the sun.
Light and weather: day / dusk / night (pool lights glow underwater, tower floodlights at night), dry / rain (rain rings the water and darkens the deck). Click the water to make a splash. prompt:
Build "Geyser Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama for a "Material Studies" series: a volcanic Icelandic island set inside a translucent block of jelly sea, viewed as a tabletop object on a pale paper studio backdrop.

- One self-contained HTML file: plain JS + WGSL, no libraries, no network requests (Google Fonts optional). WebGPU only, with a clean fallback screen if WebGPU/adapter is missing or the device is lost.

- Sea = linear shallow-water sim on a ~168² grid (heights + face velocities, a little surface tension, damping), fed by the block's tilt. Render the water with refraction of the scene behind, colored absorption through the jelly, light shafts, caustics on the bed, foam/white water, a bright meniscus on the cut faces. Cut faces of the ground show candy-coloured strata, basalt, tephra bands and turf.
- Sun shadow map, MSAA, HDR with a soft shoulder tone map. Fixed-step simulation (240 Hz bodies, 120 Hz water). Expose a debug handle on window for tests.

THE ISLAND (procedural height field + ground cover: moss, grass, sinter, scoria)
- Back-left: a scoria cone volcano with a real crater bowl holding a lava lake (dark crust plates with glowing seams), patchy summit snow. A lava channel runs from a flank vent with a spatter cone down into the sea, glowing ribbon with drifting crust; it keeps glowing under the jelly water; constant steam where it meets the sea. Warm lava light on nearby ground.
- Back-right: a grassy plateau that ends in sheer columnar-basalt cliffs on its seaward side, three basalt sea stacks with grassy tops, puffins on the ledges, a small square orange lighthouse.
- Middle: a geothermal valley — a pale sinter mound with orange bacterial runoff streaks, the geyser pool (blue over a dark vent), two milky-turquoise hot springs and one clear deep-blue one, a grey bubbling mud pot with expanding rings, fumarole steam. A timber boardwalk arcs round the front of the geyser with tourists on it, with paths to the jetty, the church and the lagoon.
- Front-left: a milky blue lagoon in white silica banks, a timber deck with a ladder, a black-timber bathhouse with a turf roof, bathers drifting up to their shoulders.
- Front-right: a meadow with three turf houses (grass roofs; white, red and tarred gables), a little white church with a red roof and spire inside a turf wall, a flagpole with a fluttering Icelandic flag, a fenced paddock with five Icelandic horses (chestnut with flaxen mane, black, grey, palomino, bay).
- A jetty on piles out to a T-head where a whale-watching boat berths; a small ticket hut. Black-sand beaches, lava boulders, kelp, urchins and sea stars on the sea floor.

THE GEYSER (Strokkur)
Cycle every ~15–20 s on its own: refill → rest (simmering, occasional bulges) → surge (three growing heaves, gurgling, wisps of steam) → a turquoise dome swells and quivers → it bursts: a white churning water column (20–35 m in the UI; 1 unit = 20 m) shoots up ballistically, hundreds of streaked drops rain back down and drift with the wind, the column breaks apart from the bottom up, a big steam cloud rolls off downwind, the sinter goes dark and wet, then the pool drains with a gurgle. Tourists raise their arms and cheer; some hold up phones during the surge.

THE VOLCANO
Tremor: the block shakes, ash billows from the crater, lava bombs fly (thud and smoke on land, hiss, steam and a splash at sea, glowing then cooling), the lava lake rises and brightens, the flow speeds up, horses bolt round the paddock, puffins take off, and the geyser goes off.

LIFE
- Humpback whale (knobbly head, long white flippers, grooved pale throat, broad flukes): cruises offshore, surfaces and blows 2–3 times (spray plumes), arches and shows its flukes as it dives, stays deep, avoids the boat and shallow water. About once a minute (or on demand) it breaches: sounds deep, turns to an open spot, rushes up, leaps clear while twisting, crashes onto its back with a huge splash, foam and a ring wave across the bay that rocks the boat.
- The boat "Hafdís" (old oak fishing boat: dark blue hull, red bottom, white wheelhouse, passengers in bright jackets): lies at the jetty ~40 s, then casts off and does a loop round the bay on a smooth filleted route, slowing right down when the whale is near, rides the waves with heave/pitch/roll, makes a wake, puffs exhaust, comes back alongside.
- Atlantic puffins: stand on the cliff edge and stacks, stretch their wings, whirr out over the bay, land on the water, dive and chase fish underwater, fly home and land.
- People: 9 tourists on the boardwalk (sometimes shuffle to another spot), walkers on the paths and jetty, 6 bathers in the lagoon. Horses graze, wander, trot when startled. A school of fish in the bay flees threats.
- Steam, ash and spray are soft translucent puffs drawn after the water with premultiplied alpha, broken up with noise, rising, spreading and drifting downwind.

UI
- Left: eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", big italic serif title "Geyser / Jelly.", subtitle "A volcanic island with a geyser, set in a block of jelly sea." Bottom-left: "How to play" with the line "Set off the geyser. Shake the volcano. Watch for the whale." and a small paragraph of hints. Top-right: status pill "WebGPU · Live".
- Right glass panel: buttons Erupt / Tremor / Breach / Cast off (→ Full ahead); disabled with labels like "Surging…", "Erupting…", "Draining…", "Refilling…" when not ready. A thin liveliness meter. Tallies: Eruptions, Tallest (m), Breaches. Status lines "Strokkur: Resting 5 s / Surging / Erupting · 24 m / Draining / Refilling 68%" and "Hafdís: Alongside 18 s / Casting off / Under way 40% / Whale ahead / Coming alongside".

- Interaction: tap the geyser, the volcano, the whale or the boat to trigger them (hand cursor on hover); Space sounds the boat's horn and puts the puffins up; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the block's side to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; wheel/pinch to zoom. On phones the panel becomes a bottom sheet with a "Controls" bar; no page scroll at any size.
- Sound: synthesized with Web Audio, only for events — surge bubbling, dome thump, eruption roar and spray hiss, drain gurgle, tremor rumble with rattles, bomb thuds and hisses, whale blow, breach rush and splash, boat horn, puffin and mud plops. No background ambience.

QUALITY BAR
Charming, legible miniature scale; nothing sticks through the water surface by mistake; no NaNs under stress (repeated tremors, eruptions, breaches, shaking, stirring). Verify with headless screenshots and an end-to-end browser test of every control, the geyser cycle order, the boat round trip, the breach, taps, flavours, sliders, pause, camera, mobile sheet and fallbacks — with zero console errors.

title: Jelly watermelon slicing simulation
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create "Melon Jelly Knife" — a single self-contained HTML file (melon-jelly-knife.html) with an interactive, physically simulated gummy watermelon slice that you can pull like jelly AND cut into pieces with a visible steel knife that animates every cut.

── Platform ──
- WebGPU + WGSL only, all JS/CSS inline, no external libraries. ES module in one <script type="module">.
- If navigator.gpu / adapter is missing, show an elegant editorial fallback card ("This specimen needs WebGPU.") with a specific explanation — never fake it with a lesser renderer. Disable the controls in that state.
- Recover from device loss (rebuild the renderer up to twice), surface WGSL compile errors via getCompilationInfo.
- Fixed 60 Hz simulation step with an accumulator (max 3 steps/frame), ¼-speed toggle, pause (Space), keyboard: N nudge, R reset, K toggle knife, H hand.

── Page design (editorial "material study") ──
- Warm paper studio backdrop #E2DFDA; the 3D floor is an infinite studio sweep that tones to exactly this colour.
- Top-left masthead: small caps label "MATERIAL STUDIES / NO. 009", huge italic serif title "Melon / Jelly." (second line indented), and a 3-line serif tagline.
- Top-right status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE / PAUSED / UNAVAILABLE".
- Right panel (thin 1px borders, translucent paper): Tool (Hand | Knife segmented buttons with small line icons), Variety swatches (Crimson, Golden, Rosé — each recolours flesh, rind, seeds, shadow tint and the UI accent), sliders Firmness (trembling ↔ set) and Internal damping (lively ↔ syrupy), buttons "Give it a nudge", Reset, Pause, checkboxes ¼ speed and Show mesh.
- Bottom-left: tool hint in italic serif, live readouts row (Mass ≈ g, Volume % of rest, Kinetic µJ, Pieces) with an "illustrative scale" footnote (1 sim unit ≈ 3.5 cm, gummy 1.3 g/cm³).
- Bottom-right collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes explaining the physics, rendering and the cutting method in plain prose.
- A dashed SVG guide line while drawing a knife stroke; small toast messages ("Missed — draw the blade across the slice.", "Too thin to cut there.", "That's plenty of pieces.").
- The camera frames the slice inside the free area between masthead, panel and readouts (lens shift), orbits on empty-space drag, zooms on wheel, double-click resets view, gently follows the slice if it is thrown far.
- Responsive: under ~860px the layout stacks (masthead, canvas ~58vh, hint, panel) with 44px+ touch targets; prefers-reduced-motion softens the intro and damping.

── The slice ──
- A thick (T ≈ 0.58) wedge of watermelon: sector with ~32° half-angle, inner radius ~1.62, all corners rounded in plane (ρ = 0.17) and top/bottom edges bevelled (~0.13).
- Layers by depth from the rind: dark green skin with irregular darker stripes, a pale cream-green band, then translucent red flesh; black teardrop seeds arranged in arcs and a few tiny air bubbles suspended inside.
- Rendered as translucent candy: screen-space refraction of the scene behind, per-pixel thickness from a back-face depth pass, Beer–Lambert absorption per refracted tap (capped by back thickness so seeds don't halo), jittered blur, subsurface-like scatter and glow toward the key light, Fresnel + GGX highlights, soft studio environment (procedural softboxes).
- Floor: PCSS-lite soft shadow from a key light behind-left-above (shadow tinted by the flesh colour), contact AO from a top-down height map. MSAA ×4, HDR, PBR-Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.

── Physics (feels like real gummy candy) ──
- Tetrahedral soft body (Delaunay of a jittered lattice inside the shape), XPBD with small steps (~10 substeps, 1 iteration each):
• co-rotational per-tet shape matching (mass-weighted covariance, Müller quaternion rotation extraction, uniform stiffness fraction) — no inversions, no ghost torque;
• per-tet volume constraints (near-incompressible);
• edge relative-velocity damping controlled by the damping slider; firmness maps to shape compliance on a log scale;
• floor contact with static/kinetic friction, light air drag, settle-damping when nearly at rest, speed cap, NaN guard with gentle reset.
- Hand tool: grab anywhere (ray pick on the skinned surface, forgiving screen-space fallback), soft patch attachment (radius ~0.4) that follows the pointer on a camera-facing plane, reach limit, never pushed into the floor; wheel or a second finger twists the held patch. Nudge = a playful impulse. Reset drops the whole slice again.
- Render mesh is skinned to the tets by barycentric embedding; normals recomputed each frame.

── Cutting into pieces ──
- The world is a list of pieces. Each piece is a convex polygon I in the slice's rest plane; its outline is I dilated by a disk of radius ρ (rounded corners), extruded to the slice thickness with the same bevels, rind layers, seeds and bubbles (seeds/bubbles kept only where they fit inside).
- A cut maps a world plane into each crossed piece's rest frame (best-fit rigid frame of the deformed piece), intersects it with the mid-plane → a straight line; clip I into two halves offset by ±ρ so both rebuilt outlines meet exactly at the cut; reject slivers ("too thin").
- All pieces are concatenated into ONE simulation (component id per particle) and ONE render mesh; each piece is its own soft body you can grab, stretch and cut again; pieces collide with each other (AABB-pruned particle–particle pushes, a few mm per pass so fresh faces ease apart instead of popping). Max 14 pieces. Built meshes are cached per piece so Reset is instant.
- State transfer on every rebuild: new rest particles are embedded in the old tets and take over interpolated positions and velocities.

── The visible knife (the star of this version) ──
- A small nakiri-style vegetable knife modelled procedurally: rectangular blade (length ~1.72, height ~0.63 — taller than the slice), straight edge with a slight lift and rounded nose at the front, thin ground bevel along the edge, flat grind to a ~0.03 spine, sharp creases (duplicated vertices), polished steel bolster, oval walnut handle that swells slightly with three steel rivets and flat end caps. Local frame: +x toward the tip, edge on y=0.
- Materials in the scene shader: brushed steel with a product-shot gradient (dark board reflected low, bright sweep high), softbox streaks, satin lighter bevel, mirror bolster; walnut with straight grain, satin oil sheen, rivets. Posed rigidly on the CPU each frame.
- The knife is drawn in the scene pass (behind the jelly surface), so the part buried in the jelly is seen refracted through it; it casts a shadow but stays out of the AO height map.
- Behaviour:
• Hover (knife tool): the knife floats ~0.42 above the slice with its edge exactly under the cursor, blade side-on to the camera, slightly rolled toward the viewer; it drops in from above when the tool is selected; hidden in hand mode.
• While drawing: it lines up along the stroke, edge just above the jelly, handle always on the left (canonical direction relative to camera right).
• On release: the stroke read on the surface it was drawn over defines a VERTICAL blade plane; the split is planned and the new pieces + new soft body are pre-built immediately (so the swap later costs only ~10 ms and there is no hitch mid-animation).
• Choreography (~1.1 s, respects ¼ speed and pause): align (0.16 s) → press: the edge sinks ~0.13 below the top and a physical collider pushes the jelly into a rounded groove under it — it squashes before it gives (to 0.42 s) → break-through: the new world is swapped in, the blade continues to the board while a wedge collider eases the two new faces apart (limited to a few mm per substep, gap growing with depth) and holds the cut lips down at the break-through depth → short hold → lift back to hover, releasing the lips so they spring back with a jiggle.
• Misses show a toast and the knife stays put; new strokes are ignored while a cut is animating; Reset cancels it.

── Quality bar ──
- Smooth 60 fps on a mid-range laptop GPU; no allocations in the frame loop except on cuts.
- Deterministic test hook on window (e.g. __melon with sim, camera, pick, planCut, startCut, advance(seconds), per-piece stats) so the animation can be stepped and screenshotted.
- Polished, calm, museum-like typography; everything readable on phone and desktop.
