title: Jelly physics simulation improvement comparison
author: vib3coded
prompt:
Create Citrus Jelly — an interactive 3D scene featuring a gummy orange slice. Everything must run directly in the browser in a single HTML file using WebGPU and WGSL shaders. Build genuine volumetric 3D geometry, not an image or a prerecorded animation.
APPEARANCE
A thick semicircular orange slice with vibrant orange flesh, a pale pith layer, and a firmer outer rind.

Visible radial segments, thin internal membranes, and tiny bubbles.
A juicy, translucent gummy material with soft highlights, light refraction, and depth-dependent color.
Avoid making it look like rigid plastic or glass.
Use a light cream background, soft studio lighting, and a contact shadow. Avoid overexposure.
PHYSICS AND INTERACTION

Let users grab any visible point with a mouse or finger and pull it.

Deformation must originate at the grab point and propagate naturally through neighboring areas.
The flesh should stretch and narrow under tension, while the rind offers more resistance.
On release, the slice should spring back gently, with oscillations gradually settling.
Use a stable soft-body simulation: a spring mesh or volumetric elastic constraints with volume preservation.
Segments, membranes, and bubbles must deform with the flesh rather than separating or floating independently.
Include ground collisions: the slice should squash slightly on impact and wobble afterward.
Prevent instant snapping back, endless oscillation, and exploding geometry.
INTERFACE

A minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace.

A large italic serif heading, “Citrus Jelly.”, on the left.
A compact control panel on the right with Firmness and Internal damping sliders.
Give it a nudge, Reset, and Pause buttons.
Show mesh and ¼ speed toggles.
Three color presets: Orange, Blood Orange, and Lemon.
A small interaction hint: “Grab. Stretch. Let go.”
All labels in English, with comfortable desktop and mobile controls.
TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS

Genuine WebGPU rendering, not a Canvas 2D substitute.

Generate geometry and materials in code without premade models.
Use a fixed simulation timestep and constraints that prevent excessive stretching.
Maintain smooth performance during grabbing, dragging, and release.
Display a clear fallback message when WebGPU is unavailable.
Test different grab locations, strong stretching, oscillation decay, collisions, and reset.
The main priority is a convincing gummy feel. The slice should look soft, juicy, and so satisfying in motion that people want to keep stretching it.

Title: "SUNNY HOLLOW: AFTER HOURS"
You are a night watchman at Sunny Hollow Studios, an abandoned 1990s children's TV studio. The show's animatronic puppet hosts were shut down after the show was cancelled (last live broadcast: May 17, 1996), but at night they still try to "finish the broadcast". Survive from 12 AM to 6 AM in a small control booth using cameras, shutters, door lights, a ceiling-vent seal and an audio lure, while managing a draining generator.

## Tech
- Single self-contained index.html (HTML + CSS + JS). Three.js r128 UMD from cdnjs (https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js). No external assets: all models are low-poly primitives, all textures are procedural canvas textures (felt, wood, rust, tiles, wallpaper, posters), all sound is generated with the Web Audio API.
- Desktop Chrome at 60 fps. Mouse controls plus keyboard shortcuts.
- Every room is its own THREE.Scene with its own camera, so only the viewed room is rendered. Pre-compile all shaders at boot (renderer.compile on every scene, with the puppets temporarily added) so the first camera flip doesn't hitch.
- Adaptive resolution: render the 3D into a render target at 0.85x. If the average frame time stays above 25 ms for 2.5 s, drop the internal scale by 0.15 (minimum 0.5).
- Add `[hidden]{display:none!important}` to the CSS so hidden overlay screens never block clicks.
- Save progress in localStorage (current night, beaten nights, stars, unlocks, custom-night sliders), wrapped in try/catch.

## Post-processing (full-screen shader)
VHS/CRT pass over everything: scanlines, film grain, chromatic aberration, a rolling tracking band, line jitter, vignette, a full-static mix, a red flash and a darkness fade. Use three presets: office (subtle), camera (strong scanlines, barrel distortion, green tint, more noise) and menu.

## Core loop
- 1 in-game hour = 60 real seconds (12 AM → 6 AM = 6 minutes).
- Mouse near the left/right 22% of the screen turns the view smoothly. Yaw is clamped to ±60°. Arrow keys work as a backup.
- Generator: 100% at start. Usage = 1 (base) + tablet 1 + each door light 1 + each closed shutter 2 + vent seal 1 + lure 1 (for 3 s). Drain = usage × 0.1% per second × night multiplier (N1 0.9, N2 0.95, N3 1.0, N4 1.03, N5 1.06, N6 1.14, custom 1.1). Show POWER LEFT % and colored usage bars.
- At 0%: shutters open, all lights die, cameras disabled. After 4–9 s Mr. Antler appears in the left doorway with eyes pulsing to a generated music-box melody (5–18 s), then 2 s of total darkness, then a jumpscare. If 6 AM arrives first, the player wins.
- 6 AM: chime, a "5 → 6 AM" rolling-digit screen, then the next night starts automatically.
- AI levels rise +1 at 2, 3 and 4 AM on nights 2+.

## Control booth (3D)
- Left and right doorways open onto dark corridors. Each doorway has a corrugated metal shutter that slides down, plus a wall panel with a red SHUTTER button and a white LIGHT button (hold).
- Without the light, a puppet in the doorway shows only faint glowing eyes. Office lights must have short range so the doorway stays dark.
- Desk: old CRT TV with rabbit ears (clickable), two static monitors, a spinning fan, a red phone (click to mute the call), a mug, papers, a desk lamp, a VENT SEAL lever box with an LED, and a tiny moose bobblehead.
- Front wall: a ceiling vent (real hole in the wall mesh, a duct behind it, angled slats, and a metal plate that slides down to seal it), a wall clock synced to game time, show posters, a "MAY 1996" calendar with the 17th circled, a kid's crayon drawing and a caution poster.
- A flickering fluorescent tube and hanging cables.

## Camera tablet
- Toggle with SPACE or by hovering the bottom bar.
- IMPORTANT, avoid a flicker bug: do NOT use mouseenter/mouseleave on the two bars (CAMERAS / LOWER sit in the same spot and ping-pong the tablet). Detect the bar zone from the pointer position inside a global pointermove handler. Flip once per visit (450 ms cooldown). Re-arm only after the mouse moves well above the bar (y < innerHeight − 110). Start each night disarmed.
- 0.22 s slide-up animation. The camera feed starts rendering once it's fully up.
- 8 cameras on a clickable schematic minimap (keys 1–8). Centered header shows "CAM 04 · WEST HALL" plus "● REC" and a timestamp. Slow camera pan in each room. A static burst on switch and whenever a puppet enters or leaves the viewed room.
- Tablet buttons: "♪ PLAY JINGLE [L]" (15 s cooldown bar) and "VENT: OPEN/SEALED [V]".
- Raising the tablet turns off held lights. Shutters can't be operated while it's up.

## Map
CAM 1 Main Stage (stage, painted sunny backdrop, teal curtains, talk-show desk, audience seats, APPLAUSE sign), CAM 2 Green Room, CAM 3 Prop Storage, CAM 4 West Hall, CAM 5 East Hall, CAM 6 Costume Closet, CAM 7 Vent Shaft (red emergency light), CAM 8 Broadcast Tower Room (equipment racks with LEDs, a wall of static/countdown CRTs, an ON AIR sign that lights up during the TV event).

## Antagonists (original, each with a unique mechanic)
Movement opportunity every ~5 s: move if random(0..20) < AI level.
1. MR. ANTLER: felt moose talk-show host (maroon blazer, yellow bow tie, palmate antlers, droopy eyelids, microphone). Route 1 → 2/3 → 4 → left door. He will NOT move while you watch his current camera. In the West Hall he walks toward the camera only while unwatched. At the door he waits lerp(10, 4.5, AI/20) s: shutter closed → loud bangs, he retreats to CAM 2/3. Open → jumpscare.
2. SPROCKET: tin robot co-host (rusty can head, bulb eyes, blinking antenna, chest dials, cassette slot). Route 1 → 8 → 5 → right door. Playing the jingle on a camera 1–2 steps behind him pulls him back there (15% chance the tape skips). Three successful lures within ~40 s each jam his tape for 25 s: red eyes, jittering, +5 aggression, lures stop working. At the right door he behaves like Antler (shutter blocks).
3. LULU: pink-striped sock marionette with button eyes, yarn hair and a wooden control bar with strings. Lives in CAM 6 with an unrest meter (+AI×0.14 per second unwatched, −9 per second while watched). Four visible poses (deeper in the closet → leaning out → staring at the camera); her pose only updates while unwatched. At 100 she enters the vent shaft, and her progress freezes while CAM 7 is watched. At the booth vent she scratches for 3.5–6 s: sealed → thump and she returns to the closet. Open → jumpscare.
4. THE UNDERSTUDY: faceless grey spare mascot suit, "SPARE #2" tag. Normally standing in CAM 3. When power is below 30% it can appear in a front corner of the booth (opposite the side you're facing), with flickering lights and breathing. Keep it out of view (turn away or raise the tablet) for 3 continuous seconds and it vanishes. Otherwise it gets you after lerp(12, 7, AI/20) s.
5. THE BROADCAST (night 5+): the booth TV turns on by itself with color bars and a countdown with beeps. Press T or click the TV before it ends. If it finishes, every camera shows "NO SIGNAL" for 10 s and Antler and Sprocket get +3 aggression meanwhile.

AI per night [Antler, Sprocket, Lulu, Understudy, Broadcast]:
N1 3,2,0,0,0 · N2 5,4,3,0,0 · N3 7,6,6,4,0 · N4 10,9,9,7,0 · N5 13,12,12,11,10 · N6 18,17,17,16,15.

## Jumpscares
The puppet lunges from 1.6 m to face distance in 0.22 s, head aligned to eye level, lit by a strong light. Camera shake, heavy chroma/jitter, a short red flash, and a loud synthesized screech (detuned sawtooths with LFO + distortion + noise). After ~1.35 s show "TECHNICAL DIFFICULTIES" over color bars and static, with who got you, a one-line tip, RETRY and MENU.

## Audio (all synthesized)
Generator hum, fan noise, camera hiss, light buzz, panned footsteps (Antler left, metallic clanks for Sprocket right), shutter slams, bangs, vent scratching, breathing, a cheerful-but-detuned show jingle (lowpassed and panned to the camera's side), the music box, a 6 AM chime with distant cheering, ambient creaks/drips/whispers/distant kids, and a menu drone. Start audio from the first click.

## Story
Each night a phone call types out 3–4 lines with a muffled formant "voice" synced word by word; it can be muted. The calls gradually reveal the lore: the nine-minute feed cut on May 17, 1996; the hosts found smiling at the camera; recordings of kids counting down; the previous watchman calling from inside the Tower Room on night 5. Night 6 is an automated station message.

## Menus and progression
- Boot screen "▶ PLAY TAPE".
- Main menu: a dark 3D stage with the hosts on the right side, a glitching yellow show logo, NEW GAME (with an erase confirmation), CONTINUE, NIGHT 6 and CUSTOM NIGHT (locked until earned), stars, and N1–N6 progress chips.
- An orientation screen with controls and host tips before night 1.
- Endings: beating night 5 shows a newspaper (studio to be demolished, the old watchman missing) and unlocks Night 6. Night 6 shows a creepy pay stub and unlocks Custom Night. A Custom Night at all-20 shows a sign-off card. One star for each.
- Custom night: sliders 0–20 for all five hosts, plus presets.
- P/Esc pauses the game; it also auto-pauses on blur.

## Style
Retro VHS look. VT323 for the UI, a chunky rounded display font for the show logo. Green/amber phosphor HUD: time and night top-right, power and usage bottom-left, key hints above them. Must also work at phone width without overflow.

## Easter eggs
- 6% chance per night that a West Hall poster reads "IT'S STILL ON AIR" with the hosts' eyes crossed out.
- Clicking the booth show poster honks.
- 1/1000 chance on switching to CAM 1 that a sun mascot appears on stage (saved as a ☀ on the menu).
- Typing "sunny" on the menu unlocks everything.

## Quality bar
- Fully playable start to finish with no console errors.
- Night 1 is beatable on the first try with plenty of power left. Night 5 needs skill. Night 6 is hard.
- Comment the code by section: utils/save, textures, puppet models, office, rooms, menu scene, post-processing, audio, game state & AI, input, UI, render loop.

title: Far Cry 3-style playable game prototype in Three.js
author: maxt3chno
prompt:
Create a visually stunning, highly atmospheric, interactive first-person 3D game set in a small tropical lagoon with a jungle survival outpost.
The game should capture the feeling of standing alone on a beautiful tropical island, similar in atmosphere and environmental design to Far Cry 3, with modern graphics, cinematic lighting, advanced shaders, and detailed environmental interactions.
I WILL PROVIDE REFERENCE IMAGES. Use the uploaded images as the primary visual references for the environment, composition, color palette, vegetation, outpost design, lighting, and overall atmosphere. Recreate the visual mood and environmental character of the references as closely as possible.
The result should be a playable, polished first-person experience, not a static scene or a simple tech demo.
1. WORLD AND ENVIRONMENT
Build a SMALL but extremely detailed tropical lagoon.
Do not create a massive open world. Prioritize visual fidelity, environmental density, atmospheric quality, and interactivity over map size.
The scene must include:

A beautiful tropical beach with sand, small rocks, driftwood, and scattered vegetation.
A stunning turquoise ocean with realistic waves and water transparency.
Shallow coastal water transitioning naturally into deeper blue water.
Dense tropical jungle surrounding the lagoon.
Palm trees, tropical bushes, vines, ferns, tall grass, and exotic plants.
Large moss-covered rocks and weathered coastal cliffs.
A small survival outpost located directly beside the beach, partially surrounded by jungle.
Natural pathways connecting the beach, outpost, and jungle.
Small environmental details that make the location feel authentic and lived-in.
The lagoon should feel isolated, peaceful, mysterious, and slightly dangerous.
The environmental aesthetic should be strongly inspired by Far Cry 3's tropical island atmosphere, but with the graphical quality and lighting of a modern high-end game.
2. THE OUTPOST
Create a small jungle survival outpost, NOT a large military base.
It should resemble a tiny improvised shelter, wooden shack, or canvas tent built by someone surviving on a tropical island.
The outpost should feel handmade, worn, and realistic.
Include:

A small improvised wooden shelter or tent.
A simple wooden table.
A small sleeping cot or military-style bed.
An AK-47 lying somewhere inside the outpost.
A survival knife resting on the table or near the bed.
Animal skins and hides hanging from the shelter or lying on the furniture.
A wooden supply crate that can be opened.
Small storage containers.
Old backpacks and survival equipment.
Ropes, fabric, wooden planks, and improvised construction elements.
Subtle environmental storytelling through scattered personal belongings.
Everything should feel physically placed in the environment rather than randomly generated.
Make the shelter visually interesting through layered materials, shadows, ambient occlusion, fabric simulation, and carefully placed props.
3. FIRST-PERSON CHARACTER
The player controls a character from a FIRST-PERSON perspective.
The player's hands and forearms MUST be visible.
Create high-quality first-person animations:

Idle breathing.
Natural hand movement.
Walking and running animations.
Looking around.
Picking up objects.
Holding a weapon.
Throwing stones.
Using a knife.
Interacting with the environment.
The camera should have subtle, natural movement.
Avoid excessive camera shaking.
Hands must feel connected to the player's actions. They should not look like floating objects or static models.
4. STONE THROWING MECHANIC
One of the most important features is the ability to pick up and throw small stones into the ocean.
The player should be able to:

Look at a small stone on the beach.
Pick it up.
See the stone in their hand.
Aim toward the ocean.
Throw the stone using a natural first-person animation.
The stone must have realistic projectile physics.
When the stone hits the ocean, create:

A visible water splash.
Expanding circular ripples.
Small water droplets.
Appropriate splash sound.
Realistic interaction between the projectile and water surface.
Stone throwing should feel satisfying and physically believable.
Allow the player to throw multiple stones without restarting the game.
5. AK-47 INTERACTION
Place an AK-47 inside the outpost.
The player must be able to approach the weapon and pick it up.
When equipped:

Display the AK-47 in a proper first-person weapon position.
Show both hands holding the weapon.
Implement realistic weapon sway.
Implement a shooting animation.
Add muzzle flash.
Add recoil.
Add shell casing ejection.
Add realistic gunshot audio.
Add environmental bullet impacts.
Add an optional reload animation.
The player should be able to shoot at rocks, trees, wooden objects, and other environmental surfaces.
Bullets should create appropriate visual and audio effects depending on the material they hit.
There is no need to create enemy AI or a combat campaign. Focus on making the weapon interaction feel polished and satisfying.
6. KNIFE INTERACTION
Create an interactive survival knife inside the shelter.
The player can pick it up and equip it.
Implement:

First-person knife holding animation.
Idle knife animation.
Knife swing animation.
Slash animation.
Appropriate sound effects.
Natural hand and wrist movement.
The knife should feel like a proper usable first-person tool, not a static object attached to the camera.
7. INTERACTIVE OBJECTS
Make the environment feel alive and interactive.
The player should be able to interact with selected objects.
Important interactions include:
Supply crate
The player can approach a wooden crate, interact with it, and open its lid.
The lid should animate naturally.
Plants
The player can approach specific tropical plants and harvest them.
Create a small first-person harvesting animation.
After harvesting, the plant should disappear from its original location or visibly lose its harvested part.
The collected plant must be added to the player's inventory.
Inventory
Create a simple but visually polished inventory interface.
Collected plants and other pickup items should appear in the inventory with their name, icon, and quantity.
The inventory must actually work and retain collected items during gameplay.
Other objects
Allow selected small objects around the outpost to be picked up or examined when appropriate.
Use subtle interaction prompts rather than oversized UI elements.
8. WEATHER SYSTEM
Implement a functional dynamic weather system.
The player should be able to switch between:

Clear tropical weather.
Cloudy weather.
Tropical rain.
Heavy tropical rain.
Rain must affect the entire environment visually.
When rain begins:

Rain particles appear.
Rain hits the ocean and creates small surface disturbances.
Sand and rocks become darker.
Leaves and wooden surfaces become wet.
Wet materials become more reflective.
Puddles appear where appropriate.
Atmospheric fog increases.
Rain audio becomes audible.
Ocean and jungle ambience change naturally.
Use wetness shaders and physically based material transitions.
The rain should feel like an actual tropical storm, not simply particles falling in front of the camera.
9. TIME OF DAY SYSTEM
Add a dynamic time-of-day system.
Allow the player to switch between:

Early morning.
Bright tropical noon.
Golden hour / sunset.
Night.
Each time of day must produce a noticeably different visual atmosphere.
Morning should include soft lighting and atmospheric mist.
Noon should feature strong tropical sunlight, vibrant turquoise water, and deep jungle shadows.
Sunset should have warm orange light, beautiful reflections on the ocean, and cinematic shadows.
Night should have moonlight, dark jungle silhouettes, subtle ambient lighting, and a peaceful tropical atmosphere.
Weather and time of day must work together.
For example, the player should be able to experience heavy rain at sunset or a cloudy nighttime lagoon.
10. GRAPHICS AND SHADERS — EXTREMELY IMPORTANT
VISUAL QUALITY IS ONE OF THE MAIN PRIORITIES.
Make the game look like a modern, high-quality tropical exploration game.
Use as many appropriate advanced graphical techniques as possible while maintaining playable performance.
Prioritize:

Physically Based Rendering (PBR).
Realistic water shaders.
Water refraction.
Screen-space or equivalent reflections.
Realistic ocean foam.
Shoreline water interaction.
Subsurface scattering for vegetation.
Detailed foliage shaders.
Wind-driven vegetation animation.
Soft dynamic shadows.
High-quality ambient occlusion.
Cinematic global illumination where supported.
Volumetric lighting.
Atmospheric fog.
Sun shafts passing through palm leaves.
Realistic wetness shaders.
Beautiful sky and cloud rendering.
High-quality tone mapping and color grading.
Subtle bloom.
Natural exposure adaptation.
High-quality material textures.
Realistic surface roughness and normal mapping.
Make the ocean and vegetation particularly impressive.
The water should look mesmerizing, with vibrant tropical colors, natural wave movement, and beautiful sunlight reflections.
Leaves and palm trees should move naturally in the wind.
The jungle must feel lush, dense, and visually rich.
Avoid flat lighting, generic low-poly graphics, cartoon-like materials, and empty environments.
Do not sacrifice the entire frame rate just to enable expensive effects. Use optimized techniques appropriate for the chosen engine.
11. SOUND DESIGN
Create immersive tropical environmental audio.
Include:

Ocean waves.
Water moving along the shoreline.
Wind passing through palm leaves.
Jungle birds.
Tropical insects.
Distant wildlife.
Footsteps on sand.
Footsteps on wood.
Stone throwing and water splashes.
Weapon handling.
AK-47 gunshots.
Knife swings.
Crate opening.
Rain hitting leaves, sand, wood, and water.
Use spatial audio and environmental sound variations where possible.
The lagoon should feel alive even when the player does nothing.
12. CONTROLS
Implement intuitive first-person controls.
WASD — Move.
Mouse — Look around.
Shift — Sprint.
Space — Jump.
E — Interact / pick up objects.
Left Mouse Button — Shoot, swing knife, or throw a held stone.
R — Reload the AK-47.
1 — Equip AK-47.
2 — Equip knife.
3 — Equip stone, if available.
I — Open inventory.
T — Change weather.
N — Change time of day.
ESC — Pause / settings.
Provide a small, elegant interface for changing weather and time of day.
Do not clutter the screen with unnecessary HUD elements.
13. VISUAL ATMOSPHERE AND ART DIRECTION
The entire experience should capture this feeling:
You are alone in a hidden tropical lagoon.
The ocean is crystal clear.
The jungle is dense and full of life.
A small improvised shelter stands beside the beach.
Your AK-47 rests near your sleeping cot.
A knife and survival equipment lie on the wooden table.
Animal skins hang from the structure.
Sunlight passes through palm trees and reflects from the ocean.
You can pick up a stone and throw it into the sea, watching the splash and ripples disappear into the waves.
You can explore the shelter, pick up your weapon, examine objects, gather tropical plants, and watch the weather change.
The scene should be beautiful enough that the player wants to stand still and admire the environment.
The visual identity should combine:
Far Cry 3 tropical island atmosphere + modern cinematic graphics + realistic water rendering + dense, detailed jungle + immersive first-person interactions.
14. IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT REQUIREMENTS
This must be a WORKING, PLAYABLE EXPERIENCE.
Do not simply create a beautiful static 3D render.
Implement the actual gameplay systems described above.
Prioritize a small, complete, polished environment rather than a large unfinished game.
All important mechanics should work:

First-person movement.
Visible animated hands.
Pickable and throwable stones.
Functional water splash effects.
Equippable and shootable AK-47.
Equippable and usable knife.
Opening supply crates.
Harvesting plants.
Functional inventory.
Dynamic rain.
Dynamic time of day.
Advanced environmental shaders.
Do not replace the requested systems with decorative placeholders.
If development limitations require prioritization, complete the core mechanics first, then add graphical polish.
15. REFERENCE IMAGES
I WILL UPLOAD REFERENCE IMAGES AFTER THIS PROMPT.
These images are extremely important.
Analyze them carefully and use them as the main visual guide.
Pay particular attention to:

Lagoon shape and composition.
Position of the ocean relative to the beach.
Tropical vegetation density.
Structure and scale of the outpost.
Color palette.
Lighting.
Water appearance.
Atmosphere.
Environmental details.
The final game should feel like a playable recreation of the location and mood shown in my reference images.
Do not blindly generate a generic tropical island.
Use the references to create a distinctive, carefully art-directed, immersive lagoon environment.

title: Magazine Cover Build
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second build of a monthly magazine cover, from blank stock to finished newsstand cover.

<inputs>
Masthead: LINTEL. Strapline: Architecture, objects and the people who make them. Issue line: October 2026 · No. 118 · $14. Lead cover line: The quiet return of concrete. Secondary lines: Six studios building with salvage; A chair that took nine years; Plus: the long table, rethought. Barcode: 9772049831006. Duotone inks: navy #1C2260 and coral #FF6B4A. Duration: 10s. If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Stage: studio grey #E4E1DB. The cover is 720×934 (x 600–1320, y 73–1007), uncoated white #FBF7F1, with a soft shadow (0 24px 60px, 18% black). Positions below are cover pixels from its top-left; margins 36px.
Cover image, drawn in code once at load, full-bleed: a concrete sphere (radius 175, center 450, 400) on a two-step plinth (upper box x 330–570, y 590–650; lower box x 300–600, y 650–700) against a wall, floor from y 700 down. Light from the upper left: the wall brightest there, the floor in shadow, the cast shadow falling right. Render in grayscale with real shading (a Lambert sphere with a soft terminator and bounce light from the plinth, three values on the boxes, a cast shadow with a 30px penumbra, fine concrete pores), then map luminance through the duotone: navy shadows, coral midtones, paper highlights, plus 1.5% grain.
Masthead: LINTEL in "Archivo" (wght 900, wdth 62), navy, tracking −0.02em, fitted to the 648px between the margins, cap tops at y 74. Draw it between wall and sphere so the sphere's crown overlaps the foot of two letters: that interlock is the cover.
Type, two families only, "Archivo" and "Newsreader":
- issue line top-left on baseline y 56: Archivo 600, 20px, tracked 0.08em, uppercase, navy;
- strapline under the masthead in a left column (x 36–255): Newsreader italic, 22px, navy;
- secondary lines below it in that column: Archivo (wght 700, wdth 75), 26px, navy, two lines each;
- lead line on the dark floor, lower left: Newsreader 500 italic, 60px, two lines, paper white, under a 2px coral rule;
- barcode: a 200×120 white panel at lower right on the floor, a correct EAN-13 encoding of the number (longer guard bars, digits beneath in Archivo 500, 20px).
Hierarchy: masthead, lead line, secondary lines, then strapline and issue line, in size and in order of arrival.
Motion is editorial and assured: elements arrive on short moves (cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.7, 0, 1), 0.45–0.7s); text lines rise 14px out of masks at their baselines; the camera starts at 1.6× on the cover's upper half and pulls back to the whole cover on cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1) over 0.8s. The real thing is a strict hierarchy, one strong image locked to the masthead and type that knows its sizes; the cheap version is a stock photo, five fonts and drop-shadowed cover lines.
Banned: drop shadows on type, outlined text, a third type family, starbursts or price-flash badges, gradients outside the image, image files, a recognizable person, real magazine names, anything flashing more than 3 times per second.
</direction>

<structure>
0.0–0.6s: studio grey; the blank cover slides up 40px into place; the camera holds at 1.6× on its upper half.
0.6–1.6s: the image develops like a two-ink proof: navy pass (0.6–1.1s), then coral pass (1.1–1.6s).
1.6–2.6s: the masthead rises letter by letter behind the sphere, 40ms apart; the issue line sets above it.
2.6–3.4s: the camera pulls back to the whole cover.

title: Vital Signs Monitor
author: AI CSS Animations
prompt:
Make a 10-second bedside patient monitor animation: the ECG sweeps with an erase bar, the pleth and respiration waves follow beat for beat, and the numbers update like a real device.

<inputs>
- Monitor: Orrin VS-7 (fictional). Bed label: "BED 07 · ADULT".
- Readings: heart rate settling from 78 to 72 bpm; SpO2 97% rising to 98%; respiration 16 per minute; a blood pressure (NIBP) measurement during the clip, landing at 118/76 with a mean of 90; temperature 36.8 °C.
- Clock: 14:31, turning to 14:32.
- Length: 10 seconds.
If I don't give you something, use the default and don't ask.
</inputs>

<direction>
Palette: screen #000000; header and soft-key bars #11151A; dividers #1F262E; ECG #3DEB5C; pleth and SpO2 #2ED3F2; respiration #F5D33B; NIBP values #F2F2F2 with their label in #FF6B7A; temperature #E6E6E6; secondary text #7C8794. Each parameter keeps one color across its wave, label and number.
Type: Saira Semi Condensed 600 for numbers: HR 168px, SpO2 120px, RR 80px, NIBP 64px, temperature 48px. Saira 500 for labels and units, 22–26px, uppercase. Draw every number digit by digit in fixed-width cells so values never jitter.
Layout: header bar y 60–120 across x 96–1824 (wordmark, bed label, clock, a battery glyph). Waveform area x 96–1336: ECG lead II in y 150–430, pleth in y 460–640, respiration in y 670–850, each labeled at its top left ("II  ×1", "PLETH", "RESP"). Numeric column x 1376–1824, boxes from y 150 to 880 separated by 1px dividers: HR 220px tall, SpO2 160, RR 120, NIBP 130 (systolic/diastolic with the mean in brackets and the time it was taken), TEMP 100. Soft-key bar y 900–1000 with six keys: NIBP, FREEZE, ALARMS, TRENDS, PATIENT, MENU (24px).
The signals are physiology computed in code. Precompute beat times at load, from t = −5s, by integrating the heart rate (78 easing to 72 bpm by 5s) at a 1ms step, with respiratory sinus arrhythmia: beat intervals shorten about 3% during each inhale of the 16-per-minute breathing cycle. ECG: each beat is a sum of gaussians around its R peak (P +0.15 mV at −0.20s, Q −0.10 mV at −0.035s, R +1.20 mV at 0, S −0.28 mV at +0.035s, T +0.32 mV at +0.25s, with the T delay scaled by the square root of the beat interval), plus seeded baseline wander (±0.03 mV at 0.25 Hz) and fine noise (±0.008 mV); 1 mV is 110px. Pleth: a pulse 0.24s after each R peak, with a fast upstroke, a rounded peak, a dicrotic notch and a slow decay, its height modulated ±6% by breathing. Respiration: a smooth asymmetric wave at 16 per minute, inhaling for 40% of each cycle.
A sweep, not a scroll: the traces never slide. A write head moves left to right at 25 mm/s (200px/s, so a pass takes 6.2s) on all three channels; each pixel column shows the signal from the last time the head passed it, and a 24px black erase bar runs just ahead of the head. Lines are 2.5px, antialiased and sampled at every pixel column, with no glow.
Numbers behave like a device: HR is 60 divided by the mean of the last four beat intervals, updated at each R wave; SpO2 updates once per pulse; values change instantly and never tween or count. A small heart glyph beside HR brightens for 0.12s on each R wave. Pressing NIBP starts a cuff cycle: its box shows CUFF and a pressure falling from 168 mmHg in 3 mmHg steps every 0.2s until the result lands.
The real thing is clinical and quiet: waveforms that agree beat for beat, a true sweep with an erase gap, and numbers that match the traces. The cheap version is a glowing heartbeat line scrolling sideways next to a heart icon.
Banned: scrolling waveforms, glow or bloom, alarm banners, red flashing, flatlines or arrhythmias, heart clip-art, real manufacturers' names or screen layouts, numbers that disagree with the traces, anything flashing more than 3 times per second.
</direction>

0.0–0.8s: black; the Orrin wordmark (Saira 600, 64px, #7C8794) fades up at the center, holds, and fades away.

5.6–7.8s: steady running; the clock turns to 14:32 at 7.0s; at 7.8s the write heads wrap to the left edge and begin erasing the first pass.
8.6–9.0s: the FREEZE key depresses and stays lit; every trace stops where it is, the numbers hold, and a FROZEN tag (22px, on #11151A) appears at the top of the waveform area.
9.0–10.0s: hold, frozen.
For other durations, keep the sweep at 25 mm/s, stretch the steady running, and keep the freeze for at least the last second.

Canvas won't fetch fonts itself: await document.fonts.load() for each face, then define window.seek. The stage is 1920×1080 (16:9), scaled to fit the window. Design for 60fps. window.seek(t), t in seconds, must compute every visual from t alone: no CSS transitions or animations, no setTimeout or setInterval, no state carried between frames, and randomness only from a seeded PRNG. Precompute the beat times, all three signals at 1ms resolution and every number's change times once at load; each trace column then reads the signal at the time the write head last passed it. <direction>
- Look: straight down on a sheet of white drawing paper on a mint laminate kitchen table, crayons scattered beside it. The drawing has to look like a six-year-old made it, not like an adult imitating one.
- Palette: table mint laminate #A9DCCB with fine seeded speckles in #9AD0BE and #C2E8DB; paper #FBF8F1 with visible tooth; crayons tomato red #E0352B, orange #F28A1F, sunflower #F7CF2C, grass green #3AA845, sky blue #2F6FD6, violet #7A4AB8, brown #8A5530, pink #F27BA4, black #2A2626; type deep green #1D4A3E. - Layout, in stage pixels: the paper, 1216 × 860, at x 560–1776, y 110–970, with a soft contact shadow; the crayons lie at left between x 120 and 500, some below the type, one rolled against the paper's edge. - Wax on tooth, the core of the look: precompute a paper tooth height field (a seeded fine 2px grain plus a softer 14px variation). A stroke deposits wax only where its pressure beats the local tooth, so lines are broken and grainy, flecked with white, denser where the child pressed harder or went over twice, with ragged edges. Later colors lay 75% over earlier ones, the earlier color showing in the gaps. Heavy patches carry a faint waxy sheen, a 4% lighter streak along the stroke.
- How the child draws:
  - outlines wobble ±4px on low-frequency noise, overshoot at corners and don't quite meet; nothing is closed cleanly or measured;
  - fills are back-and-forth scribbles 10–14px wide at about −30°, with loop turnarounds, uneven gaps and overshoots up to 20px past the outline;
  - the house: a red square leaning slightly, a lopsided brown triangle roof, a door with a round knob, two windows with crosses for four panes, a chimney sticking out of the roof slope at a slant with a smoke spiral;
  - the tree: a brown trunk as two lines with scribbled fill, a green cloud-shaped crown scribbled round and round, three red apples;
  - the sun: a yellow scribbled disc, orange rays as straight lines of uneven lengths, a black smiling face;
  - the girl (ME): a round head with dot eyes and a curve smile, violet zigzag hair, a pink triangle dress, stick arms with five-line hands, stick legs standing on the ground strip, one arm up holding the kite string;
  - the dog (BISCUIT): a brown sausage body on four stick legs, floppy ears, a tail, black dots for eyes and nose, a red tongue;
  - the kite: a violet diamond with a cross, a string down to the girl's hand and a tail of four pink bows;

- Type on the table (HTML over the canvas): kicker "THE FRIDGE GALLERY" in Lexend 600, 20px, tracked 0.16em, #1D4A3E, at (120, 140); title in Lexend 700, 64px, #1D4A3E, two lines, beneath; line in Lexend 400, 24px, #1D4A3E at 85%, at most 360px wide. - 8.0–8.6s: the motion stops on its final drawing; the camera reaches 1.0 and the kicker, title and line rise in on the table.
- 8.6–10.0s: hold, still.

</structure>
